World.title: Power minister inaugurates Fayose as REA chairman
World.content:
Former Ekiti State Governor Ayodele Fayose has formally assumed office as Chairman of the Governing Board of the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), following his appointment by President Bola Tinubu.

Fayose was inaugurated on Friday in Abuja by the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, alongside other members of the agency’s governing board.

The inauguration was announced in a statement issued by Lere Olayinka, media aide to the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike.

Other members inaugurated included Alhaji Ahmadu Abubakar, Mr. Ilyasu Makinta and three additional non-executive directors, while Mr. Abba Aliyu was formally installed as the Managing Director of the agency.

Speaking after taking the oath of office, Fayose expressed appreciation to President Tinubu for the confidence reposed in him and the other appointees.

He said his priority would be to support the agency with the political backing needed to strengthen its operations and secure funding for its programmes.

“My mission in REA is to take the agency to greater heights by providing the needed political will,” Fayose said.

He added that efforts had already commenced to mobilise support and ensure the agency obtained the resources required to execute both its immediate and long-term projects aimed at expanding electricity access nationwide.

“Work has started in earnest; we are reaching out very fast and appealing to people to ensure the work is done.

“I want to use this window to assure Nigerians that your expectation about my appointment and my colleagues will not be dashed. We will give our best to achieve the Renewed Hope of President Tinubu for the country to be better for us all,” he said.

Fayose noted that many of the problems facing Nigeria’s electricity sector are rooted in rural communities and stressed that the agency’s responsibility extends beyond simply supplying power.

“The assignment given to us is beyond providing electricity but also looking at the population of the country who need to feel the impact of the energy.

“When this happens, the people will forever be indebted to the agency,” he said.

Earlier, Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe said the country must begin to measure success in the electricity sector by the number of communities and citizens benefiting from power, rather than by megawatts generated.

“We are moving from just counting kilowatts and megawatts to how many communities and people were powered in the country,” the minister said.

Tegbe described the REA as a critical institution in Nigeria’s power sector and said its mandate covers education, healthcare, agriculture, commerce and broader economic development.

“REA is fundamentally an institution for expanding opportunity.

“Every mini-grid inaugurated, every solar home system deployed, every market, school, primary healthcare centre, farm, or productive enterprise electrified represents an investment in human capital, economic inclusion, and national prosperity,” he said.

According to the minister, the agency’s role has become even more significant as the Federal Government continues implementing the Electricity Act and wider reforms in the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry.

He said REA must serve as the link between national electricity policy and grassroots development, ensuring that rural communities benefit from ongoing reforms.

“The benefits of power reforms are being felt across the country, not only in our major cities but also in the remotest communities across the federation,” he said.

Tegbe said the inauguration of the new board reflects President Tinubu’s commitment to stronger governance, accountability and strategic oversight in public institutions.

He urged the board members to embrace transparency, innovation and prudent management of public resources while building partnerships with development agencies and the private sector to improve electricity access.

“Most importantly, I encourage you to continually ask one fundamental question whenever decisions come before the board: ‘How does this improve the lives and livelihoods of ordinary Nigerians?’

“If that question remains our compass, I have no doubt that the agency will continue to exceed expectations,” Tegbe said.

REA Managing Director Abba Aliyu also thanked President Tinubu for the opportunity to serve and assured Nigerians that the agency would continue to expand electricity access to underserved and unserved communities through its rural and off-grid programmes.

The inauguration officially marks the beginning of the tenure of the new REA governing board, with Fayose expected to provide strategic leadership and oversight for the agency’s operations.

World.title: COAS warns soldiers against substance abuse, stresses mental health
World.content:
Shaibu

By Edwin Philip, Lafia

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lt.-Gen. Waidi Shaibu, has urged personnel of the Nigerian Army to avoid substance abuse, stressing that sound mental health is essential for achieving operational objectives.

Shaibu also said Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) should not be seen as a sign of weakness but as a battle injury of the mind that requires proper attention and support.

The COAS, represented by the Commander, Army Headquarters Garrison, Maj.-Gen. John Lar, stated this on Wednesday during a four-day sensitisation seminar held at the Headquarters of 4 Special Forces, Doma, Nasarawa State.

“I want to reiterate that post-traumatic stress disorder is not a sign of weakness; it is a battle injury of the mind. We are committed to providing the necessary support system, early intervention and professional counselling to help our warriors transition successfully from trauma to triumph,” he said.

The Army chief warned that substance abuse among troops would not be tolerated, describing it as a major threat to combat readiness, unit cohesion and operational effectiveness.

“I urge commanders at all levels to intensify the fight against this menace within our barracks and formations,” he said.

The seminar, titled “Transformational Leadership, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and Drugs/Substance Abuse,” was organised by the Department of Army Transformation and Innovation.

Shaibu said the programme was designed to build trust, inspire troops through shared vision and empower personnel to adapt to unpredictable operational environments.

He added that the initiative was part of ongoing efforts by the Nigerian Army to sensitise junior and mid-level officers on effective leadership practices and values required for successful command.

“The seminar focuses on three very critical pillars of modern military operations: transformational leadership, management of post-traumatic stress disorder and the devastating effects of drugs and substance abuse,” he said.

According to him, the changing nature of security threats facing the country requires a professional, resilient and psychologically sound military force.

He urged junior and mid-level commanders to embrace transformational leadership by not only giving orders but also inspiring, mentoring and caring for the welfare of their subordinates.

The COAS commended troops for their loyalty and commitment, particularly their efforts in tackling security challenges in North Central Nigeria.

Also speaking, the Chief of Transformation and Innovation, Maj.-Gen. Peter Okoye, described the seminar as timely, given the physical and psychological demands of modern military operations.

Okoye said the programme aligned with the COAS Command Philosophy of transforming the Nigerian Army into a more professional, adaptable, combat-ready and resilient force.

“The strength of the Nigerian Army lies not only in its equipment and capabilities but also in the resilience, discipline and mental readiness of its personnel,” he said.

He added that as the Army continues to record successes in training and operations, there was a need to sustain efforts aimed at improving leadership quality, mental health, troop cohesion and operational efficiency.

World.title: Kano rejects conversion of Jambulo afforestation complex to private plots
World.content:
By Hadiza Yusuf

The Kano State Government has rejected any move to convert parts of the historic Afforestation Programme Coordinating Unit (APCU) complex in Jambulo into private residential or commercial plots, insisting that the facility must remain for public environmental purposes.

The state Commissioner for Water Resources, Environment and Climate Change, Dr Dahir M. Hashim, stated this on Friday while addressing journalists in Kano.

Hashim described the complex as an important federal environmental facility that has played a key role in coordinating afforestation activities and training forestry personnel.

He said the government was concerned by reports that portions of the property had allegedly been allocated to private interests and that there were attempts to remove federal environmental agencies operating from the facility.

“The APCU complex was established in 1988 and has, for decades, served as a centre for coordinating afforestation activities and training forest guards and other forestry personnel,” he said.

According to the commissioner, the facility should not be regarded as abandoned government property, particularly following the relocation of the operational headquarters of the National Agency for the Great Green Wall (NAGGW) from Abuja to Jambulo.

“The Kano State Government respects the authority of the courts and will not interfere with the judicial process. However, any attempt to convert this strategic environmental facility into private residential or commercial plots is against the overriding public interest,” Hashim said.

He stressed the environmental significance of the complex, noting that its mature trees help reduce heat, improve air quality, prevent erosion and support biodiversity.

Hashim warned that the destruction or fragmentation of the green area would result in the loss of vegetation that had taken decades to develop.

He called on President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice to review the reported alienation of the property and take appropriate legal steps to protect the entire complex.

The commissioner also urged the Federal Ministry of Environment to continue opposing any attempt to alienate the property and explore available legal options to preserve the facility.

He said the Kano State Government was prepared to support the Federal Ministry of Environment, NAGGW, the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) and APCU in safeguarding the complex.

“Our position is clear: public environmental assets must remain in public service,” Hashim said.

World.title: DTN@100 Heroes Awards Honour National Devt, Sustainability, Social Impact, National Global Champion Award Recipients
World.content:
The Organising Council of the Daily Times Nigeria Centenary (DTN@100) Heroes Awards has announced the recipients of four of its prestigious special honours, recognising exceptional individuals and institutions whose visionary leadership, innovation and transformational contributions continue to advance Nigeria’s economic growth, environmental sustainability, social development and global competitiveness.

The latest announcement forms part of activities leading to the DTN@100 Conference, Grand Book Unveiling and Times Heroes Awards, a landmark event commemorating the centenary of Daily Times Nigeria and celebrating a century of impactful journalism, national discourse and nation-building.

This year’s special honours recognise outstanding achievements in the categories of National Global Champion Award, National Development Award, Sustainability Award and Social Impact Award, celebrating recipients whose work continues to create measurable impact across Nigeria and beyond.

Announcing the recipients, Chairman of the DTN@100 Organising Council, Bolaji Okusaga, said the awards reflect the Council’s commitment to recognising individuals and institutions whose leadership has delivered lasting value to society and inspired national progress.

“The DTN@100 Heroes Awards were conceived to celebrate exceptional leadership, innovation and service that have contributed meaningfully to Nigeria’s development over the past century while inspiring the country’s future. These honours recognise individuals and institutions whose achievements extend beyond personal success to creating lasting impact on communities, industries and the nation as a whole,” he said.

He added that the Awards have become one of the defining legacies of the Daily Times centenary celebrations, preserving and celebrating the stories of outstanding Nigerians and institutions whose contributions continue to shape the country’s development trajectory.

The Organising Council announced that Dr Mahmoud Ahmadu, OON, President of the Nigeria Arabian Gulf Chamber of Commerce (NAGCC), was honoured with the National Global Champion Award for his exceptional leadership in advancing Nigeria’s global economic engagement and strengthening strategic trade and investment partnerships between Nigeria and the Arabian Gulf region.

Through visionary leadership, enterprise promotion and economic diplomacy, he has expanded opportunities for cross-border investment, enhanced Nigeria’s international competitiveness and contributed significantly to positioning the country as a preferred destination for global commerce and sustainable economic development.

The National Development Award was presented to Dr Olasupo Olusi, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Bank of Industry (BOI), for his outstanding leadership in driving industrialisation, enterprise development, job creation and inclusive economic growth.

Under his leadership, the Bank of Industry has continued to expand access to finance for businesses, strengthen local manufacturing, empower entrepreneurs and accelerate Nigeria’s industrial transformation, reinforcing its position as one of the country’s foremost development finance institutions.

The Organising Council also recognised Mr Abdulhamid Umar, National Project Coordinator of the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL) Programme, with the DTN@100 Sustainability Award for his outstanding leadership in driving one of Nigeria’s most ambitious climate-resilience and landscape-restoration initiatives. Under his stewardship, the World Bank-supported programme has strengthened environmental sustainability, restored degraded ecosystems, enhanced agricultural resilience, and improved livelihoods across participating states, positioning ACReSAL as a model for sustainable development.

The Council also honoured Professor Oyelaran Oyeyinka with the Social Impact Award, recognising his remarkable contributions to public policy, innovation, knowledge development and inclusive socio-economic transformation across Africa.

For decades, Professor Oyeyinka has distinguished himself through exemplary service in academia, international development and policy advisory, influencing development thinking, strengthening institutions and advancing inclusive growth across the continent.

According to Okusaga, the selection process reflected the high standards that have come to define the DTN@100 Heroes Awards.

“Our Awards Board undertook a rigorous and independent assessment of nominees, focusing on measurable impact, transformational leadership, innovation and enduring contributions to national development. The recipients announced today exemplify excellence, integrity and visionary leadership, and their achievements deserve national recognition,” he added.

The Organising Council also announced that public voting remains open for the Financial Innovation Award, encouraging Nigerians at home and in the diaspora to participate in recognising organisations that are redefining financial innovation and expanding access to financial services.

Okusaga emphasised that public participation remains an important pillar of the awards process. “These awards belong to Nigerians. Public participation reinforces the credibility, inclusiveness and national ownership of this initiative. We therefore encourage citizens to continue supporting individuals and organisations whose work is creating meaningful impact and contributing to Nigeria’s progress.”

The DTN@100 Conference, Grand Book Unveiling and Times Heroes Awards will culminate in a grand public presentation on Thursday, September 3, 2026, at the THISDAY Dome, Central Business District, Abuja, where award recipients will be formally honoured before an audience of national leaders, policymakers, captains of industry, diplomats, development partners and other distinguished stakeholders.

The event will also feature the unveiling of the Nigeria Grand Book, a landmark commemorative publication documenting the remarkable achievements of outstanding personalities, institutions and organisations whose contributions have shaped Nigeria’s political, economic, social and developmental journey over the past century.

World.title: Agbese Opposes Frequent Change of Service Chiefs, Urges Nigeria to Exit ICC
World.content:
A member of the House of Representatives, Hon. Philip Agbese, has cautioned against the frequent replacement of Nigeria’s service chiefs, saying such changes undermine military operations and provide opportunities for terrorists and other criminal elements to regroup.

Agbese, who represents Ado/Okpokwu/Ogbadibo Federal Constituency of Benue State, made the remarks in a television programme on Thursday while discussing the country’s security situation and the ongoing efforts of the Armed Forces.

The lawmaker said the military had recorded appreciable successes in tackling insecurity and deserved sustained public support rather than recurring calls for the removal of service chiefs whenever security challenges occur.

According to him, changing military commanders at critical moments often disrupts operational momentum, as newly appointed officers require time to settle into office and implement their strategies.

“Each time there are security issues, some people begin to call for the removal of the service chiefs. Those things cause setbacks because when you remove them and bring in new ones, they try to introduce different approaches, and it takes time for them to settle down. Within that period, insurgents gain mileage and launch fresh attacks,” he said.

Agbese, a member of the Labour Party, stressed that although opposition parties have a constitutional responsibility to hold governments accountable and advocate better policies, national security should remain a non-partisan issue.

“As members of the opposition, we believe government can always do more in providing leadership and security. But when it comes to the Armed Forces, they belong to all Nigerians and deserve our collective support,” he stated.

He commended Nigerians for increasingly countering misinformation and false narratives about military operations on social media, describing public cooperation as essential to the success of security agencies.

The lawmaker disclosed that based on available records, the Armed Forces had rescued no fewer than 1,000 persons from captivity this year, urging citizens to verify information before circulating reports capable of undermining national security.

Agbese also called for stronger international collaboration in intelligence sharing and counter-terrorism efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s fight against insurgency, banditry and kidnapping.

On international justice, the federal lawmaker advocated Nigeria’s withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC), arguing that continued membership no longer aligns with the country’s security realities.

He argued that while terrorist groups commit atrocities against civilians without regard for international humanitarian law, the ICC has not demonstrated the same level of commitment in ensuring that such actors are prosecuted.

According to him, there have instead been recurring concerns that Nigerian troops could face international prosecution for actions taken while confronting terrorists, despite the country’s established legal and judicial institutions for investigating allegations of human rights abuses.

“Nigeria has a functional legal and judicial system capable of addressing cases involving human rights violations. Considering the scale of security threats confronting the country, government should critically review whether continued membership of the International Criminal Court remains in our national interest,” Agbese said.

Drawing comparisons with countries such as the United States, Russia and China, he maintained that Nigeria should empower its Armed Forces to respond swiftly and decisively to security threats while reviewing international commitments that may impede effective military operations.

The lawmaker reaffirmed his confidence in the Armed Forces, urging Nigerians to continue supporting security agencies in their efforts to restore peace and safeguard the country’s territorial integrity.

World.title: Review: Josplay, Where African Music Lives
World.content:
Vanessa Obioha

For a continent of 54 countries, reducing its music to just a handful of genres hardly does it justice. This is often the experience on many global streaming platforms, where African music is largely represented by sounds from West Africa or South Africa. What, then, of the musical traditions of Lusophone Africa and the many other genres that rarely make global playlists? Africa’s sonic landscape surely goes beyond afrobeats, amapiano and house music.

Enter Josplay, an Afrocentric audio entertainment platform that delivers music, news, stories and audiobooks to listeners around the world. Since its launch in 2019, the platform has been intentional about creating a distinctly African listening experience, from its intuitive interface to AI-powered recommendations that adapt to each user’s preferences.

After signing up, users are introduced to a feature called Frames, which curates music around daily rhythms and moods. First-time users are presented with 10 Frames and asked to choose six, with the flexibility to customise their selections later. The feature tailors recommendations to different moments of the day. Select the Flow Frame, for instance, and the app curates music designed to aid concentration. Choose Unwind, and it shifts to mellow grooves suited to winding down after a busy day.

The app then invites users to select their preferred genres, and this is where Josplay truly distinguishes itself. Its catalogue reflects an impressive breadth of African music that goes beyond the genres that dominate international playlists. That diversity has only expanded through a partnership with Sony Music Entertainment, bringing a significant portion of the company’s catalogue to Josplay listeners worldwide, including recordings distributed through The Orchard and the complete catalogues of Lusafrica and Africa Nostra, comprising more than 4,000 songs.

Here, listeners will discover music they never knew existed, or knew existed but never knew what genre it belonged to. There is Tishoumaren, also known as Assouf or Desert Blues, a style that originated among the Tuareg people of the Sahara. Blending traditional Tuareg music with blues and rock influences, it creates a haunting yet captivating sound.

If Desert Blues is not quite your style, there is Sungura, the energetic Zimbabwean genre that fuses traditional Zimbabwean music with Congolese rumba, pop and rock. Driven by lively guitars, basslines and infectious percussion, it is almost impossible to sit still while listening. A good introduction is Eriki’s ‘Lost and Found.’

Those looking for smoother, romantic rhythms will appreciate Kizomba, the Angolan genre that combines traditional Angolan rhythms with Caribbean zouk and French-Caribbean compas to produce music that is both intimate and danceable.

Perhaps what is most exciting is how it celebrates a country’s musical diversity. For instance, rather than reducing Nigerian music to afrobeats and highlife, the platform also showcases Ogene, Apala, Juju, Fuji and Afrobeat, giving listeners a fuller appreciation of the country’s musical heritage.

Josplay’s homepage invites listeners into a world of culture and entertainment. Through Africa News Brief, users can catch up on news from across the continent, while Stories and Reads brings African history, folklore and personalities to life. Curious about the legendary Nigerian traditionalist Chief Pericoma Okoye? There is ‘Pericoma and the Tax Collectors.’ Prefer folklore? Then ‘How the Tortoise Got His Cracked Shell’ offers a nostalgic return to one of Africa’s storytelling traditions.

The platform also features a growing selection of podcasts, further broadening its appeal.

Josplay appears to be on track to becoming one of Africa’s most compelling music platforms. One question, however, is sustainability. Unlike most streaming services, its free tier currently carries no advertising, relying instead on limits to the number of songs users can stream each day. Whether that model proves financially sustainable remains to be seen. The company in 2021 diversified its revenue through Josplay Enterprise, which curates enterprise-grade playlists tailored to businesses and organisations, while also ensuring that creators are compensated for the use of their work.

Josplay celebrates Africa’s extraordinary musical diversity while reminding listeners that the continent’s sounds deserve far more than a corner of the world’s playlists. Whether its business model can sustain that ambition remains to be seen, but its vision is one worth paying attention to.

World.title: Debate on the Selection of Head of Service of the Federation in Perspective
World.content:
By Tunji Olaopa

In every administrative system across the world, the selection and appointment of critical officers and officials plays a very crucial role in the overall health of these systems. Indeed, the effectiveness and efficiency of any management system depend significantly on the helmsman who possesses the requisite vision, knowledge, drive and the bureaucratic competences to drive institutional reform and administrative progress. And when this discussion is situated within the context of an ongoing institutional reform process of a public administration system like the one Nigeria requires to manage the successes and consolidation of its democratic governance, then the issue of administrative leadership becomes even more cogent as it positions the public service at the very core of the building of a developmental state that Nigeria needs.

No wonder then that an extensive debate over the succession plan for the next head of the civil service of the federation (HCSF) has focused on why the HE the President needs to take a critical out-of-the-box decision on the modalities that will throw up not just the next HCSF but ground a veritable civil service leadership and administration that will serve as the basis for a functional bureaucratic institution and reprofessionalised civil service that will backstop Nigeria effectively into the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions. That this protracted concern is being championed by the leadership of the Council of Retired Federal Permanent Secretaries (CORFEPS) is even more significant. CORFEPS has over time become a veritable platform for interrogating germane issues revolving around the functionality and future of the civil service, as well as the operational mechanics and dynamics that could make for an efficient civil service.

This responsibility could have become even more grounded if the National Association of Public Administration and Management (NAPAM), the public administration professional body, is currently and sufficiently functional as to also be able to join the fray of discussions and deploy policy-engaged research agenda to deepen the conversation. This is for the sole reason that NAPAM’s expansive membership—drawing on the communities of practice and service of the numerous associations of retired heads of service and permanent secretaries across the states of the federations, public administration researchers, scholars and development workers, etc.—would have contributed an even more rounded and focused debate that pushes the issues beyond the federal civil service to the appointment of heads of service in all the states as well as how administrative leadership in the civil service can complement political leadership. My op-ed pieces over the years have provided the critical grounds for interrogating critical elements of civil service administrative leadership as reform imperatives. I have especially explored for example the generalist-professional distinction as one important item in understanding the transformation of the civil service as a world class institution in Nigeria.

For our present purpose, we take deep reflective direction from the African proverb—the fish rots from the head. This has become a metaphor for leadership vision, accountability and direction. When leadership falters, then the organization weakens and ultimately crumbles. Institutional and administrative reform is therefore ultimately about a leadership that invest frontier ideation, design thinking and policy acumen in visioning the present and future of a new civil service system that constitutes the mechanism for making the state work on behalf of her citizens. Within the Nigerian civil service, the focus and locus of this leadership template is the HCSF. And this is the most cogent reason why the administrative succession plan to install a new one is seen by those who should know to carry such a huge weight for the Tinubu administration and the bureaucracy itself.

In my modest opinion, therefore, the best way to initiate the inquiry into the matter, and beyond the generalist-professional distinction, is the urgent need to rethink the most fundamental questions around the status and operational capacity of the HCSF that enable us to probe deeper into the directions that the system needs to take in terms of a functional, ethical and strategic leadership and the reform processes the leadership needs to drive. The fundamental questions are: (a) Who is the HCSF and what does the job entail? (b) How are the two elite cadres—the administrative and professional officers from which the occupants of the office are selected—related to the challenges of leading the civil service? (c) What are the competencies required of administrative and professional officers to lead institutional reform and provide leadership to the service?

To tackle the nature of the leadership challenge and administrative succession therefore, we need to first understand what the office entails in theory and practice. The HCSF is considered the number one civil servant in the country; indeed, the HCSF is the chief policy adviser to the Federal Government of Nigeria on civil service matters. Given that the HCSF is appointed from among the serving permanent secretaries, s/he is therefore a primus inter pares charged with the responsibility of leading, administering and managing the public service through the permanent secretaries in terms of appointment, posting and performance. The managerial capacity of the HCSF is to be directed at rigorously building and professionalizing the federal workforce through the implementation of training and capacitation policies and programs, including managing the oversight of the governance of the government training institutions and manpower development institutes. The significance of the HCSF becomes glaring given the fact that she drives the civil service modernization plans and institutional reform strategies. The HCSF is the chief visionier and design/implementation officer that oversees how government’s democratic governance policies are translated through performance management into productivity.

Once we achieve this understanding of the persona and status of the HCSF, it becomes very clear why the appointment to that office would be this cogent and rigorous. But more fundamentally, it demonstrates why serious reflection has to go into the selection framework in terms of the processes, procedures and administrative philosophy that must undergird the selection into that office. It must stand to administrative reason that in choosing a visionary public administrator and manager who is in charge of the entire civil service institution, we cannot afford to play the politics of selection that install just anybody for the sake of political and administrative patronage. That will only go to damage the system and keep delaying its urgent transition into a structure at the cutting edge of professional service delivery that will backstop democratic governance and therefore the capacitation of the veritable institutional game changer-engine room in the national development change management dynamics.

The selection, by implication, must also not be undermined by administrative overreach. What does this mean? It means that in the appointment of the HCSF, we must be perceptive enough to look beyond the generalist-professional distinction that the permanent secretaries might fall into, or even the principles of seniority or geo-political balance that often play a very key role in administrative career progression. To be fair, being a generalist or a professional in this role comes with their significant advantages, in so far as merit overrides the choice, over and above the unknowing emergence of the run-of-the-mill street-wise misfits that sometimes feature in the tiny privileged bureaucratic space. A generalist is favored for such a position because of the broad and broadminded capacity for policy coordination and insight that is derived from experiences across diverse ministries and multi-sector coordination. On the other hand, the professional public servant, brings a wealth of domain technical acumen and expertise that is a sine qua non for a data-driven governance that the government requires from the civil service. Unlike the generalist, the professional comes with a specialized albeit narrow problem-solving competence rather than the presumably rounded administrative acumen of the well-groomed generalist administrative officer who are now hard to find really. And yet, each of these cadres, simply so called, lack the depth of what is demanded by that office. Indeed, the office of the HCSF is too important to be left to the limitations of these cadres and the vagaries of these two subsisting criteria for electing the head of the civil service.

The nature of the twenty-first century knowledge society, the demands of the fourth industrial revolution, and the dynamics of a developmental state require that the HCSF must possess a leadership quality and a multidisciplinary capability that is a creative mixture of tactical, strategic and operational competences not limited to any cadre. The HCSF that Nigeria and the Nigerian civil service system need must be appointed not only based on individual merit and moral characteristics, but must fundamentally be able to reflect a critical blend of technical expertise that distinguishes a pubic sector specialist, the reform passion of a change agent, and the project, program and change management acumen. These requirements provide a strategic combination of critical attitude and skills that prepares the HCSF for the leadership and administrative tasks ahead.

To possess the technical administrative skills implies that the aspirant is thoroughly grounded in the bureaucratic skills that underpin the working of government and its administrative system backend, and therefore familiar with public service rules and financial regulations, mechanics of working government business and constitutional stipulations. The candidate, in other words, should be some sort of institutional memory; an achievement that comes from possessing a minimum of ten to fifteen years of engaging and navigating the administrative dynamics of the MDAs. This has to be couple with having a track record of policy formulation experience, including the political skill of defending the policy initiatives at the Federal Executive Council, as well as implementing them.

As a change agent with a passion for reform, it is expected that the incoming HCSF must be sufficiently courageous to disrupt the subsisting bureaucratic inertia that has locked the civil service into an inefficient mode. This means that the candidate for that office must be capable of an innovative and creative vision and strategy that can drive the Federal Civil Service Strategy and Implementation Plan (FCSSIP) through the introduction of modern governance and administrative solution frameworks, from performance-based budgeting, contracting and evaluation to open data geared towards evidence-based citizen-centered service delivery. The persona of the candidate must be thoroughly investigated to determine the ability to prioritize national development goals over base ethnic objectives.

Lastly, no HCSF can ever hope to succeed in the office if she is lacking a significant amount of change management acumen, the absence of which makes the most excellent reform idea very useless. The capacity to implement policies and reform ideas is what transforms the institution into an effective one. The fundamental elements of that change management framework the candidate must possess include the experience of driving and supervising digital transformation like the ones involved in the civil service automation, digitalization and process reengineering, the Integrated Payroll and Personnel Information System (IPPIS) HR modules rooted reprofessionalisation, etc.; stakeholder management capacity; strategic capability for retraining a workforce to adopt twenty-first century competences; and should have the capacity to maneuver away from the status quo reinforcing standard annual evaluation report (APER) in favor of a result-based performance management system.

The candidate to be chosen eventually must therefore come across as a transformational permanent secretary with a track record of managing reforms, possess a clean bill of integrity, has the capacity for managing administrative and institutional crises, possess a history of meritocratic credentials team spirit and mentoring of subordinates. And then a last critical point. Making impacts as the HCSF is something that will take time, if the appointment and succession plan are strategically articulated. Given that the civil service is in a debilitated state, such a HCSF needs a minimum of three years in office. Tenure must therefore be founded on a non-renewable performance-based contract that is conditioned by certified annual performance assessment rather than by age or length of service alone. The succession plan cannot therefore start when the incumbent is just some few months away from exiting the office. A grooming framework serves the purpose, for instance, of providing sufficient time to prepare the appointed candidate to familiarize and understudy the incumbent. The pool of groomed candidates’ cohort makes it possible for the President to replace the incumbent if his performance is not encouraging and, to better plan and manage succession.

World.title: Media Experts Seek Stronger African Action Against South Africa’s Xenophobic Violence
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Veteran journalist and Editor-in-Chief of Newswatch, Ray Ekpu, Thursday, called on the Nigerian government to intensify diplomatic engagement with South Africa over recurring xenophobic attacks, insisting that Pretoria must enforce its laws, prosecute perpetrators and compensate victims.

He made the call at a Pan-African roundtable organised by League of Nigerian Columnists (LNC) in partnership with the Commonwealth Institute of Advanced and Professional Studies.

The dialogue themed, ‘From Mayibuye IAfrica to Abahambe! South Africa and Other African Countries: Reflections on the Trajectory of a Relationship’, was attended by scholars, diplomats, media professionals and policy analysts.

Ekpu, who chaired the occasion, emphasised the persistent attacks against foreign nationals in South Africa and criticised the government for what he described as its failure to decisively condemn the violence and ensure that law enforcement agencies protect immigrants.

According to him, while South Africa has laws to deal with criminal behaviour, authorities have failed to adequately enforce them.

“The South African government has not come out categorically to condemn what is going on, and the police appear to be looking the other way while these crimes are taking place. Those who violate the law should be dealt with according to the rule of law,” he stated.

Ekpu urged the Nigerian government to increase diplomatic pressure on Pretoria rather than resorting to retaliatory measures against South African-owned businesses operating in Nigeria.

He also opposed calls to target the more than 120 South African companies in Nigeria, arguing that such action would hurt Nigerians more than South Africans because the majority of employees in those firms are Nigerians.

“I do not believe in an eye-for-an-eye approach. If we go that route, Africa will only destroy itself. We should pursue coexistence and continue building Pan-Africanism,” he said.

The media icon stressed that Africa already faces numerous challenges, including economic hardship, migration, climate change and political instability, adding that the continent cannot afford further divisions.

On the plight of Nigerians displaced by xenophobic attacks, Ekpu called on the South African government to compensate victims for their losses, while urging the Nigerian government to provide support for those returning home to rebuild their lives.

“The South African government should pay compensation, while our own government should help those who have returned to resettle and start life again,” he said.

Ekpu attributed the continued migration of many Nigerians to the country’s difficult economic conditions, noting that poor wages and limited opportunities push citizens to seek greener pastures abroad, where they often face exploitation and discrimination.

He maintained that improving the domestic economy would reduce the pressure on Nigerians to emigrate.

Speaking with journalists, Jean Monnet Professor of Strategy and Development, Anthony Kila, called for coordinated diplomatic and strategic action by African governments and the African Union (AU) to bring an end to recurring xenophobic attacks in South Africa.

He warned that failure to act could have grave economic and social consequences for the country and the continent.

The persistent attacks on foreign nationals, he stated, required more than periodic condemnations, adding that African leaders must adopt concrete measures to compel South African authorities to address the crisis.

According to him, South Africa should invest in reorienting its citizens through what he described as soft diplomacy, while the AU and individual African governments should engage Pretoria more firmly to ensure that xenophobic violence is no longer tolerated.

“I think South Africans in the diaspora, South African businesses operating internationally and the government need to invest in reorientation. They need to explain to people why they should not behave in such a barbaric manner,” he said.

Kila, who is also a Political Economist, suggested that African countries could consider diplomatic measures, including boycotting selected South African events, while urging influential South African public figures to speak out more forcefully against xenophobia.

He warned that the continued targeting of other Africans would eventually deepen divisions within South Africa itself.

“Today it is South Africans against other Africans. Tomorrow it could become Zulu against non-Zulu. If this trend continues, they will eventually turn on themselves,” he said.

He also urged African governments to tackle the underlying economic conditions that force many of their citizens to migrate in search of better opportunities.

“Governments should ask themselves why their citizens are so desperate to leave their countries to seek better lives elsewhere, only to become vulnerable to exploitation and attacks,” he said.

In his remarks, veteran journalist and Media Consultant, Martins Oloja, called on Nigerian leaders to improve governance, strengthen the economy and invest in quality education as a long-term solution to the growing migration of Nigerians and recurring xenophobic attacks against Africans in South Africa.

He stated that African governments should focus on addressing the conditions that force citizens to leave their countries in search of better opportunities, rather than merely condemning attacks whenever they occur.

According to him, poverty, weak governance and poor educational outcomes have continued to drive migration across the continent, making many Africans vulnerable to discrimination and violence abroad.

“They should improve conditions at home, improve the quality of education. Quality leads to industrialisation. It is quality that leads to innovation and helps fight poverty, which is why people are leaving their countries,” he said.

Oloja described the xenophobic attacks in South Africa as a reflection of broader governance failures across Africa, blaming not only the South African government but also continental institutions, including the AU and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), for failing to provide effective leadership.

He also criticised South African authorities for allowing citizens to take the law into their own hands by attacking immigrants and destroying property, insisting that the country’s leadership must act decisively to restore order and protect all residents.

Oloja also challenged African leaders to place greater emphasis on governance, economic development and regional integration instead of concentrating excessively on politics.

He expressed concern over the slow pace of African integration, citing poor transportation links across West Africa compared to Europe, where citizens can move seamlessly by road, rail or air.

“The African Union and ECOWAS should be playing stronger roles in addressing these challenges,” he said, adding that African governments must create opportunities that discourage the mass migration of young people.

He argued that countries should focus on building globally competitive businesses capable of expanding across the continent, pointing to South Africa’s success in developing multinational companies and world-class universities.

A Tanzanian Economist and Development expert, Prof. Bravious Felix Kahyoza, urged South Africa to reinforce its commitment to Pan-Africanism by protecting migrants, promoting social inclusion and educating its citizens on the historical role African countries played in the struggle against apartheid.

He stated that many African migrants, including Nigerians in South Africa, were driven by economic hardship rather than criminal intent, adding that: “Governments across the continent must create better economic opportunities to reduce irregular migration.”

He noted that many migrants were vulnerable because they were searching for improved livelihoods and often took dangerous risks in pursuit of better opportunities abroad.

“Across Africa, particularly within the continent, we need to do better so that our citizens can feel secure and have opportunities at home,” he said. “Reducing vulnerability will also reduce the pressure for people to migrate under difficult circumstances.”

While acknowledging that migrants must respect the laws of their host countries, Kahyoza said it was equally important for South Africa to improve the way it manages migration and treatment of foreign nationals.

He called on South African authorities to sensitise citizens on the importance of Pan-African solidarity, reminding them that many African nations stood firmly behind the country’s liberation struggle.

World.title: Jessica Oji Wins Historic World U20 Athletics Championships Shot Put Gold
World.content:
Duro Ikhazuagbe

Nineteen-year-old Jessica Oji early hours of Friday became the first Nigerian to win a world title in a field event at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, United States.

Oji heaved a massive 18.08 metres to take the women’s shot put event gold, leaving the silver medal for Belsy Jenniffer Quiñonez (17.90m) of Ecuador while Emily Scherf (17.23m) of Germany settled for the bronze.

The feat of Oji is coming up barely one week after winning a silver medal at her first competition in Nigeria’s colours at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

She didn’t leave anyone in doubt about her capacity to take the gold medal at the World U20. Oji kicked off her campaign with 18.05m, before she improved to her winning throw of 18.08m. Her third effort was 17.95m, before another 18.07m . All her efforts were good enough for the gold as Quiñonez of Ecuador’s best for the silver was 17.90m.

Interestingly, Oji just last February completed her switch of allegiance from the United States of America to Nigeria.

She celebrated her 19th birthday at Team Nigeria’s training camp in Aberdeen on June 23 while preparing for the Commonwealth Games.

Oji’s best effort at Glasgow 2026 was 17.87m that earned her the silver medal. Now, she has stepped into the 18.00m mark even as a junior athlete, giving Nigeria the hope having a shot put star in the ranks of world’s best throwers .

In a chat with THISDAY at the Commonwealth Games, Oji, said that competing for Nigeria gives her joy. “If I don’t compete for Nigeria where else? I love the vibes, the atmosphere around the Nigerian camp and all around me here in Glasgow. I will go to the World U20 Championships to give my best,” Oji stressed in the interview at the Team Nigeria Maldron Hotel camp in the Scottish capital city.

Until Oji’s achievement early hours of Friday, Nigeria’s previous efforts at the U20 Championships were Esther Aghatise’s silver medal in the women’s long jump in 2002 and Chinecherem Nnamdi’s bronze medal in the men’s javelin event in 2021.

Elsewhere at the Championships, Team Nigeria continued its impressive showing in Eugene with a record-breaking performance in the mixed 4x100m relay, while Jecinta Lawrence, Faith Ezechukwu and Precious Opinion also secured progression in their respective events.

The mixed 4x100m quartet of Tejiri Godwin, Rosemary Nwankwo, Perfect Faye and Miracle Ezechukwu produced one of Nigeria’s standout performances so far, clocking 41.91 seconds to finish second in their heat and qualify for the final.

Nigeria entered the final exchange behind the leading teams, but Ezechukwu produced a sensational anchor leg, ghosting past Germany and almost catching the United States before the finish line.

Ezechukwu recorded a stunning 10.05-second anchor split as Nigeria crossed the line in 41.91 seconds, a Nigerian U20 record and the fastest U20 time ever recorded by an African team in the event.

The performance puts Nigeria firmly in the medal conversation heading into the final, with the quartet now looking to build on an impressive opening-round performance and challenge the world’s leading teams for a place on the podium.

There was further progress for Nigeria in the women’s 400m as Jecinta Lawrence and Faith Ezechukwu both advanced to the semifinals.

Lawrence battled all the way to the finish in her heat, clocking 53.97 seconds in a dead heat for third place with Eni Kuske, with both athletes credited with the same time.

Faith Ezechukwu followed with another composed performance, finishing third in her heat in 54.38 seconds to secure automatic qualification for the semifinals.

Nigeria also celebrated an impressive breakthrough in the men’s triple jump as Precious Opinion produced a new personal best of 16.02m in the qualification round.

World.title: ASUSS Raises Concerns over Attacks on Schools, Urges Govt to take Proactive Measures
World.content:
Ibrahim Oyewale in Lokoja

The Academic Staff Union of Secondary Schools(ASUSS), Kogi State chapter, has expressed serious concern over the persistent attacks on schools and educational communities in the country and the state in particular.

This was contained in a communique issued by the Executive Council(EC) of the ASUSS and copy of which was made available to journalists in Lokoja yesterday, lamenting that that schools are centres of learning and should never become targets of criminal activities.

The council therefore, called on government and all security agencies to strengthen security around schools through proactive intelligence.

The council, however, commended the Kogi State Government under the leadership of the Governor Usman Ododo, for its sustained efforts in improving security across the state and for maintaining a cordial relationship with the workforce.

“We acknowledge the government’s commitment to industrial harmony and appreciate the steps taken to promote the welfare of workers.

“The council also passionately appeals to the Kogi State Government to restore the payment of the 27.5 per cent Teachers’ Special Allowance (TSA) to secondary school teachers. This allowance was a product of a duly negotiated Collective Bargaining Agreement between ASUSS and the Government and served as recognition of the peculiar demands of the teaching profession.

‘Its restoration will greatly improve teachers’ morale and further demonstrate Government’s commitment to quality education.

“On healthcare, the council commended the Government for introducing the Kogi State Health Insurance Scheme, which has the capacity to improve access to quality healthcare for workers and their families.

“We, however, observe that some of our members have not yet enrolled in the scheme. We therefore urge all secondary school teachers to complete their enrolment without delay so they can enjoy its numerous benefits.

“The council further expresses concern over the piecemeal payment of gratuities to retired workers in the state. While we appreciate government’s efforts to settle outstanding liabilities, we respectfully appeal that gratuities be paid in more reasonable and substantial batches to enable our retired colleagues enjoy the rewards of their many years of dedicated service.

“Another major concern is the acute shortage of teachers in our public secondary schools. The shortage has placed enormous pressure on the available teachers and is affecting the quality of teaching and learning. We therefore renew our appeal to Government to urgently recruit qualified teachers to fill existing vacancies across the state.

“The council equally calls on government to establish a motorcycle loan scheme for secondary school teachers, especially those serving in rural communities where transportation remains a major challenge. Such a programme will improve teachers’ mobility, enhance punctuality, and boost productivity,” the Communique stressed.

“Despite these challenges, the council commends all teachers for their resilience, professionalism, and commitment to duty under difficult economic and working conditions. We encourage our members to remain dedicated, maintain the highest standards of discipline and professionalism, and continue to discharge their responsibilities with diligence in the overall interest of our students and the state.

“Finally, ASUSS wishes to reassure the Kogi State Government of our continued support and readiness to collaborate in advancing the development of secondary education. We remain committed to constructive engagement, mutual respect, and dialogue as the best means of addressing issues affecting teachers and the education sector.”

World.title: NAFDAC Flags Unregistered Menopause Supplement, Warns of Potential Health Risks
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake

The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) has issued a nationwide public alert over the sale and distribution of an unregistered menopause supplement, Menofix Capsules, warning Nigerians not to purchase or use the product as it is being removed from the market.

The agency said the product, marketed by PureEve as a hormone-free herbal and multivitamin supplement for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause, is not registered with NAFDAC despite being widely advertised and sold through online platforms and retail outlets across the country.

NAFDAC explained that the alert followed a complaint concerning the sale of the product and reports of possible liver-related adverse effects associated with some of its ingredients.

Following investigations, the agency confirmed that Menofix Capsules has never been registered by NAFDAC and is therefore not authorised for sale, distribution or use in Nigeria.

The regulator also cautioned consumers not to confuse the unregistered product with two legitimately approved products bearing similar names — Menofix Herbal Capsule (NAFDAC Registration No. A7-103321L) and Menofix Powder, both of which are duly registered with the agency.

NAFDAC said it has directed all its zonal directors and state coordinators to step up surveillance and immediately remove the unregistered product from circulation wherever it is found.

The agency urged distributors, retailers, healthcare providers and members of the public to remain vigilant and avoid stocking, selling or consuming the product. It also advised anyone in possession of Menofix Capsules to discontinue its use and submit any remaining stock to the nearest NAFDAC office.

Consumers who have used the product and experienced any adverse reactions were encouraged to seek immediate medical attention and report such incidents through NAFDAC’s official pharmacovigilance reporting channels.

The latest alert forms part of NAFDAC’s ongoing campaign to eliminate unregistered and potentially harmful medicines from the Nigerian market and safeguard public health.

World.title: Historic and lesser-known planetarium in Cape Town set to be restored
World.content:
The SAAF Museum's planetarium is the smallest of South Africa's five planetariums. Image: Monolithic Commons

Inside the South African Air Force (SAAF) Museum at Air Force Base (AFB) Ysterplaat in Cape Town is one of South Africa’s lesser-known planetariums – and plans are now underway to bring it back to life.

Dubbed Project Stargaze, the initiative aims to replace the facility’s ageing 1956 Spitz Model A-2 star projector with a modern digital projection system.

The goal is to transform the historic dome into a contemporary astronomy and science education centre while preserving its heritage.



The restoration project was officially launched this week during an event attended by Western Cape Minister of Cultural Affairs and Sport Ricardo Mackenzie, City of Cape Town Safety and Security Portfolio Committee Chairperson Mzwakhe Nqavashe, members of the Aeronautical Society of South Africa and invited guests.

Historic planetarium set for modern makeover

Although smaller than South Africa’s other public planetariums, the Ysterplaat facility has a long history.

Its original Spitz Model A-2 projector was designed by American inventor Armand Spitz as an affordable system for schools, universities and military institutions.

The South African Air Force (SAAF) Museum at Air Force Base (AFB) Ysterplaat has launched an ambitious campaign to restore its historic planetarium by replacing its inoperative 1956 Spitz Model A-2 star projector with a modern digital projection system.https://t.co/iQZ8aOrCm1 — DefenceWeb (@defenceWeb_Afr) August 7, 2026

The projector was first acquired by the South African Naval College before moving to 80 Air Navigation School in 1982, where it was used to train navigators in celestial navigation.

It was later transferred to the SAAF Museum, introducing thousands of visitors to astronomy over the years.



Now, after decades of service, the projector has reached the end of its working life.

“The SAAF Planetarium is more than just a dome of stars,” said Lieutenant Colonel James du Toit, Officer in Charge of the SAAF Museum at AFB Ysterplaat.

“It is a gateway to learning, curiosity and exploration.”

He emphasised how the upgraded facility would give young South Africans “a unique opportunity to engage with science, astronomy and the wonders of flight.”

The catch? SAAF’s Project Stargaze needs funding

The museum has already made progress through volunteer efforts, including repainting the dome and installing dimmable LED horizon lighting.

Project manager Major Marcel Bester said around R360 000 is still needed to complete the refurbishment.

The funding would pay for a high-luminosity Epson projector, specialised fisheye lens, surround-sound system, acoustic treatment, dehumidifier, control system and new seating.

“We really want to turn our planetarium into a world-class facility,” Bester said.

If funding is secured soon, he believes the refurbishment could be completed within two months.

The SAAF Museum at Air Force Base Ysterplaat is SA’s second-largest military aviation museum. Image: Jens Schmidtgen

Free admission

While modest admission fees could be introduced in future to help cover operating costs at the Ysterplaat planetarium, Bester said education would remain the project’s primary focus.

“The goal is to impart knowledge, not to make money,” he added. “I’d rather not charge anything and have people walk away with a wealth of knowledge.”

Mackenzie welcomed the initiative after visiting the museum for the first time, saying the attraction deserves far greater public attention.

“It’s fantastic to see what’s happening here, and this needs to be more broadcast in our communities,” Mackenzie said.

Provincial government has also pledged to explore ways to support the museum through existing education, youth and heritage programmes.

World.title: Rest In Peace: Kaizer Chiefs’ former star dies
World.content:
South African football is mourning the death of former Kaizer Chiefs midfielder Michael Nkambule. The 37-year-old died on Friday, 7 August 2026, after suffering serious injuries in a car accident approximately two weeks earlier.

Family spokesperson Siyabonga Moloi confirmed that Nkambule was travelling alone from a football tournament in Polokwane to Johannesburg when his vehicle overturned.

MICHAEL NKAMBULE LOSES BATTLE

Emergency services rushed Nkambule to Far East Rand Hospital following the accident.



He was later transferred to Johannesburg General Hospital for specialist treatment. Doctors operated on the former midfielder after he suffered severe spinal cord injuries.

Following the operation, the former Betway Premiership star returned to Far East Rand Hospital to continue his recovery.

He spent time in the intensive care unit and continued fighting despite the severity of his injuries. However, his condition eventually deteriorated, and he passed away on Friday afternoon.

Born in Etwatwa, Daveyton, Nkambule was regarded as one of South Africa’s most exciting football talents during his teenage years.

His ability attracted attention from European giants Manchester United and Chelsea before he moved to France to join the youth academy of RC Strasbourg.

Also read: Kaizer Chiefs confirm new home venue



After returning to South Africa, the talented midfielder represented SuperSport United and Black Leopards.

His most significant connection came with boyhood club Kaizer Chiefs, where he wore the iconic number 10 shirt. Known affectionately as “Ace” and “Zidane”, Nkambule never lost his passion for football after retiring from professional football.

He remained involved in the game through Ditlhake Masters FC, where he continued playing for the regional legends side. Tributes have since poured in from former teammates, football media and supporters across the country.

Widespread condolences have to been sent to the Nkambule family. Details surrounding the memorial and funeral services are expected to be announced by the family in the coming days.

World.title: FULL family statement after St Stithians pupil ‘murdered’
World.content:
Police have opened a murder investigation following post-mortem examinations into the deaths of St Stithians College Grade 11 learner Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and alumnus Ethan Coetzee. Image: ChatGPT

Police have opened a murder investigation following post-mortem examinations into the deaths of St Stithians College Grade 11 learner Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and alumnus Ethan Coetzee, who were found dead at a lodge in Sabie, Mpumalanga, earlier this week.

The South African Police Service (SAPS) confirmed on Friday that the post-mortem findings suggest the 17-year-old Waldeck-Cooks may have been strangled, while the 19-year-old Coetzee is believed to have died by suicide.

RIP | Wynberg Girls’ Grade 11 pupil dies after courageous battle



The pair were discovered at a lodge in Sabie on Monday, prompting police to initially register an inquest docket while investigations got underway.

However, following the outcome of the post-mortem examinations, detectives have added a murder charge to the investigation.

“The South African Police Service in Mpumalanga is now investigating a case of murder and an inquest following the deaths of two teenagers at a certain lodge in Sabie,” police spokesperson Lieutenant Colonel Mavela Masondo said.



“An inquest docket was initially opened. However, following post-mortem results, a case of murder was added.”

Masondo said the post-mortem findings indicated that “the 17-year-old female may have been strangled, while the 19-year-old male may have taken his own life.”

Family statement

Following the news, Derrick Cooks, father of Cameron Waldeck-Cooks, in conjunction with Cameron’s mother, Claire Waldeck-Cooks.



Our beloved daughter, Cameron Waldeck-Cooks, was a 17-year-old Grade 11 student at St Stithians Girls’ College.

Cameron was working towards the Gold level of The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment, the South African implementation of The Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award. As part of the programme, she was preparing to complete a multi-day adventurous journey. When she was invited to join two families on a hiking trip in Sabie, Mpumalanga, she saw it as an opportunity to work towards that goal.

We were notified on the morning of 3rd of August 2026 that Graham Coetzee discovered her body.



We appointed an independent forensic pathologist who has advised us that his preliminary findings indicate that Cameron died as a result of strangulation and suffocation. The police have confirmed that they have opened a murder investigation.

We are aware that conflicting and unverified accounts concerning the circumstances of Cameron’s death have been reported. We ask that speculation not be presented as fact while the investigation and forensic processes remain ongoing.

Cameron was a deeply loved daughter, sister, family member, friend and student. She was kind-hearted, warm and determined. She had a quiet strength, cared deeply for those around her, and naturally encouraged and supported younger girls who looked up to her. Her loss has left an immeasurable void in our lives.



We are profoundly grateful for the compassion and support shown to our family by the entire Saints community, including Cameron’s friends and the netball and rowing communities. Their kindness has sustained us during an unimaginably painful time.

A memorial service will be held later in August, with further details to be communicated at the appropriate time.

We are not in a position to give interviews or comment further at this stage. We respectfully ask the media and the public to protect the privacy of our family and especially the children affected by Cameron’s death, as we grieve and try to come to terms with our devastating loss.



Derrick Cooks and Claire Waldeck-Cooks

Paid tribute

The tragic deaths have sent shockwaves through the St Stithians community.

In separate statements issued earlier this week, the school paid tribute to both learners.



Waldeck-Cooks, a Grade 11 learner who had attended St Stithians since Grade R, was remembered as an accomplished rower and netball player, admired for her leadership, kindness and determination.

Coetzee, who completed his schooling at St Stithians in 2025 after 13 years at the school, was described as a talented sportsman who excelled in rugby and equestrian sport and was respected for his humility, enthusiasm and support for younger pupils.

Police have appealed to the public to refrain from speculating about the circumstances surrounding the deaths while investigations continue.

World.title: Bradley Grobler puts pen to paper on Stellenbosch FC deal
World.content:
Stellenbosch FC have strengthened their attacking options with the signing of veteran striker Bradley Grobler. Image: Stellenbosch FC website

Stellenbosch FC have strengthened their attacking options with the signing of veteran striker Bradley Grobler, who reunites with head coach Gavin Hunt as he looks to add to his remarkable Premier Soccer League goalscoring record.

One of South African football’s most prolific forwards, the 38-year-old arrives in the Cape Winelands with 129 PSL goals, leaving him within touching distance of Peter Shalulile’s all-time league scoring record.

Grobler joins Stellenbosch after spells with Sekhukhune United and SuperSport United, where he enjoyed some of the most successful years of his career, including winning the 2020/21 PSL Golden Boot.



‘It feels amazing to be here’

The former Bafana Bafana striker said joining Stellenbosch was an easy decision after seeing the club’s ambition and professionalism firsthand.

“It feels amazing to be at Stellenbosch FC,” Grobler said.

“This is a club that I’ve always admired for the way it is run and the players it has produced over the years.



“It’s a club I probably should have considered joining a long time ago. Arriving here, meeting everyone, and getting an understanding of what the club is about have made it an easy decision.”

Grobler believes the squad has the quality to compete for honours this season.

“There’s a lot of potential here in Stellenbosch. When you look at the players that have signed and combine it with the youngsters coming through, it becomes a very exciting opportunity.”



Reunion with Gavin Hunt

The experienced striker will once again work under Gavin Hunt, with whom he enjoyed success during their time together at SuperSport United.

“It also certainly helps when you’ve worked with the coach before, and I’ve worked with Coach Gavin a few times in my career, and we’ve always worked well together,” Grobler said.

“But it’s not only him. The people around and involved in the Club have all made me feel like I’ve been here for years already.”



Chasing trophies

Approaching the twilight of his career, Grobler says his motivation remains unchanged.

“I’m someone who has always taken pride in what I do, and when a club shows interest in me the way Stellenbosch has, I want to make them proud and give the fans something to celebrate.

“This is a team that I believe can compete for trophies. For me personally, nearing the end of my career, I’d also love to win more silverware, and I believe we can do that together.



“The Club is ambitious, and the coach is ambitious, so I just want to come in and add as much value as I can.”

Another major signing

Grobler’s arrival continues an active transfer window for Stellenbosch, following the return of Ashley du Preez from Kaizer Chiefs and the signing of defender Given Msimango.

The veteran striker has been handed the No 67 jersey and could make his debut when Stellenbosch host Polokwane City in their next Betway Premiership clash on Tuesday, 11 August.



Kick-off is at 19:30.

World.title: This one kitchen appliance will lower your electricity bill
World.content:
Countertop appliances can help you save money. Image: Unsplash

Electricity prices increased at the start of July. Next year, they’ll increase again. The rising cost of living is stifling many South Africans.

To reduce your spending, get creative in the kitchen.

You can become smart about your grocery spending. But using an electricity-saving kitchen appliance is a more permanent money-saving measure.



Pressure Cookers are an electricity-saving kitchen appliance

Consider replacing your stove-top cooking with pressure cooking.

Pressure cookers typically hold the equivalent of a 24cm pot.

However, unlike a stove that uses at least 2 000 watts, pressure cookers only use half that amount, 1 000 watts.

They also cook meals quicker.

So you get double the money-saving power.

You can cook meat to tender in 70% of the time.



So those beef and lamb stews will be ready in 30 minutes rather than the 3 hours it usually takes for tender meat.

Save Money by Cooking all your meals from scratch

You’ve heard it before: if you want to save money, cook every meal from scratch.

But what happens when you come home and you only have energy to use the television remote?

That’s when you turn to the pressure cooker.

Add your ingredients, push a button, wait for the jingle when your food is done and eat.

The pressure cooker will become central to your grocery list.

You’ll be able to buy all the ingredients to cook from scratch.

Multi Cookers and Slow Cookers are also Useful

The only downside is that pressure cookers come with a R1 300 price tag.

As winter ends, the appliance will go on promotion.

But when you don’t have money for a pressure cooker, turn to a more affordable appliance like a multi cooker or slow cooker.

Multi cookers work similarly to pressure cookers.

They allow you to cook multiple types of food quickly. However, they’re not as quick as pressure cookers.

They make up for that time with lower wattage. A multicooker is usually 500 watts.

The cheapest energy-saving appliance is the slow cooker.

Slow cookers use about 200 watts. They are best for stews and casseroles and not much else. They cook meat low and slow, usually four to eight hours. But they use roughly 90% less electricity than a stove-top.

Appliance Wattage Energy Saving Capacity Pressure Cooker 1 000 watts 70% Multi Cooker 500 – 800 watts 80% Slow Cooker 200 – 300 watts 90%

How Much Money Will You Save?

According to Standard Bank’s LookSee, a 3000-watt stove-top uses R7.50 per hour. If you’re cooking about 90 minutes a day, that’s R78.75 a week.

That’s R348.75 a month. If you use a pressure cooker, you’ll save about R244 a month.

If you use a slow cooker, you can save R313.87 a month.

Your money-saving ability increases because you can buy more affordable cuts of meat.

You can buy cuts that take longer to tenderise, but have them cook in 40 minutes with a pressure cooker.

Depending on how much meat you eat every month, you could save an extra few hundred.

World.title: Beyond Game Day | When Sport Loses Control: SAFA Elections Scandal Exclusive | 7 August 2026
World.content:
WHEN TRUST BREAKS, SPORT STOPS BEING JUST A GAME

Sport depends on rules, but rules alone are not enough. Every system also depends on trust: trust that selection is fair, that leadership is legitimate, that governance processes are credible and that the people responsible for protecting the game are not bending it around their own interests.

That trust can begin to unravel long before an institution formally fails.

At school level, the consequences are immediate. If parents believe money, sponsorship or influence can improve a child’s chances of selection, then merit becomes harder to defend. Coaches become vulnerable to suspicion. Schools risk being judged not only on how they develop talent, but on whether access to opportunity can be distorted by wealth or relationships.

THE DAMAGE IS BIGGER THAN ONE TEAM SHEET

Young athletes learn what systems reward. If they see influence outrank ability, that becomes part of their understanding of how institutions work. If adults become aggressive around children’s sport, that behaviour teaches something too. If racism appears in spaces supposedly built around teamwork, competition and shared identity, the question is no longer simply what happened on the field. It becomes what children are absorbing from the environments around them.

That is why one of the most uncomfortable ideas in this week’s Beyond Game Day lands so hard. The hosts ask how a teenager born long after apartheid can still know language associated with that history. The implication is obvious: discriminatory ideas do not survive by accident. They survive because they are repeated, normalised and passed down.

THE SIMPLE PRINCIPLE APPLIES HIGHER UP THE SPORTING SYSTEM

Football governance relies on process. Elections, nominations, disciplinary systems and leadership structures work only if participants believe the rules are being applied consistently and confidential information is being protected where required.

Once that confidence weakens, even a legitimate outcome can become harder to defend.

Questions raised around SAFA’s presidential nomination process illustrate why institutional credibility matters so much. If stakeholders begin wondering who knows what, when they knew it and whether information was handled properly, the issue stops being only about which candidate wins. The process itself becomes part of the contest.

THAT IS DANGEROUS FOR ANY ORGANISATION

Governance systems are designed to make leadership transitions predictable. When the process feels opaque, personalities become more important than institutions. That makes renewal harder, factionalism stronger and public trust weaker.

The leadership question is equally uncomfortable.

Sporting administrators often build immense legitimacy through historic achievements. Those achievements matter. They should be recognised.

But legacy cannot become permanent insulation from scrutiny.

LEADERSHIP HAS TO ANSWER THE PRESENT, NOT ONLY THE PAST

That applies in South African football and at FIFA. Gianni Infantino’s leadership has repeatedly placed the global governing body at the centre of political, commercial and ethical debates around the sport. The question is not whether powerful leaders will face criticism. They will. The real test is whether institutions remain strong enough to absorb controversy without allowing trust in the organisation itself to collapse.

THE LESSON REACHES FAR BEYOND SPORT

Schools, companies, governments and federations all face the same risk: once people believe access depends on influence, information is not protected or leadership no longer feels accountable, confidence drains away.

And trust is difficult to rebuild because it cannot be ordered back into existence.

It has to be earned through visible fairness, consistent rules and leadership willing to accept that authority is temporary.

Sport may provide the stage.

But the real story is what institutions reveal about themselves when the pressure rises.
