World.title: Trump says White House ballroom ruling jeopardizes lives of future presidents, vows Supreme Court appeal
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

After a panel of federal judges ordered construction on the White House ballroom to stop, President Donald Trump said he will immediately appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

In a Truth Social post on Friday, Trump decried the 2-1 decision from the the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit as "horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful."

"The Circuit Court’s decision, which is totally wrong on the vital subject of STANDING, of which the plaintiff has none, severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House — including all future Presidents of the United States, and their families, as well as the lives of all those visiting, such as Heads of State and other Dignitaries, and all Americans who wish to visit the historic, beautiful Executive Mansion," Trump wrote in the post.

He also accused the court of refusing to acknowledge that the ballroom, which he said is being built ahead of schedule and under budget, "is a Gift from President Trump and Great Patriots of the United States of America."

TRUMP WARNS JUDGE AGAINST SACRIFICING NATIONAL SECURITY BY BLOCKING WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM, DRONE BASE

"There will be no expense to the American Taxpayer. This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety," Trump wrote.

The appeals court on Friday upheld a lower-court decision that paused above-ground construction of the proposed 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom project, which replaced the demolished East Wing.

The earlier ruling allowed work to continue on underground national-security facilities and certain safety and security measures, a decision the higher court also upheld.

The appeals court said in its 136-page ruling that the decision to build a "massive ballroom" lies with Congress, not with the executive branch.

REPUBLICANS EYE PICKING UP $400M TAB FOR TRUMP'S BALLROOM AS SOME DEMS OPEN TO 'DISCUSS' IDEA

Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia wrote the majority opinion, remarking that there is no precedent for what Trump has done.

"We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now," they wrote.

The judges said their ruling does not prevent the president from building the ballroom if it is authorized by Congress in the future.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

As Trump pointed out in his social media post, the ruling was stayed for 14 days to allow the defendants to seek a Supreme Court review.

It is not immediately clear if the Supreme Court will take up this case.

World.title: Blackjack losses, a chilling phone call and a diverted flight cap a chaotic Las Vegas vacation
World.content:
*NOTE: Some names, locations, techniques and information have been withheld due to their sensitive nature.

You often don’t realize you’re in a fight for your soul until you’re deep in it.

As my loyal readers and viewers have realized, I have been fairly off the grid for roughly the past week.

Why?

It was time for my annual trip to Las Vegas, but unlike previous trips, this one was happening with the looming threat of the Iran War, death threats and the IRGC. Things were different for this working-class man this time around.

While I’m not going to get into specifics, there’s no question that due to a heightened alert status and ever-evolving threat matrices, precautions that never had been taken before were going to be necessary. It turns out some people aren’t fans of my outspoken ways, and unlike people who claim to be "threatened" by blue hair liberals (literally comical to even consider dangerous), being under the threat from a state-backed actor is a totally different ball game.

No box could go unchecked.

Wheels up to Las Vegas for a working-class vacation.

The first decision that was made was that I would move to the airport under the cover of darkness.

There are a couple of reasons why this was deemed the best option. First, it allows me to move when the city and airport aren’t buzzing yet.

Second, the streets being mostly empty provide far more tactical advantages than if they’re crowded and something goes wrong.

The plan didn’t survive me making it to the front door.

Immediately upon exiting the Hookstead Compound (location classified) with my bags, I spotted two military-age males that I’d never seen before. Keep in mind the entire point of the movements and schedule is that NOBODY is supposed to be around.

I know enough about the people who live in my vicinity to recognize most of them. I’ve never seen these two men in my life. It’s a shocking sight to behold, but they’re way more shocked to see me than vice versa.

A decision had to be made in a half of a second over whether or not this was finally it. Would the entire operation be aborted before entering the vehicle for the airport?

LUCKY TRAVELER WINS $3.3M JACKPOT ON 'WHEEL OF FORTUNE' SLOT MACHINE AT HARRY REID INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT

Ultimately, sometimes the only way to fix a problem is to go clean through it (another lesson that some people would be wise to follow for Iran).

I closed the space quickly, deemed the two men not an immediate threat showing hostile intent and got on the move as quickly as possible.

As planned, the streets are completely empty and we’re able to get into the airport without issues. From that point, the goal was simple:

Blend in as much as possible, go unnoticed and get seated on the plane as quickly as possible. Every minute spent in the open at the airport is a minute where nobody is in complete control of the situation. That’s far from ideal.

Little did I know things would only get stranger from here.

I chose a seat as close to the cockpit as possible. Unusual for someone with my blue-collar roots? For sure, but a necessity given the stakes.

What seemed like a routine and normal flight became very different in a matter of seconds. For the first time in my life, I was on a plane where a metal gate was closed off up front by the cockpit without explanation.

That’s right.

There was a metal gate rolled out making the front portion of the plane an impenetrable fortress. I tried to get a look past the gate, but found it difficult. My only guess was that one of the pilots was out of the cockpit for some reason, but I was never able to confirm that.

Fortunately, the plane touched down without further incident.

The working-class man’s Las Vegas vacation was underway.

Just as quickly as I’d gotten on the plane to Vegas, I disappeared into the crowd blending in again. Nobody knows me, and I don’t know them. The less attention the better. We’re not chasing clout. We’re chasing demons that have haunted us for a long time, and doing it while operating to survive.

Things were about to get weird (noticing a trend) very quickly.

My driver appeared like a normal woman attempting to make small talk.

It was anything but normal.

For some unexplained reason, this woman starts talking to me about sex and a sex museum. At one point, she starts asking if I like sex.

Am I on a hidden camera show? Am I being pranked? I start making very measured and careful statements assuming whatever I say is absolutely being recorded. I can’t wait to get the hell out of this taxi as soon as possible. A working-class man might not have much in life, but we do have one thing:

Common sense, and common sense dictates asking a stranger about sex in a vehicle is about as strange as it gets.

I get out at the Cosmopolitan in Las Vegas with one clear goal in mind:

Get to the blackjack table as quickly as I can.

I dumped my stuff into my room, which for a working-class guy who had to fight for everything in life, I can tell you was pretty shocking. It featured a massive bedroom, a living room area, huge walk-in shower, a hot tub and a balcony overlooking Las Vegas.

I’m not going to lie to you all. It was epic. I guess life occasionally hands the downtrodden a win in life.

To the tables I went.

I pulled out a roll of working-class money and set it down at a blackjack table in the high-limit room. Now, some of you might be asking, "David, what is a guy like you doing in the high-limit room? That doesn’t seem like it’s your speed."

Fair question, and the answer is simple:

Privacy.

The high-limit room at the Cosmo is one of the nicest in Las Vegas, and it’s also fairly secluded.

Remember, I have significant threats I have to worry about, and unlike the unhinged clowns roaming around, the people who want me dead actually have the means to carry it out.

Head on a swivel.

I sit down at a double-deck table, and immediately go on a nice little run earning more money in a matter of minutes than a regular working-class guy does over the course of a few weeks.

When you don’t come from much, you know when to walk away with the win the universe gifted you (this energy won’t last for long). I push back from the table for the time being and keep the operation rolling.

Next stop? Stage Door for a hot dog and a cheap beer. The hot dog, while not amazing, is certainly worth the money and it’s also a tradition. It hits the spot, and I soon get word a second seasoned Las Vegas operator has arrived. For the sake of the story, he is identified as VO2. VO1, another seasoned Las Vegas operator, won’t arrive until the next day.

From here, things progress rather normally. We hit up the arts district for a couple beers and did a little exploring.

I was about to hit my next unexpected hurdle, and while I’m on a high alert status, I didn’t see this kind of roadblock coming.

I decide to head back for some more high-limit blackjack, and am promptly informed the casino needs extra information from me. I’m not going to share the specific information in a public setting, but it appears the amount of working-class money that I’ve put on the table in one day has possibly triggered some money laundering tripwires.

Me? The working-class guy from rural Wisconsin? You have to be kidding me.

After a brief conversation with the casino bosses, it’s smoothed over and the gambling continues.

Remember the win I had early in the day? That’s wiped out in about an hour, and then go ahead and tack on a few paychecks on top of that.

Now, this is where most people would start panicking. Those kinds of swings at the tables break most people, but most people aren’t from my rural Wisconsin background.

I’m in the fight, and while the IRGC hasn’t taken its shot yet, the casino is drawing financial blood.

Just like knowing when to walk away when you win, you also need to know when to not chase losses. I cut the cord, push back and live to fight another day.

I grab a burger on my way back to the room, crush it and pass out as soon as my head hits the pillow.

Day two brings chilling phone call.

Day two started like any other day in Las Vegas. All was quiet in the streets and casinos and people were still asleep by the time I was on the move with enough caffeine in my system to kill a rhino. I guess I’m just built differently. If chugging Celsius was a skill, I’d be the Tom Brady of getting it done.

The day started with biscuits and gravy at Ellis Island, followed by getting kicked in the shorts at the blackjack tables. Fortunately, the losses this time around aren’t nearly as vicious, but it’s still not great. I’m now deep in a gambling hole. Not great, but it’s only a loss once you actually leave the city.

What happened next nobody could see coming…….most of all me.

The bat phone buzzes to life, and I see a name that stops me dead in my tracks. I know something serious must be happening for me to be receiving this call, and I now have a major issue:

I can’t take this call outside of a completely secure location.

My hotel room, which would get the job done, is too far away and time is of critical importance.

The decision is made for VO2 and myself to relocate to a closer secure location, and with the doorway secure, I answer the phone.

A serious flow of information starts flooding in.

Seconds feel like hours.

There are times when years pass without anything happening, and then there are times where decisions are made in seconds that can change everything.

This is the latter.

I try to process the information as quickly and as efficiently as I can, and it ultimately boils down to one call:

Go or don’t go.

You could hear a pin drop in the secure room. Based on the information I was hearing, I simply was not confident with going.

It’s a no go with the door left open for a decision to be made at a later time.

With my head spinning with a million thoughts, I get word that VO1 has touched down and is on his way to the rendezvous point. After a brief conversation, we head over to Ole Red (Blake Shelton’s establishment) for nachos and a beer.

The nachos were absolute fire. The best nachos I’ve ever had? No, but definitely very solid and delicious with some added brisket.

Next up was Golden Tiki in the Chinatown area of Las Vegas. Golden Tiki is another tradition every single year for us. It’s an outstanding tiki bar with a unique vibe, and some bathroom wallpaper that is a bit shocking at first sight. Seeing as how this is a family website, I won’t share further details. I have myself a couple tiki drinks, and both are well worth the money.

As a working-class guy, I can really only afford cheap domestic beers, but this is vacation. Let’s live a little. Plus, with the death threats, I simply can’t be living for the future. Much like fighting the demons, any day could be the last, and we’re leaving it all out on the field.

Now, there is one location in Las Vegas I’ve been more than eager to get to, and with the full trio locked in, it’s time to execute the plan.

Hogs & Heifers.

For those of you who don’t know, Hogs is an absolutely insane Las Vegas institution. It’s not for the faint of heart or easily offended. It’s a bar for true American patriots and it has the most entertaining bartenders in Vegas by orders of magnitude. They’ll insult you in the most vulgar way possible, but it’s all in the name of good fun.

It was closed last year, and that was the first time since discovering the gem that we weren’t able to go. That needed to change and it did.

It’s now located at the Plaza while its new permanent home is built.

The bartenders were as rowdy and fun as ever. While it’s an outpost location, it felt just like the old Hogs so many have come to know and love, and the Coors Banquets were as cold as ever.

Oh, did I mention the insults and jabs were flying in all directions? It felt good to be back, and as always, you meet some insane characters in there.

We rotate between playing blackjack and hopping in and out of the bar as the day stabilizes following the phone call in the secure location.

I’m actually feeling fairly good about it as I head back to my hotel room, but I’m also starving. I order room service and get hit with one hell of a surprise:

The full room service experience is a $160 minimum spend.

I honestly think what I’m hearing can’t possibly be true. I’m trying to order a wrap. I don’t need the full room service experience. Bring it to me in a bag and a plastic container and I’ll be fine. That’s exactly what ended up happening.

How is a working-class guy supposed to be able to afford a $160 minimum spend? It’s simply not possible. We’re lucky just to have food on the table. Forget the fancy stuff. Save that for the millionaires and billionaires, not guys like myself.

First, I have to operate under new procedures thanks to the Iranians. Second, I am gutted at the table. Third, I am reminded of just how blue-collar I am when ordering room service. The losses keep piling up.

Having said that, the wrap was delicious and the portion sizes were excellent.

Day three: bring out the machine guns.

Tuesday started just like any other day. I filmed a short war update and crushed a couple Celsius cans, and the vibes were high.

I’m also very excited for one very simple reason:

The schedule has a portion blocked off for letting it rip with some machine guns.

Generally speaking, I hate indoor shooting ranges and shooting ranges in general. I had a private outdoor one at my house growing up, and the idea of strangers with guns around me at a range has never been something I’ve really enjoyed. I know how good I am with a gun (most working-class men from Wisconsin can say the same), but I don’t know how good these random people are or what stupid stuff they might do. Add in the fact foreign tourists don’t know an AK-47 from a Beretta M9, and I think you get the point.

Well, when in Vegas, you do things you don’t do at home. I grabbed a PKM machine gun and PPSh-41 Soviet submachine gun.

Both were absolutely awesome. The PKM was shockingly light, and the rate of fire was exceptional.

The PPSh-41 was cool mostly because it’s the submachine gun the Soviets used in WWII against the Germans.

I wouldn’t say it’s a particularly impressive submachine gun or special, but it can’t be beat from a historical standpoint if you’re looking for foreign WWII guns. I can’t recommend both enough if you ever get a chance to shoot them. You won’t regret it. We also met some cool Welsh dudes at the range who absolutely loved America. It was a humbling reminder just how good we have it here in the USA. Foreigners would give anything to be part of our club, and none of us would give it up for anything.

Next, the trio filed over to El Cortez where I had a very mediocre bratwurst before, yet again, getting my wallet crushed at the blackjack tables.

I hope my wife is okay being solely responsible for the bills for the foreseeable future because this has turned into a catastrophic gambling nightmare.

What do you do when the world is against you and the demons are starting to sing? You numb the pain with a little Coors Banquet, and that’s exactly what we did by swinging by Hogs, where the bartenders were in rare form. I say that as a compliment. I can’t wait to visit next year once it’s in its final home. I can only imagine how glorious it will be.

The day wound down with a stop in the Arts District for a delicious espresso martini and some insanely good Mexican food, followed by a short stop at Ellis Island before closing beers at Stage Door. I eventually found myself back in the high-limit room with my blue-collar money (no money laundering concerns this time) and actually came out a little ahead. Slowly but surely, I’m crawling out of the hole I created.

However, my winning wasn’t the highlight of day three coming to an end. The dude sitting next to me at the table was hysterical. I legit couldn’t stop chuckling at every word coming out of this guy’s mouth, and a woman (I believe girlfriend but can’t say for sure) shows up and sits down next to him. Turns out she’s a former golf superstar and was at one point one of the top golfers in the world. Admittedly, I have no idea who she is, but I also couldn’t recognize any golfer other than maybe three or four. That’s a sport for rich people, and I’m anything but wealthy, no matter what the rumor mill says.

They were both a ton of fun, and then a Canadian showed up ripping cigs. What a night at the high-limit blackjack table. I wouldn’t have cared if I lost every penny because the dude was so funny that it made the whole thing entertaining, no matter the outcome. Fairly certain I also saw him tip several thousand dollars to the dealers in the time I was with him.

Day four: An unexpected vehicle nightmare.

Day four was the final full day in Las Vegas, and after breakfast and some more blackjack, we decided to catch a ride to Fremont.

We’re not 50 yards down the street when the right front tire of the vehicle blows out, and the driver declares an emergency. It’s in the worst possible location. We’re nowhere near a parking garage or the safety of a building.

Is this how it ends for me? Have plans been set in motion that can’t be stopped?

I don’t know and I’m definitely not going to wait to find out. VO1 and I bail out of the vehicle, and I start scanning in all directions for threats. I don’t see anything, but we’re completely in the open and exposed. Nowhere to run. Nowhere to hide. I took a look at the guy’s vehicle, and as VO1 noted, "His right tire is f****d."

I peered over, and assessed the situation.

His right tire was completely destroyed. I don’t even understand what happened. I never heard a pop or any kind of blast.

It was fine when we entered the vehicle, and it was anything but fine now. Every second matters. The longer we stay exposed, the more risk we’re assuming.

A backup vehicle - a big black SUV - whisks in and we’re in it without hesitation racing towards where we’re going.

I still have absolutely no idea what happened with the original vehicle, and I doubt I ever will. Some questions are best left unasked.

We grab a couple beers and attempt to win some money. VO1 pulls an absurd four card blackjack split and hits it. The craziest part is it wasn’t the first time. He did the exact same thing earlier in the day at Ellis Island.

Two successful four card splits in one trip? Good luck replicating that at any point in the near future.

I also noticed at one point in the night that my phone all of a sudden had a crack in the screen protector, which VO2 and myself found extremely odd. It was never dropped and never left alone. None of us could explain it. Maybe there was a perfectly ordinary explanation. Maybe there wasn't. Either way, it became one more strange thing on a trip that seemed determined to keep getting stranger.

Fortunately, the night didn’t feature any more unexpected surprises, and instead focused on some honest conversations about some theories we have about relationships and life. Those aren’t my stories alone to share, so I won’t out of respect for the other parties involved.

Day five: time to exfil and get home.

I wake up, bang out another video update for the Hookheads (what my fans call themselves on YouTube) and grab a stack of cash to hit the high-limit room one final time before leaving.

That’s when there was an unexpected change of plans.

I’m well over a thousand miles from home, and I get a call learning that my HVAC system is still not only not fixed, but getting the company to show up and do it has become a nightmare for my wife, who is running point at home.

It’s enraging. We’re now weeks into this situation without a resolution, and my patience has officially run out.

Instead of spending some blue-collar money one last time at the tables, I’m now dealing with this issue and then I run into a major computer problem.

What seemed like a successful trip is unraveling into a nightmare as I sit on the one-yard line waiting to punch the ball in.

You remember the start about a fight for your soul? I successfully avoided detection in Las Vegas (major win), clawed back some losses to an acceptable point (huge win) and was ready to roll one last time.

One final engagement at the tables.

Instead I’m in a hotel room dealing with infuriating nonsense.

It’s not the bright moments when you have to remember to save your soul. It’s the dark ones, and that’s what I’m left doing as the clock ticks down.

I eventually get enough of it smoothed out, but now I have to race to catch my plane. With a Burger King burger and some fries in my stomach, it’s time to go home.

I spent five days dancing with the demons, battling the highest stakes I’ve ever gambled and made it out alive.

Little did I know the biggest fight yet was only hours away.

The plane ride straight from the depths of Hell.

In the final stretch of my plane ride home I start to notice something that I don’t think many other people are:

The plane is flying in a holding pattern.

We’re not getting any closer to our final destination. We’re holding.

A brief holding pattern is one thing. A holding pattern that carries on for an extended period of time is rarely a good thing.

Then the pilot comes over the PA system and gives us all the devastating news. The plane is being diverted to a completely different airport due to the final destination having a ground closure.

You have to be kidding me, right? I just made it out of Las Vegas alive and am supposed to be landing back home in minutes.

Instead, we’re bound for an airport much further away from my home, and while that’s bad enough, what’s looming is an experience so hellish that I can only pray I never have to repeat it again.

Once the plane lands, we’re just stuck on a runway for hours. It feels like Lord of the Flies. Discontent is growing. Now, I will say none of this is the fault of the crew. I’m not blaming them. I’m blaming the universe.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK CULTURE COVERAGE

We finally pull into a parking spot…..that is nowhere near a gate. The next problem? A stairs vehicle is blocking the bus from coming to get us.

It just drags on and on. I’ve seen darkness in life. I’m not even sure what words could accurately sum up this situation. I want to be anywhere else on the planet right now.

Eventually, we get off and are unloaded in a terminal to find a way home. Absolute disaster on all levels.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

I make it home and my wonderful wife has pizza waiting. It’s the small victories that really make you smile. The highest of highs. The lowest of lows. All in a span of a few days. I fought the demons and won only to be dragged back down in the closing moments. Fortunately, I was able to pry victory away from the brutal jaws of defeat.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

What comes next? I don’t know, but I do know someday I will lose this fight. That day just isn’t today. We ride again at dawn. Let me know your thoughts at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

World.title: GOP senator breaks with Trump over 'woke' Smithsonian history battle
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, is splitting from the majority of Republicans on the GOP's pushback against the Smithsonian Institution's teaching of American history.

The moderate Republican senator sent a letter to the Trump administration alongside Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., asking for more information on President Donald Trump's directive to install "temporary signage" outside the National Museum of American History, after he accused the museum of teaching historical accounts with an inaccurate and hyper-partisan lens.

"As Chair and Ranking Member of the Senate Interior Appropriations Subcommittee, we write to express our concern and to request more information regarding the role the Department of the Interior (DOI) will have in implementing Executive Order (EO) 14416, ‘Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution,’" the letter said.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

Republicans have heaped scrutiny on the Smithsonian Institution, which gets roughly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars from Congress annually, for exhibits that the GOP has argued are inherently political.

But Murkowski appeared to refute that in her bipartisan letter, writing to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, "For the past 180 years, the Smithsonian Institution has been committed to sharing objective historical evidence through research and education, not political narratives."

"The Smithsonian Institution has worked tirelessly to present a comprehensive narrative of our nation’s amazing history, from its many triumphs to its trials. There is nothing more American than telling our story truthfully," the senators said.

Trump signed an executive order late last month directing Burgum to utilize existing avenues "to restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution," including installing "temporary exhibits or signage on [federally owned] sidewalks, walkways, and land used by the public that corrects inaccurate information presented in the Museum."

Murkowski and Merkley are asking the administration for information on whether there's any precedent for federal land or funds being used to communicate "conflicting information" to a nearby entity's operations, who is compiling the information and what the timeline and cost of the signage will be.

Examples Republicans have seized on include an exhibit that described Disney's "Steamboat Willie" as representing "vestiges of long-standing traditions of blackface minstrelsy," while accusing the broader curation of the museum of being "anti-white" and "woke."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

It's led several conservatives on the House Appropriations Committee to tell Fox News Digital they would like to see new guardrails on the Smithsonian's federal funds to force the museum to change controversial exhibits or risk losing its government dollars.

World.title: Sen. Bill Cassidy, a critical Republican holdout, backs Todd Blanche for attorney general
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., announced Friday he will vote for President Donald Trump’s pick of Todd Blanche for attorney general, likely assuring his confirmation.

“All considered, I will vote for Mr. Blanche. I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” Cassidy said in a floor speech after outlining concerns he said he weighed.

Cassidy’s decision is likely to be decisive in helping Blanche get confirmed to the powerful job.

While he’s “concerned about episodes of apparent lawfare,” Cassidy said, “even critics admit that Mr. Blanche knows the law and is a hands-on administrator.”

Republicans need support from 50 of their 53 senators to confirm Blanche.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, came out Friday against Blanche, joining fellow centrist Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, to oppose the president’s choice. With Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., out indefinitely, and Democrats expected to vote no, a third GOP opponent would have blocked the nomination.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska. Allison Robbert / AP file

Despite the “numerous constructive meetings” she’s had with Blanche, Murkowski said in a statement, “I will oppose his nomination.”

“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she said.

Murkowski also warned of the “politicization” and “even weaponization” of the Justice Department, which she said has accelerated under the Trump administration.

The senator cited the Justice Department’s handling of the release of files in the case of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and questioned whether the Trump administration’s proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund, which she called a “slush fund” in her announcement, would remain off the table.

A McConnell spokesperson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment Friday about how he would vote if he were able to be present and cast a vote.

The retiring Kentucky senator is not a guaranteed proponent on Blanche; he has voted against some high-profile Trump nominees, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

In an interview with Punchbowl News on Thursday, before Murkowski’s announcement, Trump lashed out against the moderate GOP senator.

“Murkowski, I was against. I’m against Murkowski,” he said in the interview, released Friday. “I do more for Alaska than any any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s she’s not good.”

Blanche, the acting attorney general, has already faced a bumpy confirmation process after Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., both withheld their support for the nomination over their concerns about his leadership at the Justice Department.

Cornyn and Tillis had expressed concerns about the fund, which was intended to compensate alleged victims of politically motivated prosecutions. The fund was created as part of Trump’s settlement with the IRS over a leak of his tax records. The settlement also included a guarantee that he and his family business would be sheltered from tax audits.

The senators had sought written assurances that the fund would be rescinded and the scope of the audit immunity clarified, which Blanche ultimately provided. Tillis had also insisted that Blanche meet with Epstein survivors, which he had previously not agreed to do.

After Blanche’s contentious confirmation hearing last month, during which Tillis and other senators aired their concerns about the Justice Department’s handling of the Epstein case, the acting attorney general did meet privately with a group of victims. Epstein survivor Dani Bensky told NBC News, however, that the meeting was “not productive” or “substantive,” while Blanche described it in opposite terms.

Democrats have denounced the Justice Department’s failure to redact personal information about the survivors, but not that of people who may have participated in their abuse. They have also raised concerns the “anti-weaponization” fund is not dead and that loopholes exist to resurrect it.

World.title: Senate passes sanctions bill on Russia and Iran named for late Sen. Lindsey Graham
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Senate voted overwhelmingly to pass legislation to impose sanctions against Russia and Iran after months of fits and starts, with the death of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham providing the final push.

The 61-page legislation, renamed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, in honor of the bill’s biggest proponent, is designed to punish major buyers of Russian oil and gas. It also features additional sanctions on Russian leaders, family members and oligarchs.

Smoke rises over the city following a Russian air attack on Kyiv in July. Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images file

And it allows for targeted tariffs on products from countries that buy most Russian oil and gas, limiting them to the five biggest importers.

The vote was 86-11.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the bill would help protect Ukraine against Russian aggression.

“Ukraine is now the largest conflict, literally, since World War II in Europe,” Thune said in a recent floor speech. “And the Ukrainian people have been resilient, worked really, really hard to try and bring this war to an end. But as long as Putin has Russian oil and gas money, he’s able to continue this war. And what this sanctions bill would do would basically cut that off.”

Rescuers work at a nine-story residential building in Kyiv's Podilskyi district after a Russian missile strike in July. Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos via Getty Images file

After a last-minute demand from President Donald Trump, it also extends sanction authority designed to limit funding toward Iran’s weapons and energy sectors.

The bill has been criticized by a group of Democrats and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., with the Democrats arguing that it would give Trump too much tariff authority.

It now goes to the Republican-controlled House, where it faces an uncertain future.

The Senate deal was announced Tuesday morning by Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the late senator’s sister and appointed successor, as well as Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Katie Britt, R-Ala.; Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H.; Roger Wicker, R-Miss.; and Jim Risch, R-Idaho.

A couple walks past a recruiting placard in Kyiv in June. Sergei Supinsky / AFP via Getty Images file

The senators struck the deal July 28, less than two weeks after Graham’s unexpected death, saying there was “no greater way to honor” the South Carolinian’s legacy.

“We are proud to announce an agreement on legislation to stop purchasers of Russian oil and gas from fueling Putin’s war machine and to continue restricting the Iranian regime’s ability to support terrorism and build its nuclear program,” the senators said in a joint statement.

Senate passage was all but guaranteed after the chamber voted 86-12 to advance the bill procedurally last month, shortly after reaching the deal.

World.title: Rep. Andy Ogles loses his Republican primary in Tennessee
World.content:
Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee has lost his Republican primary, NBC News projects, falling to a former state official in a primary season that has seen an unusually high number of incumbents lose renomination.

See live results

Charlie Hatcher, the former state agricultural commissioner, rode support from prominent establishment Republicans to a victory over Ogles, a controversial congressman backed by President Donald Trump. He is a heavy favorite in the general election in the deep-red district.

Congressional candidate Charlie Hatcher speaks at a campaign event at Southall Angus in Franklin, Tenn., on July 13. Alan Poizner for The Tennessean / USA Today Network via Reuters

Ogles was outraised and outspent on the airwaves, largely because of a massive ad effort from a pro-clean energy group — a last-minute campaign Ogles criticized in an interview with Fox News.

While Ogles had arguably the most important endorsement in a GOP primary in Trump’s, Hatcher had backing from Gov. Bill Lee, former Gov. Bill Haslam and other prominent Republicans, like former Trump Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue.

Ogles has faced various controversies over the years. He said this year that Muslims don’t belong in American society, deleted a homophobic social media post after having blamed a staffer and argued last year that the federal government should revoke future New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s citizenship and deport him.

He was also investigated on suspicion of campaign finance violations; he has not been charged with any crimes. Ogles told The Associated Press that the Justice Department returned his cellphone, which it had seized during the investigation.

But while Ogles had fended off a well-funded primary opponent before, he couldn’t do it this time. Hatcher didn’t run away from Trump, either, despite Trump’s support for Ogles. Hatcher aligned himself with Trump and his policies and sought to contrast himself with Ogles.

“Think what President Trump could do if our congressman spent less time talking and more time doing,” reads a quote on Hatcher’s website.

Ogles is the ninth House member — six Democrats and three Republicans — to lose a primary this year. That’s the most in a nondecennial redistricting year since 1970, according to Vital Statistics on Congress.

Two senators, Republicans Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas, also lost their primaries, and an additional House member — Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas — finished second in his primary and then decided to drop out of the race and resign before a GOP runoff.

World.title: Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins the Republican primary for governor of Tennessee
World.content:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn has won the Republican nomination for governor of Tennessee, NBC News projects, defeating Rep. John Rose in a race in which President Donald Trump declined to endorse.

Blackburn, 74, became the first woman to represent Tennessee in the Senate after she won her current seat in 2018; she had served in the House since 2003. If she wins the governor’s race, she would be the first female governor.

She will be a heavy favorite in the general election in the red state to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Bill Lee. Jerri Green, a member of the Memphis City Council, won the Democratic nomination.

Blackburn is considered one of the most conservative members of the Senate, known for her stances on abortion and transgender rights and her criticism of China’s influence.

While Trump stayed out of the race, Blackburn and Rose both leaned on his name.

The Tennessee Freedom Fund, a pro-Blackburn outside group, has spent heavily to tie her to Trump, airing s featuring clips of Trump referring to her as “an incredible person” and saying: “Fantastic job you did. We’re proud of you.”

At a rally in Washington in January, Trump praised Blackburn, saying, “Unfortunately, she’s running for governor,” and adding: “I’d love her not to. I begged her: ‘I said, ‘Marsha, don’t. We don’t want to lose you in the Senate.’”

But the Nashville Banner reported that Trump told members of Tennessee’s congressional delegation on a flight to Memphis on Air Force One that he would not endorse Blackburn because of his relationship with Rose, according to two members of Congress who were present for the conversation. Rose, who represents Tennessee’s 6th District, is a former state agriculture commissioner who also positioned himself as a loyal Trump ally.

Rep. John Rose, R-Tenn., arrives for a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on in 2024. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images file

It makes the race a rare Republican contest in which Trump has stayed on the sidelines. Trump has even double-endorsed GOP candidates in past races, like in South Carolina, where he added an endorsement of state Attorney General Alan Wilson to his backing of Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette ahead of a runoff Wilson won.

Rose spent almost $13 million self-funding his gubernatorial bid.

Blackburn is part of an unusually large group of senators running for governor in this election cycle.

GOP Sen. Tommy Tuberville won his party’s gubernatorial nomination in Alabama this year, while Democratic Sen. Michael Bennet lost his primary in Colorado. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar will be on the ballot for governor in Minnesota next week.

World.title: Idaho police release chilling new video of In-N-Out mass shooting
World.content:
Police released new surveillance footage of the mass shooting at an In-N-Out in Idaho on Friday, showing the clearest account yet of the horrific scene that unfolded last week.

The Twin Falls Police Department showed the surveillance video — which contains detailed voiceover from law enforcement — of the shooting at a press conference.

The shooting at and around the newly opened Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out on Saturday left three people dead and seven others wounded. The 24-year-old gunman, Chad Williams, fatally shot himself.

Surveillance video with voiceover audio from authorities shows Williams pulling up to the In-N-Out drive through in a white Honda Civic. When he stops at the payment window, he rolls down his window and shoots employee Ashley Garibay, 23, who later died of her injuries.

He then pulls up slightly in the drive through, parks and exits his car, then shoots and kills Christopher Claunch as he’s sitting in his vehicle, according to the video.

The video then shows a man, who authorities identify as former police officer Austin James, running towards Williams before getting shot. James survived the shooting, but is shown retreating back to his car while losing blood.

Williams then returns to the payment window and observes other employees rendering aid to Garibay before firing into the window, according to the video. His handgun jams, prompting him to return to his vehicle and retrieve a rifle, according to the video.

Inside the restaurant, an off-duty Idaho State Police Trooper assists evacuating patrons and employees while searching for the gunman, according to the video. Authorities said they were not releasing the off-duty trooper’s name at this time.

The surveillance footage shows about half a dozen uniformed In-N-Out employees crawling on the ground, and over each other, to escape.

Williams then fires at fleeing patrons in the parking lot and returns to the drive-through window, where he exchanges gunfire with the off-duty trooper who’s still in the restaurant. The gunman briefly retreats, then returns to the window and fires inside again, injuring a good samaritan who was trying to help the trooper and render aid to Garibay.

A woman seen in the video fleeing from the restaurant encounters the gunman, then seeks shelter behind his car, where she finds the discarded handgun. She picks it up and then discards it when she realizes it’s jammed, according to the footage.

The gunman then walks from the In-N-Out to the street and fires at cars stopped at a red light, striking three victims, the video shows.

He then can be seen firing at Tesla vehicles parked at a nearby charging station, shooting three people as they sat in the vehicles. One of the three who were shot, Dale Schultz, 66, died from his injuries, the video states.

Williams then walks into the nearby Twin Falls Visitor’s Center, according to the footage. He then leaves the visitor center store and encounters two employees of nearby businesses on a walking trail behind the visitor center.

One of the employees engages with the gunman, talking with him and allowing others coming down the trail time to escape, according to the video. As they separate, Williams fires at the employee, the video shows.

Body camera video from police officers responding to the scene and running towards the gunman is then shown.

“Hey! Show me your hands!” an officer shouts as he points his rifle towards the gunman.

The voiceover then states that Williams fatally shot himself and fell into a canyon.

On Friday, police said that they still have not identified a motive, and that there is no reason to believe there was another shooter.

“To our victims and their loved ones, this community grieves with you,” said Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks. “We will never forget what happened here. We will never forget those that were hurt.”

The In-N-Out location opened on July 24, according to a news release from the California-based chain.

Lynsi Snyder, the president of In-N-Out Burger, addressed the shooting and the death of Garibay.

“She was taking care of our most important asset — our customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own,” Snyder said.

“He shot both on our property and off and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our associate and customers, innocent people who never saw it coming,” she added.

World.title: A quandary for the Fed: Dealing with hot inflation and cool job growth
World.content:
What a difference a day can make for monetary policy.

On Thursday, interest rate futures were decidedly tilted toward the Federal Reserve hiking its benchmark rate in September, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks traders to forecast the central bank's policy decisions. But after Friday morning's dismal July jobs report, which showed that employers unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs last month, that probability has now flipped, with the Fed expected to hold steady next month.

The latest employment figures suggest the labor market may be much weaker than previously thought. On Friday, the Labor Department also revised down hiring data for May and June by a combined 103,000. The suddenly wobbly job market complicates the Fed's dual mission of maximizing employment while keeping consumer prices stable.

The Fed typically cuts interest rates when the labor market slows sharply because cheaper money stimulates the economy by spurring consumer borrowing and business investment. At the same time, the central bank is also trying to douse inflation, which continues to run hot.

Elevated inflation is typically addressed by the Fed raising rates, as higher borrowing costs put the brakes on spending, tempering economic demand and price increases.

"The chances of holding just went up pretty significantly today," Indeed Hiring Lab senior economist Cory Stahle told CBS News about next month's Fed meeting. "What we see in the jobs report maybe says that the Federal Reserve, at the very least, might have to think about the timing of a potential rate hike, if not think about some rate cuts on the table as well, if we continue to see this type of deterioration in the labor market."

On Friday, the probability that the Fed will hold its benchmark rate steady next month rose to 56%, from 45% the previous day, according to CME FedWatch.

Fed faces a quandary

In June, inflation rose at an annual rate of 3.5%, higher than the Fed would like but a decline from 4.2% in May. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has signaled that he's determined to drive inflation back down to the central bank's 2% annual target.

But whipping inflation back to 2% by raising interest rates gets a whole lot trickier for the Fed if officials also need to prop up a weakening job market with lower rates, according to economists.

"The U.S. labor market is stalling again, and that is going to make the Federal Reserve's job harder and life for job seekers rough," said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in an email. "The Federal Reserve has to stay focused on inflation, but the labor market is vulnerable to any downturn."

July's Consumer Price Index report, set to be released on Aug. 12, is forecast to show inflation eased slightly last month to an annual pace of 3.4%, according to FactSet.

Americans are struggling not only with a tepid labor market, but also with inflation outpacing wage gains, Long noted. This gap represents a continuation of a longer-term trend, with much of workers' wage gains over the past seven years largely consumed by inflation, according to a CBS News analysis of Census data.

The typical full-time worker earned $1,250 a week in the first half of 2026, the analysis found. That's up $342 from the year before the pandemic, amounting to a hefty 38% pay raise. But prices in the U.S. climbed nearly as fast. Consumer costs have jumped 30% over that same seven-year period, swallowing about 80% of the typical worker's raise.

"Most Americans are getting squeezed by high inflation," Long said. "Many Americans will have to tighten their belts this fall."

What's behind the hiring slump?

Employers are holding off on hiring amid economic uncertainty sparked by high energy prices caused by the Iran war, steeper U.S. tariffs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, Indeed Hiring Lab's Stahle said.

"There's just been a lot of policy uncertainty, geopolitical uncertainty, that is weighing on the minds of businesses and households," he told CBS News. "Wrestling with this uncertainty makes it hard for businesses to commit to a long-term hire."

Some economists are still penciling in rate hikes later this year, citing the imperative to tame inflation, which they believe the Fed will prioritize over shoring up the job market.

"We agree that the July jobs report was a bit dovish on net," Bank of America economists said Friday. "But we are sticking with our call that the Fed will hike by [0.75 percentage points] this year, starting in September. The Fed is likely to remain more focused on inflation than labor."

World.title: More than 50 decomposing bodies found at Far South Side funeral home
World.content:
Chicago authorities are investigating a Far South Side funeral home after more than 50 decomposing bodies were found in the facility.

Its funeral director's license was suspended when state regulators found decomposing bodies were being kept in "deplorable conditions" that included rodent and maggot infestations.

Chicago police were seen going in and out of South Chicago Chapel, at the corner of 95th Street and Exchange Avenue, on Thursday evening.

A Chicago Police Department spokesperson referred questions to the Cook County Medical Examiner's Office, which confirmed it was notified by city and state officials about bodies improperly stored at the funeral home.

The Cook County Medical Examiner's Office said investigators and forensic pathologists who went to the facility "found more than 50 decedents in various states of decomposition at this time."

The medical examiner's office said investigators were still assessing the conditions of the bodies and searching for documents to identify them, including death certificates, a process that could take several days.

According to the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation records, the state suspended the license of funeral director Johanna Morgan due to a finding that the facility's "continued practice is a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare."

Records show Morgan had been "allowing multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies."

Morgan was funeral director at South Chicago Chapel as late as May of 2025, but it was unclear from current records if she was still funeral director there as of Thursday.

One neighbor, who wanted to be identified only as "V," said she's lived directly behind South Chicago Chapel for about a year and has constantly experienced what she describes as a disturbing smell.

"It just, like, stinks all the time. Like, it's so bad," she said. "I don't know, like a dead mouse. Like, it stinks."

Another neighbor said the smell has been ongoing.

"I have a 3-year-old, I live right next door," Valkiery Velez told CBS News Chicago. "I lived there for like a year, so, like, I could smell it the whole year."

On Thursday evening, staff from Emmanuel Funeral Home & Cremation Services arrived at South Chicago Chapel to retrieve a body, unaware of the investigation. The staff said they had spoken with South Chicago Chapel earlier but had not heard from them since.

"We stopped by to get someone. We don't know what's going on at the moment," Pastor Christopher Jennings said. "We talked to them the first time, they picked up, they talked to us, they said they'd give us a call back. After that, there was no call. We kept calling, so we decided to do a wellness check to see what was going on and this is what we come to."

According to the Illinois Secretary of State's website, the active business license of South Chicago Chapel lists Johanna Morgan's husband, Clark Morgan, as president.

The funeral home's owners did not respond to messages left by CBS News Chicago.

Clark Morgan previously owned and operated Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights, which was shut down last year, accused of mishandling the bodies of people who had recently died.

The crematory agreed to shut down its operations amid a probe by the Illinois State Comptroller's office, which regulates the cremation industry.

CBS News Chicago obtained photos from inside a trailer at the crematory where bodies were being stored. The trailer is located on the property belonging to Heights, and the photos show deceased people partially wrapped in sheets or clear plastic bags, with their faces and body parts sticking out.

CBS News Chicago also found bodies in bags moved from another trailer on the site, and there are questions about storage areas without proper refrigeration at the business.

World.title: Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy's psychiatrists testify at her murder trial
World.content:
Psychiatrists who treated Lindsay Clancy before she killed her three young children in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on Jan. 24, 2023, began testifying in her high-profile murder trial on Friday.

Clancy is facing first-degree murder charges in the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. The defense says she was overmedicated and suffering from an extreme episode of postpartum psychosis when she strangled the children.

Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan said the jury should expect a full day of testimony Friday.

You can watch the trial live in the embedded video, on CBS News Boston or on the CBS News Boston YouTube page while court is in session.

Lindsay Clancy's first psychiatrist testifies

Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Clancy's first psychiatrist, took the stand just before 12:30 p.m. Clancy had begun seeing Tufts in September of 2022.

Dr. Jennifer Tufts testifies at Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 7, 2026. CBS Boston

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague began by questioning Tufts about whether Clancy had tried medication before, specifically during her time in nursing school. Tufts testified that Clancy had reported trying an SSRI and did not report any side effects while taking it.

Sprague asked Tufts if Clancy ever said she was hearing voices telling her to hurt herself, hurt other people, or kill someone. Tufts said that Clancy answered "No" to all of them.

Tufts testified that Clancy's biggest concern was anxiety when she came in originally, and she had recommended she go to individual therapy and take sertraline, otherwise known as Zoloft. She said that Clancy was concerned about side effects from the medication.

"I recall that she was generally reluctant to take medications, but at this point she was considering it and was interested in learning about what medications might be helpful for her," Tufts said.

Clancy had also said she had tried Zoloft while she was postpartum with her second child, Tufts testified. Tufts said Clancy told her that she had some common side effects, such as appetite issues and upset stomach, when she initially took the medication.

During a follow-up appointment later in September, Tufts said that Clancy had told her she elected not to take the Zoloft because she was able to sleep a bit more.

Tense moment in courtroom

Before testimony resumed just after noon on Friday, Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, claimed he heard prosecutors say "shut her up" on a hot mic, as Clancy cried during autopsy testimony on Thursday.

Judge wants to go to sidebar and Reddington exclaims "I don't want to go to sidebar!" Now attorneys are talking at sidebar. Seems emotions are heightened. Lots of hands waving. — Kristina Rex (@KristinaRex) August 7, 2026

"This is not like 'Handmaid's Tale.' You can't tape her mouth shut," Reddington was heard saying to Judge Sullivan before heading to sidebar.

Right before the lunch break, Sullivan said he wanted to make something "crystal clear."

"There is to be no inappropriate comments or disruptive comments to be made inside of this courtroom. If anybody is found to make those, they will be immediately escorted out and barred," Sullivan said. "There are microphones all around, so if I get a report of that, there's going to be some serious issues and serious problems ... There's going to be no warnings, no yellow card. You're out."

Lindsay Clancy's McLean psychiatrist testifies

The first psychiatrist to testify Friday was Dr. Alia Goodheart of McLean Hospital, a psychiatric hospital in Belmont where Lindsay Clancy was admitted for voluntary inpatient treatment on Jan. 1, 2023. She left early, after nearly five days, to attend her daughter Cora's birthday party. Clancy then had follow-up outpatient treatment at McLean up until the murders on Jan. 24.

Dr. Alia Goodheart of McLean Hospital testifies at Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 7, 2026 CBS Boston

Goodheart said Clancy told her she was having side effects from medication and found it hard to sleep without medicine. The doctor testified Clancy was a low-level risk patient who was "anxious" and her diagnosis was "major depressive disorder, severe without psychotic features."

When prosecutor Shanan Buckingham asked Goodheart about her observations of Clancy's mental status, the doctor told the court, "I can't remember certain elements ... she was appropriately dressed, speech was normal rate and volume, she was polite and cooperative."

Buckingham also asked Goodheart if she observed any signs of psychosis with Clancy, and the doctor replied, "No." She also said Clancy was specifically asked if she had a plan to kill herself or harm others and "she denied it," the doctor said.

"I did not have any concerns about her safety or a risk for anybody else," Goodheart testified about discharging Clancy on Jan. 5, 19 days before the murders. "She had never stated that she had any thoughts of harming anybody else."

Clancy was then sent home with a two-week supply of Ativan and Trazodone, medicines to treat depression, anxiety and insomnia.

Goodheart testified for about an hour before Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington began his cross-examination of her around 10:45 a.m. She left the stand just before 12:30 p.m. on Friday

"How many women have you treated that are suffering from postpartum psychosis?" Reddington asked her. After a long pause, Goodheart replied, "I haven't seen any."

Clancy's mental health is a key issue at trial. Her ex-husband Patrick Clancy testified last week that she started making suicidal statements and told him she had thoughts of hurting the children after switching to a new medication in December 2022.

Lindsay Clancy at her trial in Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 7, 2026 CBS Boston

Lindsay Clancy trial day 9

The first witness on the stand Friday morning was Kimberlee Hardy, the former director of the Kingsbury Club, a fitness center in Kingston. She testified briefly about Cora and Dawson spending time in the playroom there in 2022 and early 2023 and that Lindsay Clancy "seemed happy to be with them" and always picked them up on time.

She was followed by the 58th witness for the prosecution, Sarah Carney of Duxbury, a friend of the Clancy family for several years. Carney was on the stand for about 10 minutes and spoke about seeing Lindsay Clancy after her treatment at McLean. Carney said Clancy appeared to be quiet and thinner.

Lindsay Clancy trial this week

On Thursday, a childhood friend testified that Clancy texted her and said she had been taking a medication that caused some "dark thoughts." Clancy said she was trying to wean herself off the medication and try new ones to remove the side effects. Another friend said Clancy told her that she was feeling "like a zombie" shortly before the murders, and a coworker said Clancy reported "negative side effects from the medication."

Clancy also wrote about her mental health struggles in diary entries that were read aloud in court on Monday.

"I feel like I'm drowning every day," Clancy said in one entry.

On Tuesday, prosecutors showed the prescription pill bottles seized from the Clancy home after the murders. They say that while Clancy was prescribed several drugs for her mental health, she was not taking many pills from each bottle.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Energy company sues data center over who should pay for AI buildout
World.content:
The largest energy provider in Nevada, NV Energy, is suing data center developer Tract Capital Management, accusing the company of trying to pass costs onto consumers.

At issue is who pays to expand energy infrastructure when a data center needs as much electricity as a midsize city.

Tract's two planned campuses near Reno would together draw more than 2 gigawatts of power, nearly a third of NV Energy's generating capacity. NV Energy, which powers 90% of the state, warns it may have to raise rates if Tract does not shoulder more of the infrastructure costs.

The case marks the first time that a major utility company has sued a data center developer, and could influence who is responsible for the costs of building infrastructure needed to power the AI boom.

"Projects that create new infrastructure or energy costs must pay those costs and cannot shift them onto Nevada families, small businesses, or existing customers," NV Energy spokesperson Katie Jo Collier told CBS News. "Residential and small business customers cannot be left on the hook for these investments now or in the future."

The dispute traces back to agreements signed by NV Energy and Tract's local contracting entity, Reno Power, which established terms for delivering electricity to data centers. According to a statement from Tract, NV Energy is refusing to deliver power it had promised to provide, while still demanding that the Denver-based data center developer begin $1 billion in grid upgrades.

In June, Tract called for private arbitration to settle the matter. Weeks later, NV Energy sued to stop it.

In its lawsuit, NV Energy argues that Tract is calling for private arbitration to circumvent public scrutiny. It alleges that this is no longer a contract dispute, but one over how much power Tract will be able to draw and who will pay for the massive infrastructure investments needed to deliver it.

These questions, NV Energy argues, can only be legally decided by the state regulator, the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada, because the answers will affect every ratepayer in the state, not just the two companies at the table.

Nevada's rules require large power users to go through the commission, which determines their energy and infrastructure needs on the principle that big customers will fund their own expansion rather than shifting the burden onto average ratepayers already on the grid. Opening it up to a public forum would also allow consumer advocates, community members and other stakeholders to participate.

NV Energy says it had no choice but to sue to stop the arbitration. Utility companies are legally obligated to provide power to anyone in their territory that requests it. NV Energy cannot turn Tract away, and says it would have to raise rates if the infrastructure isn't increased to meet the added demand.

Tract says that NV Energy is launching a "public relations blitz stoking anti-data center sentiment." It points out that it has already invested more than $127 million in infrastructure projects in Nevada and committed to nearly $1 billion in network infrastructure upgrades that it says will benefit all of NV Energy's customers. The real problem, Tract told CBS News, is that NV Energy failed to adequately plan for the power it promised to provide, and is now invoking "the commission's jurisdiction as a shield."

Until now, the AI boom has made fast friends of data centers and energy companies eager to reap the profits of their vast energy demands. Nevada, in particular, has touted its relatively low energy rates, which are cheap compared to neighboring California, to court data centers: the state has 22 operating data centers and 20 more in the works.

But this case is an early fissure in that alliance, a sign that utility companies fear being blamed for rising rates and in this case are pressuring data centers, and the tech companies behind them, to shell out to subsidize their strain on the grid.

World.title: Trump mounts new effort to fire Fed's Lisa Cook after Supreme Court ruling
World.content:
Washington — The White House has informed Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, that President Trump is considering firing her from her post because of allegations of mortgage fraud, according to a letter to Cook that was obtained by CBS News.

The move comes after the Supreme Court in June blocked Mr. Trump from firing Cook while a legal challenge to her attempted removal last year moves forward. The high court said in its 5-4 decision that the president failed to afford Cook the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice and the opportunity to respond to the accusations against her, before she was fired.

Mr. Trump said in the wake of the decision that his administration would "take appropriate action" to fire Cook, and the White House now appears to be attempting to remedy the issues raised by the high court. In the letter obtained by CBS News, dated Aug. 5, White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino laid out the allegations against Cook and set an Aug. 26 deadline for her to provide a response to the claims.

"Pursuant to the Supreme Court's opinion from June 29, 2026, you are hereby provided notice that the President is considering removing you from your position on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve due to there being sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements," he wrote.

ABC News first reported that Mr. Trump is considering firing Cook again.

The allegations against Cook were raised by Bill Pulte, a senior housing official in the Trump administration, in a criminal referral he sent to the Justice Department nearly one year ago. Pulte claimed that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage filings related to two properties, one in Michigan and a second in Georgia, before she was nominated to the Fed Board by former President Joe Biden in 2021.

Cook has denied wrongdoing and she has not been charged with a crime.

Scavino claimed in his letter to the Fed governor that the alleged actions "may be sufficient to demonstrate that you committed a crime."

"There is a distinct nexus between a basic level of trustworthiness and care in financial matters and the duties of a Member of the Board of Governors," he wrote. "Because the allegations in the Criminal Referral reflect on your honesty, trustworthiness, and competence to perform the duties of the office you currently hold, the President has determined that there is reason to believe they constitute cause to remove you from your position on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve."

Mr. Trump first attempted to fire Cook last year over the claims she committed mortgage fraud.

She swiftly filed a lawsuit challenging her removal and asked a federal court to reinstate her to the role. Cook prevailed in blocking her firing in district court and a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. The Supreme Court in June also allowed her to remain in her post as a Fed governor as her lawsuit moves forward.

To accept the government's arguments that Mr. Trump can fire Cook "would in effect transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment — an interpretive leap out of step with the statute Congress enacted and our Nation's tradition of central banking protected from political interference," Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the five-justice majority.

He was joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, Brett Kavanaugh and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

World.title: Senate passes long-stalled Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham
World.content:
Washington — After more than a year of negotiations, the Senate on Friday finally passed a bill to impose punishing new sanctions on Russia for its war on Ukraine, approving the measure with overwhelming bipartisan support.

Senators had pushed for months for a vote on legislation that would penalize top Russian figures and the biggest buyers of Russian oil to dial up the pressure on Moscow to end the fighting.

The Senate voted 86 to 11 to approve the bill, sending it to the House.

Over the last year, prior versions of the measure — championed by Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina — were on the verge of moving forward, only to meet resistance from the White House or to be put on the back burner for other priorities or alternate courses of action.

The effort to impose fresh sanctions on Russia received another burst of momentum after Graham's sudden death in July. Graham died shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv and announcing that a deal had been reached with the White House to move forward on an updated version of the legislation.

GOP Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who filled her brother's seat after his death, said the late senator "believed that this was the most consequential piece of legislation that he had ever led."

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who spearheaded the sanctions legislation with Graham, called it a "momentous day."

"I'm not even going to try to channel my inner Lindsey Graham, except to say, as he said to me in some of his last words, 'This is a big effing deal,'" Blumenthal said.

The bill, titled The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. There are exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are taking "significant" steps to reduce the imports. It also includes sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, officials within his government, oligarchs and Russian banks and financial institutions.

China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air think tank. Europe has historically been Russia's largest natural gas customer, though the European Union has cut its imports significantly in recent years and is aiming to fully wean itself off Russian gas by next year.

The bill also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors. The Iran sanctions were added at the urging of President Trump.

It gives the president authority to waive the sanctions if he certifies to Congress that it's in the national interests of the U.S.

The vote came together after most opposition faded this week. With any one senator having the ability to slow the path forward, GOP Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky secured a vote on an amendment to strip the tariff authority from the bill, which failed.

Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia also dropped his opposition after securing a commitment from U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer. Speaking on the Senate floor Friday morning, Warnock entered a letter from Greer into the record that he said closes a loophole that would expand the president's tariff authority, calling it a "small but meaningful victory for all Americans who continue to suffer under this president's reckless tariffs."

After attending Graham's funeral in Washington, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy watched from the Senate gallery as senators advanced the long-stalled sanctions in a June 29 vote. Zelenskyy said it was "deeply symbolic" that Graham's last trip abroad was to Ukraine, adding that the "best way to honor his memory" was to pass the measure.

Its potential passage in the House will be delayed since the lower chamber is on its five-week August break. And it's likely to meet resistance from some Democrats who are skeptical about the tariff provisions.

In a statement after the bill's Senate passage, Democratic Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York and Don Beyer of Virginia said "the current text is unacceptable."

"This bill's sanctions still contain the broadest possible waiver authority for President Trump, who already has the power to impose these sanctions on Russia under U.S. law but has refused to do so," said Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Beyer, a member of the Joint Economic Committee.

"What the bill does grant, however, are sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past," they said.

Blumenthal acknowledged that the measure faces issues in the House, but emphasized that "this bill is the bill that will pass" and be signed into law by the president.

"He supports it," Blumenthal said in a news conference after the vote. "It has taken some time to gain his support, but now that we have it, we need to move forward as quickly as possible to make sure we stand with the people of Ukraine."

Blumenthal said Senate negotiators have had conversations with House leaders, as well as Meeks.

"I hope we'll continue those conversations," he said. "I think it's a historic opportunity. Time is not on our side, and I hope the conversations will take place quickly."

Before the House left, Speaker Mike Johnson said he was "heartened to hear" that a deal had been reached with the White House.

"We're happy to receive and process that," the Louisiana Republican said.
