Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Circuit: When to Go Where

8 pm – Pick your seated show. Ginger and The Peppers at Blue Note on Paulista, or Amaro Freitas and his sextet at Sesc Pinheiros if you want the jazz.

10 pm – Tirambaço play samba in the basement room at Casa de Francisca, by Metrô Sé. Book; the Porão is small.

10 pm, the free option – Sara Hebe at Sol y Sombra 13 in Bixiga, part of the Flipei independent-publishers festival that runs until Sunday. No ticket needed.

Midnight – Ride-share to Barra Funda for D-Edge or Clash Club. Neither posts a line-up far in advance, so look at their Instagram feeds first.

Saturday, 4 pm – Alessandra Leão sings Alceu Valença in the vão under MASP, free and outdoors. It opens a season of free Saturday concerts running to November.

Saturday and Sunday – Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour at Parque Villa-Lobos, gates from noon. Saturday is sold out; Sunday tickets were still on sale at the time of writing.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba and MPB — Casa de Francisca has Tirambaço tonight and a Seresta tribute to Arlindo Cruz tomorrow. Sesc Belenzinho has Demônios da Garoa, the city’s oldest samba group, free in the Comedoria at 8 pm. Where: Casa de Francisca, Sesc Belenzinho

Jazz — Amaro Freitas brings his sextet to Sesc Pinheiros at 8 pm, and the Renato Pestana Quinteto plays JazzB near Metrô República at 9 pm. Blue Note has rock tonight, so go there for the room rather than the genre. Where: Sesc Pinheiros, JazzB

Electronic and clubs — D-Edge in Barra Funda is the city’s long-standing house and techno room, with Clash Club a few streets away for indie and themed nights. Neither publishes its Friday bill far ahead. Where: D-Edge, Clash Club

Forró and northeastern — Canto da Ema in Pinheiros has Janayna Pereira from 10 pm, and Raphaela Santos plays the Centro de Tradições Nordestinas in Limão. Both are dance floors rather than seated rooms. Where: Canto da Ema, Centro de Tradições Nordestinas

Free and festival — Flipei, the eighth Festa Literária Pirata das Editoras Independentes, runs to Sunday across central venues with free gigs including Sara Hebe tonight. El Majadero plays cumbia free at the Centro Cultural Vila Itororó at 7 pm. Where: Sol y Sombra 13, Espaço Cultural Elza Soares, Centro Cultural Vila Itororó

Megashows — Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour takes Parque Villa-Lobos on Saturday and Sunday, with gates at noon on both days. Arena tickets start at R$200 (US$39.20) full price and R$100 (US$19.60) at the half rate. Where: Parque Villa-Lobos

Pick Your Night

Date night: Casa de Francisca. Eat upstairs from 8 pm, then take a table for Tirambaço at 10 pm in the Porão.

Solo and safe: Blue Note on Paulista. Assigned seating, attentive staff, and Metrô Consolação directly underneath when you leave.

Dance till late: D-Edge in Barra Funda, with Clash Club as the fallback if the bill does not suit. Check both feeds first, and book your ride home from inside.

Meet locals: A Vila Madalena bar crawl along Aspicuelta and Mourato Coelho. Nothing needs booking and the street does the work for you.

Spend nothing: Sara Hebe at Sol y Sombra 13 in Bixiga, or El Majadero at Vila Itororó. Both free, both part of a genuinely good week for free programming in the centre.

Where to Go

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro An intimate music house in a 1902 palacete, with a main Salão upstairs and a smaller Porão below. Seated shows, serious sound, and the city’s best room for MPB and samba at close range. Tonight: Tirambaço, samba, 10 pm in the Porão. Also this weekend: Seresta à Arlindo Cruz on Saturday, at 5 pm and 9 pm, also in the Porão. Cost: Ticketed per show, with a dinner menu available before the set. Prices are published with each show on the venue’s own programme page. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, Sé Website: casadefrancisca.art.br Getting there: Metrô Sé, about five minutes on foot. Take a ride-share home rather than walking through the centre after the show. Good to know: Book ahead; both rooms are small and sell out. Arrive early if you want to eat first.

Blue Note São Paulo — Avenida Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York club, in the Conjunto Nacional on Avenida Paulista. Proper seated concerts, decent cocktails, and a crowd that is dressed up without being stiff. Tonight: Ginger and The Peppers, rock, at 8 pm. This is not a jazz night. Also this weekend: Paula Morelenbaum with Moreno Veloso and Jaques Morelenbaum on Saturday, at 8 pm and 10.30 pm. Cost: Ticketed per show and priced by seat; buy through the club’s own site. A service charge is added to food and drink. Address: Av. Paulista, 2073 (Conjunto Nacional) Getting there: Metrô Consolação is directly beneath the building. The avenue is busy and well lit at any hour. Good to know: Book online; seating is assigned. Smart casual.

D-Edge — Barra Funda Open since 2003 and still São Paulo’s best-known electronic club, with a Funktion-One rig and a crowd that treats dancing as the point. Mixed, unpretentious, and reliably late. Tonight: A Friday club night, but the house has not published a line-up we could verify. Check its Instagram or ticket page before travelling. Best time: Thursday to Saturday. Things do not really start before 1 am. Cost: Entry is priced per event; expect roughly R$40–R$80 (US$7.84–US$15.68) and drinks around R$20–R$35 (US$3.92–US$6.86). Drinks go on a comanda card. Address: Al. Olga, 170, Barra Funda Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro, about 10 minutes on foot. Ride-share is the better call on the way out. Good to know: No dress code. Buy online to skip the queue.

Clash Club — Barra Funda A 1930s warehouse on Rua Barra Funda given over to indie, pop and themed parties across two floors. Younger crowd than D-Edge and an easier door. Tonight: A club night is expected but no bill has been published. Look at the venue’s Instagram before you commit to the trip. Best time: Friday and Saturday. Arrive around midnight. Cost: Priced per party; expect roughly R$30–R$60 (US$5.88–US$11.76) on the door and R$15–R$30 (US$2.94–US$5.88) for drinks. Address: Rua Barra Funda, 969 — the street sits on the Barra Funda and Santa Cecília boundary Phone: (11) 3661-1500 Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro, then a short walk or a ride-share. Same approach as D-Edge. Good to know: Casual dress is fine. Advance tickets are usually available online.

Sardosa Bar — Vila Leopoldina A countryside-São Paulo boteco that ran as Bar da Adelaide until October 2025, when it was renamed. Roughly 200 covers between the dining room and a veranda, with a XV de Jaú shirt on the wall giving away where the kitchen learned to cook. Tonight: Open from noon straight through to midnight. Friday is churrasco day, served from noon to 10.30 pm. Best time: Friday and Saturday evenings. The veranda tables go first. Cost: Skewers from R$14–R$16 (US$2.74–US$3.14), a fraldinha with rustic potatoes at R$65 (US$12.74), and the house Caipirinha do Thiago at R$34 (US$6.66). Any caipirinha can be made without alcohol. Address: Rua Carlos Weber, 1750, Vila Leopoldina — not Vila Madalena, and about 25 minutes by car from Avenida Paulista Phone: (11) 97659-0326 Getting there: No metro nearby; take a ride-share. It is a destination in its own right rather than a stop on a crawl. Good to know: No reservations needed for the bar. Go early on a Friday if you want the churrasco.

Bourbon Street Music Club — Moema One of the city’s longest-running live-music rooms, programming blues, jazz, rock and MPB with table service. An older, well-dressed crowd that comes for the band rather than the scene. Tonight: A Friday booking is likely but we could not confirm tonight’s act. Check the club’s programme before you book a table. Best time: Thursday to Saturday, with dinner service before the show. Cost: Ticketed per show and published with each booking. Full dinner menu on top. Address: Rua dos Chanés, 127, Moema Getting there: No metro station within walking distance; ride-share is the practical option. Quiet, safe neighbourhood. Good to know: Reservations recommended. Book by phone or through the website.

MASP — Avenida Paulista Lina Bo Bardi’s museum on its red concrete legs, with a covered public square underneath known as the vão. The free concerts staged there are a São Paulo ritual. Tonight: No concert. The museum’s own evening hours apply; check before making a special trip. Tomorrow: Alessandra Leão sings a set drawn from Alceu Valença’s songbook in the vão at 4 pm, free. It opens the Música no Vão season, which runs on Saturdays through to November with Assucena, Maria Beraldo and Paola Ribeiro to follow. Cost: The vão concerts are free and unticketed. Museum admission is charged separately and priced on the museum’s own site. Address: Av. Paulista, 1578, Bela Vista Getting there: Metrô Trianon-MASP, one block away. Ride-share pickup on the avenue is straightforward. Good to know: For the vão show, just turn up. Go early if you want to be near the front.

Parque Villa-Lobos — Alto de Pinheiros The riverside park that has become São Paulo’s default site for very large open-air shows. Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour lands here this weekend. Tonight: Nothing on. The park is a weekend fixture, not a Friday one. This weekend: Anitta on Saturday 8 and Sunday 9 August, gates from noon on both days. Saturday has sold out. Cost: Arena from R$200 (US$39.20) full price and R$100 (US$19.60) half price; Front Stage from R$360 (US$70.57) full and R$180 (US$35.28) half. Address: Av. Professor Fonseca Rodrigues, 2001 Getting there: CPTM to Jaguaré, then a walk, or a ride-share booked well in advance. Roads around the park close on show days. Good to know: Gates at midday means a long day outdoors. Take water and sun cover.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena: Tree-lined streets packed with bars, galleries and a young creative crowd. Aspicuelta and Mourato Coelho are the two streets that matter.

Barra Funda: Industrial-chic club district anchored by D-Edge and Clash Club. Safe on the club strip, dead two streets away.

Avenida Paulista: The city’s spine, with MASP by day and Blue Note by night. Busy enough to walk at any hour.

Sé and Bixiga: The historic centre, with Casa de Francisca and the Flipei venues. Go with a destination in mind and ride-share between them after dark.

Moema and Vila Leopoldina: Comfortable residential districts with destination venues rather than crawls. Bourbon Street and Sardosa Bar are the reasons to make the trip.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

D-Edge — A mixed floor with a long-standing queer presence. There is no dedicated gay night, but the room is reliably welcoming.

Clash Club — Younger and more varied, with themed parties that are sometimes explicitly LGBTQ+. Check the venue’s Instagram for tonight’s billing.

Vila Madalena bars — Broadly LGBTQ+ friendly without any dedicated gay bars. Aspicuelta is comfortable on any night.

Money & How Paying Works Dollar figures in this guide use the Banco Central PTAX close of 6 August 2026, R$5.1014 to US$1. Menu and ticket prices attributed to a named venue come from that venue; club door and drink figures are typical ranges rather than quoted tariffs. Comanda card system: clubs such as D-Edge give you a card on entry, charge drinks to it, and settle the total as you leave. Losing it costs a fixed penalty. Couvert artístico is common at seated music venues and is not optional once it is on your bill. Expect roughly R$30–R$60 (US$5.88–US$11.76) where it applies. Cards and Pix are taken almost everywhere, but a few small bars remain cash-only. Carry R$100–R$200 (US$19.60–US$39.20) as a fallback. Tipping: 10 per cent is standard and usually appears on the bill as ‘serviço’. Anything beyond it is optional.

Getting Home Safe

The metro shuts around midnight on a Friday and reopens early on Saturday morning. If you want to use it, leave the venue by 11.30 pm.

99 and Uber both work well across the city. Barra Funda to Paulista after midnight typically runs R$25–R$40 (US$4.90–US$7.84), with surge worst between 2 am and 4 am.

Wait for your car inside the venue or in a lit doorway. Do not stand on an empty street with your phone out.

Avenida Paulista is walkable at any hour. In the centre after dark, move venue to venue by ride-share rather than on foot.

Barra Funda’s club strip is fine, but the streets around it are empty and industrial. Stay on the main drag and go door to door.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a comanda card?

It is a plastic card handed to you at the door of a club. You charge drinks to it through the night and pay the total on the way out; losing it means paying a fixed penalty instead.

Is it safe to walk at night?

On Avenida Paulista, yes, and it stays busy until late. In Vila Madalena stick to the main bar streets, and everywhere else take a ride-share between venues.

Do I need to book ahead?

For seated rooms such as Casa de Francisca and Blue Note, yes, and tonight both are small enough to sell out. For clubs, buy online to skip the queue; for bars, just walk in.

Sources: Ao Vivo (São Paulo listings, 3–9 August 2026), flipei.org, Parque Ibirapuera, Caderno Pop (Música no Vão), Guia Caju (Bar Sardosa), Diário do Grande ABC (PTAX, 6 August 2026)

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 7, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Carioca da Gema A small, brick-walled samba house that has been booking live bands on Avenida Mem de Sá since 2000. Doors open at 6.30 pm on Fridays, the happy-hour set starts at 7 pm and the main band at 9.30 pm.

Tonight at a Glance — Pedra do Sal Free open-air roda de samba in Saúde, from about 6 pm; the same roda also runs on Mondays — Carioca da Gema Lapa’s classic samba house; door charge R$35 (US$6.86) on Fridays, main band at 9.30 pm — Rio Scenarium Antique-furnished club on Rua do Lavradio, open 7 pm to 2 am on Fridays; live Brazilian music across three floors — Trapiche Gamboa Long-running port-district samba house; no programme published for tonight, so ring ahead before you travel — Lapa’s street bars Rua do Lavradio and Avenida Mem de Sá fill up from about 9 pm; no cover, no booking, no plan required

Rio’s Friday does not depend on one-off bookings, and that is the point. The weekly samba circuit through Saúde, Lapa and the old port district runs whatever else is or is not on.

Pavement tables outside bars on a Rio de Janeiro street at night. File photograph, not taken tonight. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Circuit: When to Go Where

6 pm – Head to Pedra do Sal as the roda starts. It is free and outdoors, the musicians set up on the stone steps, and the crowd spreads into the surrounding streets.

8 pm – Beer and caipirinhas from the vendors around the largo, most of them cash-only. Expect roughly R$8–R$10 (US$1.57–US$1.96) for a large beer and R$15–R$20 (US$2.94–US$3.92) for a caipirinha.

9.30 pm – Short taxi or rideshare to Carioca da Gema in Lapa for the main band. The door is R$35 (US$6.86) on Fridays and Saturdays, R$30 (US$5.88) from Tuesday to Thursday.

Midnight – Walk down Rua do Lavradio to Rio Scenarium, three floors of antique-strewn dance floors. The house closes at 2 am on Fridays, so this is a late stop rather than an all-nighter.

After 1 am – If Trapiche Gamboa has a band on, the old port warehouse is the best dancing in the city. No programme for tonight has been published.

Sunrise – Recover with an água de coco at Posto 9 in Ipanema. The beach kiosks along Leme and Copacabana open early, though hours vary and none of them advertise a fixed time.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — Friday is the strongest samba night of the week: a free street roda in Saúde and live-band houses in Lapa and the port district. This is the working circuit, not a tourist show. Where: Pedra do Sal, Carioca da Gema, Rio Scenarium, Trapiche Gamboa

Gafieira and choro — Rio Scenarium programmes samba, gafieira and choro across its three floors from Wednesday to Saturday. The upper floors are quieter if you want to hear the band rather than dance to it. Where: Rio Scenarium

MPB — Carioca da Gema books singers rather than cover bands, on a small stage in a room that holds a couple of hundred people. The happy-hour slot at 7 pm is voice and guitar; the main set at 9.30 pm is a full band. Where: Carioca da Gema

Electronic — Thin tonight. Rio’s electronic scene runs on one-off warehouse and beach parties that cluster on Saturdays, and neither Circo Voador nor Fundição Progresso lists a Friday event this week. Where: check Circo Voador and Fundição Progresso listings before travelling

Bossa nova and choro — Bip Bip in Copacabana is the city’s smallest and best-loved jam room, but its regular nights are Tuesday, Wednesday and Sunday rather than Friday. Worth knowing about for the rest of your stay. Where: Bip Bip, Copacabana

Theatre and high culture — Nothing on tonight, but two things are worth booking now. Florian Zeller’s “O Filho” opens on 13 August at the Teatro Fernanda Montenegro in the Copacabana Palace, with Gabriel Braga Nunes and Maria Flor; the Theatro Municipal’s ballet stages “O Corsário” from 20 August. Where: Teatro Fernanda Montenegro, Theatro Municipal

Pick Your Night

Date night: Dinner in Santa Teresa, then a table for two at Carioca da Gema for the 9.30 pm band. Book the restaurant; the samba house does not take reservations after 9 pm.

Solo and safe: Start at Pedra do Sal, where the crowd is open and you can stand with a beer and listen. Move to Rio Scenarium later; its multi-floor layout makes arriving alone feel unremarkable.

Dance till late: Rio Scenarium until it closes at 2 am, then Trapiche Gamboa if it has a band on. Nothing in Lapa reliably runs past about 3 am on a winter Friday, so plan your ride home rather than assuming a sunrise.

Meet locals: Pedra do Sal, without question. The Friday roda is a neighbourhood event first and a tourist attraction second, and Cariocas are generous with translations.

Chill and conversation: A corner table at a Botafogo bar such as Comuna or Hocus Pocus. Quieter than Lapa, closer to Zona Sul, and you can actually hear each other.

Where to Go

Pedra do Sal — Saúde A quilombo site in the old port district, recognised as Rio cultural heritage, where a free roda de samba plays on the stone steps. The crowd is young, largely local, and spills across the largo and into the surrounding streets. Tonight: Free open-air roda de samba from about 6 pm. No cover, no booking, outdoors. Best time: Mondays and Fridays are the two traditional roda nights; Riotur lists music at the site from Thursday to Sunday as well. Arrive by 7 pm for a spot near the musicians. Cost: Free entry. Street vendors sell beer and caipirinhas; expect roughly R$8–R$10 (US$1.57–US$1.96) and R$15–R$20 (US$2.94–US$3.92). Bring cash. Address: Largo João da Baiana, off Rua Argemiro Bulcão, Saúde Instagram: @pedradosaloficial Getting there: VLT or metro to the Praça Mauá area, then a short walk. A rideshare from Zona Sul is around R$30 (US$5.88) outside surge hours. Good to know: No booking and nowhere to sit. Wear shoes you can stand on cobbles in, and keep your phone in a front pocket.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa A samba and choro house that has been running on Avenida Mem de Sá since 2000, in one of the old townhouses that gave Lapa its second life. Small stage, exposed brick, and a crowd that mixes regulars, music students and visitors who did their homework. Tonight: Doors 6.30 pm, happy-hour voice-and-guitar set at 7 pm, main band at 9.30 pm. The house has not published tonight’s act; check its Instagram on the day. Best time: Fridays and Saturdays for the full band. Tables are held only until 9 pm, so arrive before then if you want to sit. Cost: Door charge R$35 (US$6.86) on Fridays, Saturdays and the eve of a public holiday; R$30 (US$5.88) Tuesday to Thursday. Beer and cocktails on top; expect roughly R$12–R$16 (US$2.35–US$3.14) for a beer and R$22–R$28 (US$4.31–US$5.49) for a caipirinha. Address: Av. Mem de Sá, 79, Lapa/Centro Phone: +55 21 2221-0043 Instagram: @cariocadagema Website: barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then a 10-minute walk. Rideshare pickup on Avenida Mem de Sá is busy and well lit. Good to know: Tables can be reserved through the venue’s website. Smart-casual is plenty.

Rio Scenarium — Centro/Lapa Seven rooms over three floors, furnished out of an antiques dealer’s warehouse, with a stated capacity of 2,000. The crowd is more dressed-up and more international than the street rodas, and the sound is the best in Lapa. Tonight: Open 7 pm to 2 am. Live Brazilian music across the floors; the house does not publish a per-night line-up in advance. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday only — the house is closed on Sundays, Mondays and Tuesdays. Saturday adds a feijoada session from noon to 6 pm. Cost: Entry is ticketed and the price varies by night; buy through the venue’s ticket page rather than relying on a quoted figure. Drinks are charged to a comanda tab settled on the way out. Address: Rua do Lavradio, 20, Centro Phone: +55 21 3147-9000 Instagram: @rioscenarium Website: rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then a five-minute walk down Rua do Lavradio. The street is lively and policed on Friday nights. Good to know: Book a table online to skip the queue. Dress smart-casual.

Trapiche Gamboa — Saúde/Gamboa A three-storey 1860s townhouse near Pedra do Sal, open since 2004 and one of the few rooms in the city where the whole floor dances. Less touristed than Rio Scenarium and considerably less polished. Tonight: No programme has been published for tonight and the listings we can find are years out of date. Ring the house on +55 21 2516-0868 before you travel. Best time: Friday and Saturday have historically been the main samba nights, with doors from about 7.30 pm and the band on around 10.30 pm. Closing time is variously reported between 1 am and 3 am. Cost: A couvert is charged at the door and has historically been modest by Lapa standards. We could not confirm a current figure; ask when you call. Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral, 155, Saúde Phone: +55 21 2516-0868 Instagram: @trapichegamboa Getting there: Rideshare is the sensible route from Zona Sul, roughly R$20–R$30 (US$3.92–US$5.88) from Copacabana. The surrounding streets are industrial and empty at night. Good to know: Over-18s only on Fridays and Saturdays. Order your ride home from inside the building.

Circo Voador — Lapa The tent-roofed concert hall under the Arcos da Lapa, capacity around 3,000, and the venue most Rio bands want to graduate to. Standing floor, narrow mezzanine, no air conditioning. Tonight: No event listed for tonight. Check the venue’s own calendar before making the trip. Best time: The house runs Wednesday to Sunday. Doors are usually two hours before the headliner; get in between 8 pm and 9 pm to avoid the box-office queue. Cost: Tickets typically run R$60–R$200 (US$11.76–US$39.20) depending on the act. Drinks are on a comanda card; the box office does not always take Pix. Address: Rua dos Arcos s/n, Lapa Phone: +55 21 2533-0354 Instagram: @circo_voador Website: circovoador.com.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then about 12 minutes on foot through the Arcos. Traffic on Rua dos Arcos seizes up after 11 pm, so get dropped on Rua do Lavradio. Good to know: Over-18s on most nights. Buy online; shows sell out.

Theatro Municipal — Centro (Cinelândia) Rio’s gilded opera house, modelled on the Palais Garnier and still the city’s grandest room. Opera, ballet, classical concerts and the occasional popular-music special. Tonight: Nothing scheduled. The house is dark this evening. Best time: The next run is the company ballet’s “O Corsário”, staged from 20 August, with evening performances at 7 pm and matinees at 5 pm and 2 pm on selected dates. Book ahead. Cost: Varies by production and seat. Prices are published with each run on the theatre’s own site. Address: Praça Floriano s/n, Cinelândia, Centro Phone: +55 21 2332-9191 Instagram: @theatromunicipalrj Website: theatromunicipal.rj.gov.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia; the station exit faces the theatre steps. Rideshare pickup on Praça Floriano is well lit. Good to know: Smart dress, black tie for galas. Arrive 30 minutes early for the foyer.

Bip Bip — Copacabana A Copacabana institution the size of a front room, where musicians sit around a table and play unamplified. No stage, no PA, and famously little tolerance for talking over the music. Tonight: No Friday session is advertised. Its regular nights are choro on Tuesdays, bossa nova on Wednesdays and samba on Sundays. Best time: Wednesday bossa nova from about 7 pm. There are only a handful of seats, so early is the only way. Cost: No cover; you pay for what you drink and the musicians pass a hat. Expect roughly R$8–R$12 (US$1.57–US$2.35) for a beer, cash only. Address: Rua Almirante Gonçalves, 50, Copacabana Getting there: Metro to Siqueira Campos or Cantagalo, then about 10 minutes on foot. Easy rideshare drop-off on the street outside. Good to know: No booking and no dress code. Take cash; the bar has never taken cards.

Fundição Progresso — Lapa A cavernous former foundry next door to Circo Voador, used for touring acts, club nights and cultural programming. When it is full it is one of the best rooms in Rio; when it is empty it is a shed. Tonight: Nothing listed. The venue’s published calendar currently shows only a handful of dated shows, none of them this week. Best time: Whenever it has a booking, which is usually a Friday or Saturday. The mezzanine has good sightlines and its own bar. Cost: Ticket prices are set per show and published with each announcement. Drinks go on a comanda card. Address: Rua dos Arcos, 24, Lapa Phone: +55 21 2220-5070 Instagram: @fundicaoprogresso Website: fundicaoprogresso.com.br Getting there: Metro to Cinelândia, then about 12 minutes on foot. The Arcos area stays busy on event nights and empties fast when there is nothing on. Good to know: Buy online where possible. No strict dress code.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: Rio’s bohemian heart, loud and chaotic, with samba halls along Avenida Mem de Sá and Rua do Lavradio under the Arcos. Everyone from students to old-school malandros.

Saúde and Gamboa: The old port district, cobbled and half-restored, with Pedra do Sal at its centre. Grittier and more local than Lapa, and quiet the moment the music stops.

Copacabana: Beachfront classic with old botecos, the tiny Bip Bip jam room, and a steady tourist crowd. Safe and walkable if you stay on the main drags.

Centro and Cinelândia: Belle Époque facades and the Theatro Municipal, busy by day and quiet at night except around the cultural venues. Good for a dress-up evening.

Santa Teresa: Hillside arts enclave with bohemian restaurants and views over the bay. Perfect for a sunset drink before you drop down into Lapa.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Rua Farme de Amoedo, Ipanema — The centre of gay Rio by day, and the bars around the street draw a mixed, friendly crowd on Friday nights. Nothing here needs booking; walk the block and pick a table.

Lapa — The samba houses are not gay venues but are entirely unbothered, and the street crowd on Mem de Sá is as mixed as Rio gets. One-off parties are announced on Instagram rather than in listings, so check on the day.

Money & How Paying Works Dollar figures in this guide use the Banco Central PTAX close of 6 August 2026, R$5.1014 to US$1. Door charges quoted against a named venue come from that venue; drink prices are typical ranges for the neighbourhood, not quoted tariffs. Comanda card system: the bigger venues give you a card on which drinks are tallied, and you settle at the cash desk on the way out. Do not lose it, as the penalty for a lost comanda is set high on purpose. Couvert artístico: a per-head music charge, either added to your bill at the table or built into the door price. On a ticket it will say ‘couvert artístico incluso’. Cash versus card: Pix is now the default across Rio and cards are widely taken, but the street vendors at Pedra do Sal and old-school botecos including Bip Bip are cash-only. Carry R$100–R$150 (US$19.60–US$29.40) in small notes. Tipping: 10 per cent service is almost always printed on the bill as ‘serviço’. You can round up, but nothing further is expected.

Getting Home Safe

The metro runs late on Friday nights but not all night. If you are still in Lapa or Centro after midnight, plan on a rideshare or a taxi rather than the train.

99 and Uber are both reliable here. Pickup in Lapa is safest on the main avenues — Avenida Mem de Sá, Rua do Lavradio, Praça Floriano — where the lighting and foot traffic are good.

Late-night surge: between 1 am and 4 am, a ride from Lapa to Zona Sul typically runs R$25–R$45 (US$4.90–US$8.82). Prices spike when the big venues empty at once, so walk two blocks and order from a quieter corner.

Lapa is busy and generally fine on a Friday, but stick to the main streets and avoid the stairways up to Santa Teresa on foot after midnight. Pickpocketing in a crowd is the realistic risk; phone in a front pocket.

The port district around Trapiche Gamboa is industrial and empties out completely at night. Go straight from the venue to a pre-ordered car and do not go looking for an after-party on foot.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do I wear to a samba club?

Smart-casual works almost everywhere: closed shoes rather than flip-flops, jeans or chinos, a shirt or a clean t-shirt. Skip high heels for Lapa’s cobblestones; wedges or flats are the sensible choice.

Is it OK to go out alone?

Yes, and Rio is easier than most big cities for it. At Pedra do Sal the crowd is communal and open, and at a table in Carioca da Gema you may well be adopted by the couple next to you.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not much, but a little goes a long way: ‘uma cerveja, por favor’, ‘quanto custa?’ and ‘obrigado’ or ‘obrigada’ will carry you through the night. At Pedra do Sal and the smaller samba clubs very few people speak fluent English.

Sources: barcariocadagema.com.br, rioscenarium.com.br, Riotur, Visit Rio, fundicaoprogresso.com.br, Diário do Grande ABC (PTAX, 6 August 2026)

World.title: Half of Brazil’s Municipalities No Longer Have a Bank Branch
World.content:
Brazil · Banking

Key Facts The gap. 2,649 Brazilian municipalities — 48 percent of the country — have no in-person bank service at all, affecting 19.7 million people.

2,649 Brazilian municipalities — 48 percent of the country — have no in-person bank service at all, affecting 19.7 million people. The closures. The branch network has shrunk 42 percent since 2015, from 22,928 branches to 14,381. That is roughly thirty closures a week.

The branch network has shrunk 42 percent since 2015, from 22,928 branches to 14,381. That is roughly thirty closures a week. Last one out. 638 municipalities have lost their final branch since 2015, leaving about 6.9 million people with none.

638 municipalities have lost their final branch since 2015, leaving about 6.9 million people with none. The jobs. Santander cut 6,100 posts in a year, Itaú 4,600 and Bradesco 3,000 — nearly 14,000 between them, with Banco do Brasil shedding a further 1,400.

Santander cut 6,100 posts in a year, Itaú 4,600 and Bradesco 3,000 — nearly 14,000 between them, with Banco do Brasil shedding a further 1,400. What replaced them. Contracts with banking correspondents rose 49 percent between 2015 and 2025.

Contracts with banking correspondents rose 49 percent between 2015 and 2025. The profits. The five largest banks made 124 billion reais (about US$24.5 billion) in 2025.

Brazil’s branch network has shrunk 42 percent since 2015, and 2,649 municipalities — nearly half the country — now have no in-person bank at all.

Brazil bank branches are disappearing at about thirty a week, and the arithmetic has reached a point worth stating plainly: 2,649 municipalities, 48 percent of the country, no longer have any in-person banking service. That is 19.7 million people. Six hundred and thirty-eight of those towns lost their last branch after 2015.

Brazil had 22,928 bank branches in 2015. By 2025 it had 14,381. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where Brazil bank branches have gone

The numbers come from Dieese, the union-linked research institute, working from central bank data, and they were put to the banking federation at a national bargaining session in July. Fenaban declined to suspend the closures.

Between 2015 and May 2026 the network shrank by 9,500 branches, or 42 percent. In the most recent comparable year the five largest banks closed 1,345 between them: Santander 579, Itaú 319, Bradesco 296, Caixa 138 and Banco do Brasil 13.

The employment side moved with it. Across the sector 93,300 net posts have gone since 2015. In the year to May 2026 the three big private banks shed nearly 14,000 between them. Of the posts eliminated since 2020, 25,500 — about 79 percent — were held by women, and women fell from 49 percent of the workforce to under 47 percent in a single year.

Half the country now banks without a bank

This is the number that should stop you: 2,649 municipalities, 48 percent of all of them, have no in-person banking service. That is 19.7 million people, roughly nine percent of Brazil’s population. Six hundred and thirty-eight towns have lost their last branch since 2015.

What has taken their place is not nothing, but it is not a branch either. Contracts with correspondentes bancários — lottery agents, shop counters, small retailers authorised to handle basic transactions — rose 49 percent over the decade. Credit cooperatives have expanded into the same gaps.

Juvandia Moreira, who heads the bank workers’ confederation, puts it this way: the work is not being eliminated, it is being transferred to correspondents, and that opens space for cooperatives in the areas the banks have abandoned. What a correspondent cannot do is resolve anything complicated.

The banks are not hiding why

Febraban’s own technology survey, published in June, records that 83 percent of all banking transactions in Brazil now happen through digital channels and 78 percent through mobile. Brazilians made 240.8 billion banking transactions in 2025, of which 187.5 billion were on a phone — up 11 percent in a year and 169 percent over five. Seventy-six percent of customers do more than four-fifths of their banking digitally.

The economics follow. The five largest banks made 124 billion reais (about US$24.5 billion) in 2025; the three big private ones made 87 billion reais (about US$17.2 billion) between them, up 16.4 percent. Bradesco’s efficiency ratio improved 2.8 points to 48.4 percent on exactly this kind of cost reduction.

The union’s counter-argument is not that digitisation is wrong but that fee income alone now covers around 150 percent of the banks’ payroll, and that the dismissals were carried out without the prior negotiation the courts have required. That argument is live and in litigation.

What it means if you live in Brazil

If you are in a state capital, very little. If you are not — the Bahian coast, the interior of Minas, most of the Northeast — the practical consequence is that anything requiring a physical branch means travelling. Opening an account, clearing a compliance block on a CPF, dealing with an inheritance or a court-ordered transfer: these are the things a lottery agent cannot fix.

The realistic answer for most foreign residents is a digital bank. Nubank, Inter, C6 and Mercado Pago all work without a branch, and 83 percent of the country already banks that way. The trade-off is worth knowing: some of them, Mercado Pago included, hold a payment-institution licence rather than a full banking licence, which changes the deposit protection you get.

If you are choosing where to live in Brazil and you are not in a capital, it is worth checking whether the town still has a branch before you sign a lease. Increasingly, the answer is no. This is general information, not financial advice.

World.title: Washington Fast-Tracks Military Cooperation With Colombia’s New Government — Nothing Signed Yet
World.content:
Colombia · Defence

Key Facts Nothing is signed. There is no treaty, memorandum or basing accord. What exists is planning, a Pentagon meeting and an official’s social-media post.

There is no treaty, memorandum or basing accord. What exists is planning, a Pentagon meeting and an official’s social-media post. The name. “Plan Patriota 2.0”, used by US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas Joseph Humire on 21 July after meeting Colombia’s incoming defence minister.

“Plan Patriota 2.0”, used by US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas Joseph Humire on 21 July after meeting Colombia’s incoming defence minister. What is discussed. Intelligence sharing, extradition, helicopters and counter-drone equipment, a regional training centre in Colombia, and a possible return to aerial coca spraying.

Intelligence sharing, extradition, helicopters and counter-drone equipment, a regional training centre in Colombia, and a possible return to aerial coca spraying. The money. US security assistance to Colombia fell from about US$400 million to roughly US$187 million in the first year of Trump’s second term.

US security assistance to Colombia fell from about US$400 million to roughly US$187 million in the first year of Trump’s second term. Still in place. Gustavo Petro, his family and former interior minister Armando Benedetti remain on the US sanctions list. Washington has not asked for that to be reconsidered.

Gustavo Petro, his family and former interior minister Armando Benedetti remain on the US sanctions list. Washington has not asked for that to be reconsidered. Who came today. Nine US officials at the inauguration, almost all security and counter-narcotics. Marco Rubio was not among them.

Washington and Colombia’s incoming government have been planning an expanded security partnership since July. Nothing has been signed, and the sanctions on Gustavo Petro are still in force.

US Colombia military cooperation is being rebuilt, and it is worth being precise about what that means today. There is no signed agreement. There is a Pentagon meeting in July, a name — “Plan Patriota 2.0” — used by a US official on social media, and reporting that planning began before Abelardo De La Espriella took office on Friday.

US security assistance to Colombia fell from about US$400 million to roughly US$187 million in the past year. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What US Colombia military cooperation actually amounts to right now

The reporting is real and the caution is warranted. The New York Times wrote on Friday, the day Abelardo De La Espriella was sworn in, that the Trump administration and the incoming Colombian government have been planning an expanded military, intelligence and counter-narcotics partnership. The planning began before the handover. The timetable for joint operations is undefined.

The hard, documented core is narrower than the headline suggests. On 21 July, Joseph Humire, the US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, posted that after meeting Colombia’s incoming defence leadership at the Pentagon the previous week, “we plan to take this partnership to new levels with Plan Patriot 2.0”. Present were vice-president-elect José Manuel Restrepo and defence minister-designate General Jorge Eduardo Mora López, who called it a new stage of cooperation, integration and joint action.

The State Department has said on the record that it is ready to support Colombia’s efforts to strengthen its security forces and defeat narco-terrorists. The Pentagon declined further comment. That is the whole documented record. No agreement has been published.

What is on the table

The elements under discussion, as reported, are: US intelligence sharing and support for Colombian operations against trafficking organisations; extradition of captured traffickers; replenishment of the helicopter fleet and counter-drone systems; a regional counter-narcotics and counter-terrorism training centre based in Colombia; and Colombia joining the inter-American coalition against drug cartels created in March, with Medellín designated as its regional seat.

The most consequential item is the possible return of aerial coca eradication, suspended in Colombia in 2015 over the health effects of glyphosate. Restarting it would mean rebuilding the logistics and clearing the legal restrictions that stopped it. Nobody has said it will happen.

Where this comes from

The relationship broke down badly under Gustavo Petro. In September 2025 the White House determined Colombia had failed demonstrably on counter-narcotics — the first decertification since 1997 — while issuing a waiver that preserved most assistance. In October the US Treasury placed Petro, his wife, his son and then interior minister Armando Benedetti on the sanctions list, and Trump announced an end to payments and subsidies.

As of mid-July, a US under secretary confirmed the White House has not asked for those sanctions to be reconsidered. They are still in force today.

One correction to the usual framing: cooperation never actually stopped. Petro continued intelligence sharing and counter-narcotics work with Washington throughout the rupture. What is being described is an acceleration, not a restart from zero.

What it means if you live in or invest in Colombia

For residents in Bogotá, Medellín or Cartagena, nothing here touches immigration, banking or property. The effect, if it materialises, is regional: more joint operations in the coca and trafficking corridors of Catatumbo, Cauca, Nariño, Putumayo and Chocó, with the road closures, checkpoints and airspace restrictions that come with them.

The caveat that matters is retaliation. A harder military line has historically produced urban responses. Police intercepted a bus carrying around 450 kilograms of explosives intended for military and police targets during inauguration week, which is the concrete illustration. Armed-group combatants have risen from about 13,000 in 2022 to roughly 27,000 in 2025.

For investors, the resolution of the Washington relationship removes the sharpest tail risk hanging over Colombian assets since October — the tariff threat and the sanctioning of a sitting president. That discount is plausibly reversing. But the sanctions themselves have not been lifted, so compliance screening for anyone with Colombian counterparties has not got easier yet. This is general information, not investment advice.

World.title: Procuraduría Freezes the SIC Fine Against Ecopetrol Hours Before Colombia’s Handover
World.content:
Colombia · Energy

Key Facts What happened. The Procuraduría sent an urgent letter ordering the competition regulator to answer its questions before ruling on a near-final sanction against Ecopetrol.

The Procuraduría sent an urgent letter ordering the competition regulator to answer its questions before ruling on a near-final sanction against Ecopetrol. When. The letter followed an inspection visit on 4 August and became public on 7 August — the morning of Colombia’s presidential handover.

The letter followed an inspection visit on 4 August and became public on 7 August — the morning of Colombia’s presidential handover. Who is charged. Ecopetrol and its subsidiaries Cenit and Ocensa. The helicopter operator Helistar is not.

Ecopetrol and its subsidiaries Cenit and Ocensa. The helicopter operator Helistar is not. The case. Six air-transport tenders between 2011 and 2023, worth more than 400,000 million pesos (about US$110 million), allegedly written to favour the incumbent.

Six air-transport tenders between 2011 and 2023, worth more than 400,000 million pesos (about US$110 million), allegedly written to favour the incumbent. What it does not do. This is not an injunction and it does not close the case. The file now waits on the regulator’s reply and an advisory committee opinion.

This is not an injunction and it does not close the case. The file now waits on the regulator’s reply and an advisory committee opinion. The consequence. If the answer does not arrive in time, the decision falls to the incoming government.

Colombia’s inspector general froze a near-final competition ruling against Ecopetrol hours before the government changed — leaving a nine-figure decision to the incoming administration.

The Ecopetrol SIC sanction was days from being issued. Then, on the morning Colombia changed governments, the Procuraduría made public an urgent letter ordering the competition regulator to answer its questions first — and warned that ruling without doing so would leave the decision open to being struck down in court.

What the Procuraduría actually did to the Ecopetrol SIC sanction

The instrument is an oficio urgente from Marcio Melgosa, the Procurador Delegado for preventive oversight of public functions, sent after his office carried out an inspection visit on Tuesday 4 August.

It does not suspend anything. What it does is require the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio to answer the Procuraduría’s questions before it issues its ruling. The warning attached is the point: ruling first would leave the act legally defective, open to annulment in court, with what the letter calls significant financial consequences for the state.

The file now waits on two things — the regulator’s reply, and the opinion of its advisory committee, which is mandatory but not binding. A source at the regulator told El Tiempo that if the reply does not come within what remains of Petro’s term, the decision passes to the incoming administration. On the morning Abelardo De La Espriella was sworn in, that is the whole story.

The case itself

The Superintendencia’s delegate for competition, Francisco Melo Rodríguez, had recommended a finding of liability. The head of the regulator is Cielo Rusinque.

The allegation covers six tenders for air transport to oilfields between 2011 and 2023, worth more than 400,000 million pesos, roughly US$110 million. The claim is that the terms were written so only the incumbent could win: an aircraft-age ceiling that moved from five years to fifteen, then ten, then twenty, dropped in 2023 as having no legal basis; and a requirement that aircraft already be in Colombia, armoured and equipped.

Internal messages from 2021 are quoted in the file. One official proposed framing a requirement around security; another suggested a fifteen-year age cap because with it “there would only be one bidder”.

Ecopetrol has raised two procedural objections. It says the regulator’s company visits were carried out under a preliminary enquiry rather than a formal investigation, and that it ordered forensic imaging of a mobile device without a judicial order, under threat of fines.

A company without a permanent chief executive

The timing lands on an organisation already in transition. Ricardo Roa Barragán left definitively on 30 July after a period of unpaid leave, and Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra has been interim chief executive since 31 July while the board runs a selection process.

The board changed the same day. Luis Felipe Henao Cardona took the chair on 31 July, and De La Espriella has already named Jorge Mario Velásquez as an incoming board member.

The underlying numbers are strong. Second-quarter revenue was 40.2 trillion pesos (about US$11.1 billion) and net income 6.1 trillion (about US$1.7 billion), up 235 percent, with Brent averaging US$96.7 a barrel against US$66.7 a year earlier.

One number worth reading carefully. Ecopetrol’s 2026 plan, approved last November, expected to hold lifting cost below US$12 a barrel. First-half lifting cost fell 3 percent in pesos, to 47,249 pesos a barrel — but in dollars the second quarter came in at US$13.68, up 14.3 percent. The plan assumed 4,050 pesos to the dollar; the peso has been trading nearer 3,613. It is the exchange rate breaking that target, not the cost of pumping oil.

What it means if you hold Colombian assets

Ecopetrol is the largest weight in the COLCAP and a core holding in most Colombian pension portfolios. Two things changed this week: a competition case carrying a nine-figure potential fine has been pushed past the handover, and the company enters a new administration without a permanent chief executive.

For residents, the practical line is the exchange rate rather than the lawsuit. A peso near 3,613 makes Ecopetrol’s dollar costs look worse and makes your dollar income buy less in Bogotá.

World.content:

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief for August 7: American payrolls fell 23,000 and a summer of job gains was revised away, shares rose to near a record anyway, and Washington moved to redefine birthright citizenship.

Rio Times · USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 7

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 7 — Key Facts —Payrolls fall American employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, against forecasts of an 83,000 gain. —A summer revised away May and June were cut by a combined 103,000 jobs, with May reduced from 129,000 to 63,000. —Participation slides The share of Americans working or looking for work fell to 61.4%, the lowest in over five years. —Shares rise anyway By early afternoon the S&P 500 was up about 0.5% and the Nasdaq 1.1%, after both closed lower on Thursday. —Citizenship orders President Trump signed two executive orders narrowing who is born a United States citizen, which lawyers expect to be challenged in court. —Canada hires Canada added 75,000 jobs in July against forecasts of 15,000, and unemployment fell to 6.4%, a two-year low.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 7 — America received three messages on Friday morning, and none of them agreed with the others.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 7. (Photo internet reproduction)

The data said weakness, the markets said records, and Washington spent the day arguing about who is born American.

United States – The Summer That Was Revised Away

Jobs lost, and months rewritten

American employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, where economists had expected a gain of 83,000. Worse, May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000, with May falling from 129,000 to 63,000.

Private employers added 30,000 posts, well below the 78,000 expected, while government shed 53,000. Retail and hospitality were weak and healthcare grew more slowly than usual.

The quiet version of failure

The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% from 4.2%, which sounds like relief and is not. It fell because the share of Americans working or looking for work dropped to 61.4% from 61.5%, the lowest in more than five years.

This is not a country being fired, it is a country quietly giving up the search. Temporary layoffs rose by 153,000 to 921,000, and hourly pay rose just 0.1% on the month, taking annual growth to 3.2%, the weakest since May 2021.

United States – Washington Rewrites Who Is American

Two orders on birthright citizenship

President Trump signed two executive orders narrowing who is born a United States citizen. The first draws on a Supreme Court ruling from 30 June to widen the categories of people whose children would not qualify, including those the administration classes as alien enemies, members of foreign terrorist organisations and people acting for foreign governments.

A second order targets what the White House calls birth tourism. The American Civil Liberties Union responded that birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution and cannot be altered by executive order.

The louder argument

Trump called the June ruling a very unfortunate decision, saying the constitutional guarantee had been written for the children of freed slaves. Legal challenges are considered certain.

On the morning its labour market shrank, the country’s loudest argument was not about work but about belonging. Those two conversations were held in the same city and did not touch.

Markets – Relief at Bad News

Shares up, yields down

The market read the weak report as a reason to buy. By early afternoon in New York the S&P 500 was up about 0.5%, the Nasdaq 1.1% and the Dow 0.3%, with technology doing the heavy lifting and Nvidia up 1.9%.

Government borrowing costs fell, the ten-year yield to 4.654% and the two-year to 4.204%, its lowest since 17 July. Every major index was heading for a weekly gain, having closed lower on Thursday with the S&P at 7,709.96.

A central bank with no good option

What the report means for interest rates is genuinely disputed. One reading has traders paring back bets on a September increase, while another shows the probability of a September cut falling to 42% from 55% the day before, and Wall Street still expects at least one rise by year-end.

The Federal Reserve held rates last week on a nine to three vote, and the split has not healed. One investment chief called the combination of shrinking employment and stubborn inflation a conundrum, which is the polite word for it.

The economy said it was weakening, the market answered by climbing toward a record, and the government spent the morning debating who is born American — three conversations in one country, none of them listening to the others.

Canada – Competence Without Permission to Enjoy It

Five times the forecast

Canada added 75,000 jobs in July, where economists polled by Reuters had expected 15,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 6.4%, its lowest in two years, and the country is now up 181,000 jobs since April.

Wholesale and retail added 21,000 posts, finance and property 18,000, and professional services 17,000. Public administration lost 15,000 and agriculture 9,600.

A country that will not let itself celebrate

The reaction from Canadian economists was immediate and deflating. One called the labour market not yet strong, noting unemployment is still higher than normal and wage growth slowed, while another said the road to recovery remains long.

They are right that 6.4% remains well above the American 4.1%, and one month settles nothing. But the mood is also the habit of a country that has learned not to look pleased too early.

United States – Courts, Committees and Regulators

A nomination in trouble

Senator Lisa Murkowski said she will vote against Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department. His confirmation now turns on Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, whom the president helped defeat in a primary.

The Senate Homeland Security Committee voted eight to five along party lines to hold Dr Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress. He had declined to answer members’ questions at a hearing last week.

A fine and a deregulation

A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay a further 567 million dollars in a child safety case, ruling that most of the money should fund treatment services for young people. Separately, the Federal Communications Commission voted to lift limits on how many television stations a single company may own.

Corporate results moved violently in both directions. The Trade Desk fell 18.1% and Seagate 8%, while the healthcare platform Doximity jumped 81% after beating expectations and raising its outlook, and the software group Atlassian rose 32.1%.

Canada – A Calendar Kept, a Deadline Approaching

By-elections at the end of the month

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called by-elections for 31 August, in seats including Beaches–East York and Chicoutimi–Le Fjord. It is the ordinary business of a country carrying on with its own schedule.

Ottawa has spent the summer reacting to decisions taken in Washington. Setting its own dates is a small assertion of normality.

Twelve days to the tariff

A 50% United States tariff on roughly 20 billion dollars of Canadian goods takes effect on 19 August. That is twelve days after a jobs report that beat every forecast.

The second quarter is estimated to have grown at an annual rate of 3.4%, which is the strongest evidence yet that the economy has steadied. Whether it survives contact with the tariff is the only question that matters here.

The Bigger Picture Friday delivered three American messages that refused to agree. Employers cut 23,000 jobs and a further 103,000 were revised out of May and June, while participation fell to a five-year low of 61.4%, which is what a country looks like when people stop searching rather than when they are fired. The market answered by rising through the session, reading weak employment as a reason to expect cheaper money. And the government spent the same morning signing orders on who is born a United States citizen, a debate about belonging held alongside a debate about work that never met it. Canada had the simpler day and trusted it less. It added 75,000 jobs against a forecast of 15,000, cut unemployment to a two-year low, and its own economists spent the afternoon explaining why nobody should get excited, with a 50% tariff twelve days away.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief August 7: What We Are Watching

Coming weeks – Legal challenges to the two executive orders on birthright citizenship.

19 August – The 50% United States tariff on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods takes effect.

31 August – Canadian by-elections, including Beaches–East York and Chicoutimi–Le Fjord.

September – The Federal Reserve meeting, where the committee remains split three ways.

Coming weeks – Whether Senator Cassidy’s vote decides the Blanche nomination.

Ongoing – Whether American participation recovers or the retreat from the labour force continues.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the July United States jobs report show?

Nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 in July against expectations of an 83,000 gain, while May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000, taking May from 129,000 to 63,000 and June from 57,000 to 20,000. The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, but the labour force participation rate fell to 61.4%, its lowest in more than five years, and annual wage growth slowed to 3.2%, the weakest since May 2021.

Why did share prices rise on a weak jobs report?

Investors read a softer labour market as reducing the pressure for higher interest rates, and by early afternoon in New York the S&P 500 was up about 0.5% and the Nasdaq 1.1%, while the two-year Treasury yield fell to 4.204%, its lowest since 17 July. The implication for Federal Reserve policy is contested, with some reporting traders paring bets on a September increase and other data showing the probability of a September cut falling to 42% from 55% the previous day.

What do the new executive orders on birthright citizenship do?

President Trump signed two orders narrowing who is born a United States citizen, the first drawing on a Supreme Court ruling of 30 June to widen the categories of people whose children would be ineligible, including those the administration classes as alien enemies, members of foreign terrorist organisations and people acting on behalf of foreign governments, and the second targeting what the White House calls birth tourism. The American Civil Liberties Union said birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution and cannot be changed by executive order, and legal challenges are widely expected.

How strong was Canada’s July employment report?

Statistics Canada reported 75,000 new jobs in July against a Reuters poll forecast of 15,000, split between full- and part-time work, with unemployment falling to 6.4%, its lowest in two years, and employment up 181,000 since April. Canadian economists were cautious nonetheless, noting that the rate remains well above the American 4.1% and that wage growth slowed, with a 50% United States tariff on roughly 20 billion dollars of Canadian goods due to take effect on 19 August.

World.title: Argentina’s Senate Strips the Foreign Land Chapter — the 15% Cap Stays
World.content:
Argentina · Property

Key Facts What passed. The private-property inviolability bill cleared the Senate 37–33 in the early hours of 7 August, after a session that ran nearly twelve hours.

The private-property inviolability bill cleared the Senate 37–33 in the early hours of 7 August, after a session that ran nearly twelve hours. What was cut. Two chapters were removed before the vote: foreign purchases of rural land, and amendments to the fire-management law.

Two chapters were removed before the vote: foreign purchases of rural land, and amendments to the fire-management law. The land cap. The plan to lift the foreign ownership ceiling from 15 to 25 percent is gone from this text. Ley 26.737 stands unchanged.

The plan to lift the foreign ownership ceiling from 15 to 25 percent is gone from this text. Ley 26.737 stands unchanged. Who killed it. Allied governors withdrew support at the last minute. The government pulled the chapter on 5 August to save the session.

Allied governors withdrew support at the last minute. The government pulled the chapter on 5 August to save the session. Next stop. The Chamber of Deputies. It is not law.

The Chamber of Deputies. It is not law. Outside. Police cleared a protest at the Congress with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets on the evening of 6 August.

Argentina’s Senate passed the private-property bill 37–33 after the government cut the chapter that would have raised the foreign land cap to 25 percent. The 15 percent ceiling stands.

The Argentina foreign land cap is not moving. The government withdrew the chapter that would have raised the ceiling from 15 percent to 25 before the Senate voted in the early hours of Friday, and the remaining private-property bill passed 37 to 33. Ley 26.737 is unchanged, and every restriction a foreign buyer faced last month still applies.

Argentina’s 15 percent ceiling on foreign ownership of rural land survives, along with the 1,000-hectare cap and the water-frontage ban. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Argentina foreign land cap vote actually decided

The bill the Senate approved is the Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada, filed by the executive in March and promoted by Deregulation Minister Federico Sturzenegger. It amends the Civil and Commercial Code on evictions and expropriations. It passed 37 votes to 33 and now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

What it no longer contains is the part most foreign buyers were watching. Chapter III, on purchases of rural land by foreigners — the chapter that would have raised the national ceiling from 15 percent to 25 — was stripped out before the vote. So was Chapter IV, on the fire-management law, pulled during the debate itself.

The government withdrew the land chapter on 5 August, after allied governors pulled their support. That detail matters more than the vote count: the measure was not defeated by the opposition. It was abandoned because Milei’s own coalition would not carry it.

What still applies if you want to buy Argentine land

Ley 26.737, in force since December 2011, is untouched. Every limit in it still binds.

Foreigners may not hold more than 15 percent of rural land nationally, and the same 15 percent ceiling applies province by province and municipality by municipality. No single foreign nationality may hold more than 30 percent of that 15 percent. There is a 1,000-hectare cap in the núcleo zone.

Two other restrictions catch people out. You cannot title or possess rural land that contains or borders a large permanent body of water — which rules out a good deal of what buyers picture when they picture Patagonia. And rural property inside a border security zone requires prior consent from the Interior Ministry.

If you were told this was about to loosen, it was, and then it was not.

The night outside Congress

The march went ahead on 6 August even after the government announced it was dropping the land chapter. Unions, teachers’ organisations and social groups gathered at Plaza del Congreso under the slogan “the land is not for sale, not for burning, not for eviction”.

It was peaceful for around six hours. From about 5 p.m. the Federal Police cleared the area using tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets, with Gendarmería also deployed. Some protesters threw stones. The clashes ran more than two hours and spread through central Buenos Aires.

The counts do not agree. Outlets have reported between eight and more than twelve detentions, two people hit by rubber bullets, three officers injured and an unspecified number affected by gas. No official tally from the Security Ministry has been published.

What it means if you are buying or invested in Argentina

The practical answer is that nothing changed, and you should plan on that. If you are looking at farmland, a vineyard or an estancia, run the same checks you would have run last month: the national, provincial and municipal 15 percent ceilings, the nationality sub-limit, the water-frontage prohibition and the border-zone consent.

The political read is more useful than the legal one. Milei’s government has spent much of its term deregulating by decree and by omnibus bill, and it could not get a modest loosening of foreign land rules past its own allies. Rural land is a sovereignty question in Argentina in a way it is not in Uruguay or Paraguay, and that is unlikely to shift in this Congress.

For anyone weighing Argentine farmland against a neighbour, that is the datapoint. The rules are stable because they cannot be moved, not because anyone has decided they are right. This is general information, not legal or investment advice.

World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts The warning. Codelco chairman Bernardo Fontaine told a mining conference in Santiago on Thursday the company faces “four difficult years” in production.

Codelco chairman Bernardo Fontaine told a mining conference in Santiago on Thursday the company faces “four difficult years” in production. The plan. The five-year investment programme is US$34 billion, and Fontaine says there is no possibility of financing it given the debt.

The five-year investment programme is US$34 billion, and Fontaine says there is no possibility of financing it given the debt. The debt. Gross debt rose from US$17.6 billion in 2021 to US$26.3 billion in 2025. Net debt to EBITDA is 3.8 times, against roughly 0.7 for global peers.

Gross debt rose from US$17.6 billion in 2021 to US$26.3 billion in 2025. Net debt to EBITDA is 3.8 times, against roughly 0.7 for global peers. The trend. Comparing the last four years with the previous four: production down 16 percent, costs up 82 percent, liabilities up 50 percent — with copper 30 percent more expensive.

Comparing the last four years with the previous four: production down 16 percent, costs up 82 percent, liabilities up 50 percent — with copper 30 percent more expensive. Not for sale. Fontaine has ruled out a listing. What he wants is partners and minority stakes, and changes to the laws governing Codelco.

Fontaine has ruled out a listing. What he wants is partners and minority stakes, and changes to the laws governing Codelco. Meanwhile. Development at the Andes Norte project inside El Teniente was suspended on 4 August after six months of unusual seismic data.

Codelco’s chairman told a Santiago conference the state miner faces four difficult years and cannot finance its US$34 billion investment plan against nearly US$26 billion of debt.

The Codelco chairman has said out loud what the balance sheet already showed. Speaking in Santiago on Thursday, Bernardo Fontaine told a mining summit that the company’s US$34 billion five-year investment plan cannot be paid for, and that Chile should expect four difficult years of production while it is reworked.

Codelco’s gross debt rose from US$17.6 billion in 2021 to US$26.3 billion in 2025. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Codelco chairman said

Bernardo Fontaine spoke on Thursday at the third edition of Ecos de la Minería, a summit run by El Mercurio in Santiago. He did not soften it. “Codelco’s investment plan for these five years is US$34 billion, and there is no possibility of financing US$34 billion given the debt Codelco carries.”

And on what follows: “This plan is going to bring us four difficult years, difficult years in production.” Every scheduled investment is being re-evaluated, and only those that “effectively add value” will survive the review.

He set out four priorities: raise safety standards, maximise contributions to the state without taking on more debt, put the house in order with greater transparency, and strengthen sustainability. Fontaine was appointed by the Kast government and took the chair on 27 May. The chief executive, Jorge Gómez, has been in post since 13 July.

The numbers behind the warning

Fontaine’s case rests on a four-year comparison. Against the previous four years, production is down 16 percent, cost per tonne is up 82 percent and liabilities are up 50 percent — all achieved while copper was 30 percent more expensive.

Gross debt went from US$17.6 billion in 2021 to US$26.3 billion in 2025, and total accumulated debt now stands near US$26 billion. Net debt to EBITDA is 3.8 times; global peers sit around 0.7. Interest costs crossed US$1,022 million in the twelve months to the first quarter of this year.

His most pointed argument is about the money Codelco sends the treasury. Free cash flow after costs, expenses, investment and interest was negative across those four years despite US$7 billion in fiscal contributions — which, he argues, were financed by borrowing rather than earned.

What he is proposing, and what he is not

This is worth stating precisely, because it is easy to misreport. Fontaine has ruled out a public listing: “It is not in the plan.” Codelco stays entirely state-owned.

What he wants is to revise the rules and laws governing the company to make it easier to find partners, and to evaluate selling stakes Codelco holds in private companies. There is precedent: a June agreement with Anglo American over Andina and Los Bronces could add 2.7 million tonnes of copper over two decades. There has also been political friction over the opacity of minority-stake sales at El Abra and Quebrada Blanca.

The union is not persuaded. The Federación de Trabajadores del Cobre argues that every government has taken money out of Codelco without a long-term view, and rejects Fontaine’s dismissal of declining ore grade as a myth, saying falling grade is a principal cause of falling output. Its president says he will seek dialogue first, while leaving street action open.

El Teniente, and why this lands now

Four days before the speech, Codelco suspended development and construction at the Andes Norte project inside the El Teniente division near Rancagua. Six months of data had shown what the company called an emerging seismic phenomenon with characteristics different from the risks it has historically managed, linked to the greater depth of the works. At least four contractors and more than twenty contracts are affected.

The timing sharpens the point. Copper passed US$14,000 a tonne this week and Chile’s treasury stands to collect billions above budget, while the state miner that generates a large share of that money is telling the country it cannot fund its own future.

For anyone holding Chilean pesos, a Chilean pension or Chilean sovereign paper, this is a fiscal story rather than a mining one. Codelco pays the state directly, and a chairman saying out loud that the plan is unfinanceable is a signal about future transfers — and therefore about the deficit, the peso and the risk premium. This is general information, not investment advice.
