However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: Albanese returns to a gambling debate ready to catch fire
World.content:
Drugs, sex and multi-million dollar high rollers are themes more often featured in a Hollywood film than a parliamentary hearing, but this week's gambling inquiry has been the exception.

The explosive evidence heard at the opening of a two-day inquiry into Labor's proposed crackdown on wagering advertising has proved a watershed moment for the increasingly friendless bill.

The Greens and crossbenchers have long opposed the federal government's draft, but this week the Coalition also joined the chorus calling for significant changes.

Mere weeks ago, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used the last Question Time before the winter break to pour ice-cold water on the prospect of his government strengthening its legislation.

He implored parliament to pass the reforms, which curtail ads on television and radio at certain times, bans them in stadiums and on player uniforms, and require an online opt-out, but offered a bleak alternative to those who wanted more.

"If they don't (vote for the bill), then they do have the option of the status quo," he said.

Multiple senior Labor figures have this week referred journalists back to those same words even as the push for stronger measures has grown.

They insist that beyond carefully calibrated changes to improve existing measures in the bill, a wholesale rewrite dramatically expanding restrictions is not on Albanese's agenda.

Despite ministers publicly playing down the chances of Labor shelving the bill entirely, that confidence is more borne of the belief that the Coalition will buckle rather than the PM.

A sprinkling of Labor MPs have publicly called for the government's bill to go further — longtime advocate Mike Freelander, as well as Louise Miller-Frost and Alicia Payne among them — but even more are making noises privately that inducements must be addressed. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Few believe PM would go much further

It is unfortunate that Albanese has been on a rare week of leave at the same time the gambling debate has gone from simmering discontent to white-hot anger.

If Albanese returns to parliament on Tuesday armed with the same dismissive response to questions about tougher measures, his words will surely prove the match that sets the whole tinderbox alight.

But given he has been absent as the emotional drumbeats have ratcheted up the stakes over recent days, there is every chance that is exactly what will happen.

Albanese believes the government's bill gets the balance right, and while industry sources have told this column there appears to be growing consensus among stakeholders to tinker with a few elements, such as the current plan to ease TV ad restrictions at the seemingly arbitrary time of 8.30pm, few believe the PM would go much further.

There are also some inside Labor concerned that pushing too far on gambling would open the government to criticism about intruding on the lives of average Australians, particularly at a time when many people are flirting with the prospect of a One Nation protest vote.

Many in the Coalition party room are also far from enthusiastic about encroaching on personal freedoms.

But advocates remain confident Australians understand the difference between their right to place a bet and the desire of others to not be bombarded with promotions.

Loading...

A crunched timeline for platforms

There are also a number of technical and implementation concerns this column won't bore you with, but having read the bill's 136-page explanatory memorandum can say with some authority that the complaints from broadcasters about its complexity are valid.

In particular, the crunched timeline expecting the so-called online "triple lock" to be in place by January 1 seems almost impossible to meet.

It means streamers, social media and other platforms would have only months to prepare before they were required to restrict gambling ads to logged-in users who have verified they are aged over 18, while also giving every adult user a simple way to "opt out" entirely.

This difficulty, along with concerns many Australians won't know they could access an ad kill switch, has driven the push to invert the whole plan and instead require platforms to create an "opt in" system.

Proponents argue this would remove perennial libertarian concerns around age verification, such as the much-feared digital ID.

They also quietly acknowledge an "opt in" effectively amounts to a shadow advertising ban, for what would ever possess the majority of Australians to proactively 

It's this latter reality that makes the idea totally unpalatable to the wagering industry and sporting codes, and likely veers into the territory the government would consider a writ-large change to the bill.

Therefore a nonstarter.

Former NRL player and recovered gambling addict Luke Bateman told this week's inquiry that VIP account managers at wagering companies had previously offered him access to illegal drugs. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Bateman's surprising testimony

But a mere few months ago the idea of tackling what are generally referred to as "inducements" was also unthinkable.

Now the issue has been enshrined in Labor's national policy platform and has not only the backing of many inside the federal caucus, but the support of the Greens and Coalition.

A sprinkling of Labor MPs have publicly called for the government's bill to go further — longtime advocate Mike Freelander, as well as Louise Miller-Frost and Alicia Payne among them — but even more are making noises privately that inducements must be addressed.

Support on this has crystallised in the days since former NRL player and recovered gambling addict Luke Bateman told this week's inquiry that VIP account managers at wagering companies had previously offered him access to illegal drugs.

Alliance for Gambling Reform chief advocate Reverend Tim Costello also claimed he was aware of a gambling addict who was offered drugs and sex workers, while another witness suggested this type of relationship building between customers and betting company reps was common.

Gambling companies have strongly refuted those allegations and asked for evidence to investigate the matters.

Some have also taken aim at Bateman, who failed to tell the Senate inquiry he had previously worked for six months as an account manager for the now defunct Southern Cross Bet, shortly before going into rehab.

That Bateman ought to have disclosed his past employment in the interests of complete transparency is obvious, but not doing so at the time does not automatically negate his testimony.

Those who seized on the potential conflict to suggest otherwise, rather than confront the broader allegation that the friendly courting of high spending punters and widespread use of bonus bets and other incentives was problematic, hardly covered the industry in glory.

As they say in sport, play the ball not the man.

Loading

A united position could still buckle

But soon the only politics that will matter will be those playing out inside the parliament.

Communications Minister Anika Wells is currently waiting on amendments from the various opposing camps.

If Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young's public statements to date are anything to go by, it's hard to see the minor party reaching a compromise with Labor.

So too the suggestions from independent ACT Senator David Pocock, though his effective advocacy has certainly rattled Labor representatives in Canberra increasingly at risk of succumbing to a teal-style wave in the territory.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

Which leaves the Coalition, led on this issue by Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson, though with plenty of backbench commentary to complicate the matter.

Labor has privately bemoaned the disparate approach of the Coalition, with cynics speculating the most active proponents of change, like Liberal MP Simon Kennedy, will soon run into difficulty when his National Party colleagues turn their mind to the issue.

But at least some of the lack of cohesion behind the Coalition's position is because there has not yet been a joint party room meeting to discuss the bill as Labor only introduced it on the last day of parliament before a five-week break.

Still, even a united position could buckle under sustained pressure from broadcasters and sporting codes.

Both stakeholders have worked hard to convince the government of the risk the reforms pose to their viability.

Then there's the blame shifting argument.

But the prime minister should be wary of a change in wind direction since he first made the "status quo" threat, lest the flames turn and ignite his own side.

World.title: Bessent's to-do list reveals the unpredictable state of US economic policy
World.content:
When the Trump cabinet met at Camp David last week, the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, ostentatiously put a "to do" list in front of him, where it could be seen by journalists.

"To Do," it said. "Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5 — $10 bill."

Bessent used to make big currency bets for George Soros in his former life as a Wall Street banker, so knows full well the power of such signalling, even before you actually do anything.

Japan and the US later announced that they had jointly intervened to prop up the yen after it had fallen to a 40-year low.

Bessent portrayed the move as the act of an ally and partner of Japan. But the US also has a huge vested interest in a stronger yen.

Not only does a weak yen make Japan ultra-competitive against the US, it poses risks for the US Treasury bond market.

Japan is the largest holder of US Treasury bonds. If those bonds get sold off to support the currency, it puts their price down and, conversely, long term US interest rates up.

That's seen as one of the reasons why this particular intervention happened by the US selling euros, rather than US dollar, in exchange for yen.

Loading...

Warnings from the 1997 crisis

There is also a regional dimension to this story. A crash in the value of the yen was a contributing factor in the lead up to the Asian financial crisis in 1997.

A competitive devaluation wave across South East Asia now could be ugly.

The 1997 crisis was primarily a result of structural weaknesses like rapidly deregulated financial sectors and volatile short term capital flows.

There are new, different but also dangerous flaws in some Asian economies right now.

Most notably, South Korea — which should be enjoying the absolute economic sunshine of its dominance of the microchip and memory market — is instead flailing under share market volatility fed by over-leveraged investors, and also a share market too heavily dominated by a couple of the largest manufacturers of semiconductor technology, like Samsung.

The result has been a 40 per cent drop in the market's value in the space of just 27 days, leaving thousands of investors who had borrowed in order to invest facing financial oblivion.

The very volatility of the market — which so far in 2026 has had 33 days of movements of at least 5 per cent — has now made South Korea look like a highly risky investment.

Indonesia also has problems stemming from an overly ambitious and expensive government spending program.

Not all the news is bad out of Asia.

Vietnamese President To Lam will visit Australia in the next few days. (Reuters: Minh Hoang)

Vietnamese President To Lam will visit Australia in the next few days. His country has been the fastest growing economy in the region in the past couple of years with growth rates of around 8 per cent a year.

That's despite initially being one of the biggest targets of Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs last year.

Malaysia and Singapore — which were also in the firing line — are also booming in the way that South Korea should be, thanks to their big presence in IT hardware.

And that's despite them being among the most energy intense economies, and/or the biggest importers of oil and gas at a time when the Middle East conflict has both pushed up prices and cut supply of both commodities from the Gulf.

So the IMF has still been predicting that Asia will remain the main driver of global growth, with India and China accounting for about 70 per cent of that.

Perhaps more than any other part of the world, Asia is now riding the impact of all the biggest disruptions to the global economy.

There's the continuing uncertainty about energy supply; a boom in AI investment of such magnitude that central bankers discuss its potential to destabilise the financial system; and inflation.

Loading

Not just an energy price shock

It's not just inflation stemming from an energy price shock either.

The sudden escalation in government spending in the name of building defence capabilities is creating pressures around the world, prompting governments to massively expand their spending even when inflationary surges suggest they should be cutting back.

Japan is at the epicentre of these pressures. Once the stand-out growth economy, the "miracle" economy in the 1980s, it has struggled to find its way back from decades of deflation to growth, only to now find itself suffering from inflation partly driven by the fact its low interest rates have depressed its currency and delivered high prices and inflation across the economy.

While it is making a mark in robotics, it is not the leader in AI that competitors in the region have proved to be.

And it has been rapidly escalating its military spending amid the fears — shared by many US allies — of abandonment even as China projects its power into the region.

That all creates big tensions in economic policy between an expansionary fiscal (or government spending) policy and a monetary policy ambition which should see interest rates rising to curb inflation.

Loading...

The Bank of Japan has raised rates five times from their record lows, halving the differential with US interest rates.

But it now faces the difficulty of choosing between a path which raises rates to further reduce that differential — and hopefully stop further devaluation of the currency — but at the cost of killing off nascent growth, or stalling for time.

Unlike many other central banks, the BoJ's charter requires its actions to be mutually compatible with government policy.

Which is perhaps why it has instead been buying yen in the market to boost its value — an intervention which some analysts have estimated could have amounted to 13.8 trillion yen or $US87 billion over just two days.

So many conflicting economic signals usually demand some clear economic signals from central banks and economic ministers.

But if there is another trend at play just now it would seem to be a shift away from clear signals, and even from central bank independence.

The well-respected governor of Bank Indonesia Perry Warjiyo suddenly resigned last month in a move which unsettled markets at a time when the government's budget policies have kindled inflation.

There is much more disquiet, though, about just what is happening at the US Federal Reserve.

Kevin Warsh announced a new communications strategy which does not indicate where monetary policy might be heading, which has done nothing to settle financial markets. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Central bank's independence in question

Trump's appointment of Kevin Warsh as Fed chair came after his regular attacks on Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, who Trump regularly threatened to fire for not cutting interest rates fast enough.

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal last December, Trump said he wanted the Fed chair to consult with him on where to set interest rates.

"I'm a smart voice and should be listened to," he said.

Now this week the WSJ has reported that the president has repeatedly spoken with Warsh since he became chairman of the Fed three months ago.

That, and the fact that Warsh has announced a new communications strategy which does not indicate where monetary policy might be heading has done nothing to settle financial markets.

Confidence in central bank independence is not on a good trajectory now.

The decision to intervene in the yen was also marked by a lack of coordination with others.

The Financial Times reported on Friday that "Washington's sale of euros to boost the yen late last week blindsided the European Central Bank, with the US only informing its counterparts in Frankfurt after the historic currency intervention".

"Typically, the US would have been expected to use dollars in such an operation," the FT reported.

"Some senior ECB officials viewed the US decision to use euros in its trade as an unprecedented breach of longstanding conventions on co-operation between western monetary authorities, the people said."

Washington's sales of euros, carried out by the New York Federal Reserve on behalf of the US Treasury, were "very striking" and "sad", one person familiar with discussions among European policymakers told the FT.

Global economic policy now seems at the mercy of an exceptionally casual approach to information, scribbled on a note pad, awaiting an update on Scott Bessent's to-do list.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: Cory Doctorow thinks Australia should be worried about digital sovereignty before AI
World.content:
Cory Doctorow is the science fiction author, activist, and technology critic who coined the term "enshittification" to describe how digital platforms seem to get worse over time as they prioritise profit. He's back with a new book, The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, warning AI isn't a revolution rather it's a financial bubble and sooner or later it'll burst.

He's visiting Australia this month, appearing at The Festival of Dangerous Ideas and The Wheeler Centre. Ahead of his visit, he tells the ABC what a life online could look like after the AI bubble and what still brings him joy on the internet.

You say science fiction writers like yourself are lousy at predicting the future but they can be pretty good technology critics. Why is that?

So, the point of science fiction, at least science fiction that's good — I'm sure you can find colleagues of mine who disagree with me about this, but they're wrong — is not to describe gadgets. It's to interrogate who the gadgets do things for and who the gadgets do things to. The characteristics of gadgets, obviously they matter, but who cares if there's a time machine if all it ever does is go back in time and make things worse for you. So, what's really important are the kind of techno-politics.

There's a very famous example where Robert Moses, who was the famous power broker in New York City, and built a lot of its infrastructure, deliberately built overpasses on the motorway to the public beach so that public buses couldn't go under them in order to stop black people from going to the beach, right, to affect a kind of permanent segregation. And so, there's clearly some techno-politics built into that overpass, right? But it's not that the overpass is racist, right? If someone were to invent a bus with a lower profile, all of those techno politics would change. It's just a piece of architecture that's contingent on other mechanisms in society. And what science fiction writers do is they do things like imagine a lower profile bus and what might happen to the techno-politics of the things around us. And so, this makes us very well equipped to observe the claims made by tech executives, which are often very self-serving, very absolute, and very inevitable.

So this story that we're being told about AI by tech companies — that it's going to change our world, It's going to replace a lot of human labour, it might even reach super intelligence. You argue in your new book that that story isn't inevitable. Why is the future still up for grabs?

Well, I think we can tease apart two different things because there's two kinds of claims you made in there, one of which is just impossible, and the other one is self-serving. So, the impossible one is we teach the word-guessing program too many words and it becomes super intelligent. Yes, it's true, if you use an AI-enabled auto-complete on your phone, it can probably make good guesses about which words you're going to say. And if you're married to someone, your spouse can probably make good guesses about which words you're going to say. But the first one is just a statistical analysis, and the second one is understanding. And the fact that statistical analysis and understanding sometimes produce the same output doesn't mean that they're the same thing. And you can tell because if you turned around to your spouse and said, "I want a divorce", your spouse could have some ideas about where that thought was coming from and the chatbot wouldn't have any idea where that thought was coming from because it just wants the future to be like the past. It's doing statistical inference. So that's one half of that.

The other half of that is this inevitablist doctrine that says that automation has to be driven by capital in order to improve throughput. That what you want to do is fire as many workers as possible and have the remainders pick up the slack by serving as peripherals for machines that do most of the work but then ask a human to do the parts of it that they can't do. And there's another way of arranging automation. And we see both in the historic record of how automation is adopted. When labour drives adoption rather than capital, what you see is not improvements in throughput, but improvements in quality.

So, like you as a writer might choose to use a spell-checker in order to sometimes catch words that you don't know how to spell without having to stop in the middle and look them up. And your editor might say, well, now you've got a spell-checker. Why do you need a sub-editor? And so, you're going to write, we're going to publish it to the internet without an intermediary sub, and you're going to take the blame for the typos. And we can see that neither of those are built into the technology. This is about whether your boss thinks that your readers will accept a lower quality product. And we live in an environment that is the end stage of 40 years of lax competition enforcement in which cartels, monopolies, and duopolies dominate most sectors of our economy. And they believe correctly that when there are fewer options to shop for, you can lower quality without losing sales because you're the only game in town. And so, in a world of statistical inference tools and monopolies, firing workers and replacing them with software to produce lower quality outputs, is not an unreasonable bet that you could make it work, but there's nothing inevitable about it.

No one came down off a mountain with two stone tablets saying "in thine future, everything shall suck". This is just the kind of end stage of a long run program to transfer value and power from labour and democratically accountable institutions to capital.

It's a fear though that a lot of people have right now. But how does this outrage over AI replacing workers actually benefit big tech companies?

So, we should distinguish here between AI replacing workers because bosses know that you will accept a lower quality product and so they can fire workers and replace them with AI and blame the workers for the mistakes. And AI replacing workers because they can do the workers' job. Or put more succinctly, there's two different cases. AI can do your job and an AI salesman can convince your boss to replace you with an AI that can't do your job. And I think it is absolutely reasonable to worry about the second one. But if the way that you phrase it is as the first one, AI can do my job, then you help AI companies raise money and you help AI salesmen convince bosses to fire workers. We have to really be focused on that fine distinction because it is in that distinction that the narrative that drives the investment, that drives the bubble, it's in that, that's where it lives.

In your new book, you argue that what we're heading towards is not this future that we're being sold by tech companies, but instead it's the bursting of this AI bubble. So, if and when that happens what comes next? I mean it seems hard to imagine right now that AI is going away. It's already part of our lives.

Hold on is it part of our lives? Because we have these digital sovereignty debates everywhere. I know it's a hot button issue in Australia. It's a big deal in Canada. I'm a Canadian, we're like cold Australians. And I was just on a panel in Toronto and we were talking about digital sovereignty and everyone on the panel, it kind of blew my mind because they all talked about how important it is for there to be Canadian AI. I was like, "wait a second, guys. If Donald Trump turned off all of our chatbots tomorrow, what would change? Which government ministry would be unable to do his job? Which important firm would go out of business?"

Whereas we actually see the chief prosecutor of the international criminal court kicked off the internet. He loses his Microsoft accounts and everything else he connects with that account.

If Office 365 went away tomorrow in Australia, Mad Max would come to life, right? Every ministry would cease to work, every firm would cease to function, every household would collapse. So, AI is not a part of our lives in like an important sense. AI is a part of our lives the way Tamagotchis were a part of our lives. Let's have some perspective here. Especially because there is a real digital sovereignty risk and it's nothing to do with AI.

So, what would be different after the AI bubble bursts? So, we still have the machines, and you can buy them at a bankruptcy for 10 cents on the dollar, which is why if like Australia wants a national AI strategy, it should be do nothing until the hardware is 10 cents on the dollar. Jesus Christ, don't buy this shit at the top of the market. What are you, a sucker?

Bubbles are really evil. They transfer money from everyday savers to insiders who lie about market opportunities. And those everyday savers are just trying to avoid like, being homeless and starving to death in their old age. And so, they do leave behind some residue. And so part of this is they trained a lot of people, some of whom were already technical and some of whom dropped out of or changed from other trades to learn all the different parts of the stack, whether it's programming, advanced statistical analysis, data labelling, prompting, all of those things have been kind of inculcated through society.

And that's a little like what happened with the web. Where the web bubble took a bunch of humanities undergraduates and convinced them to become Perl programmers and HTML jocks. And so, when the web burst around 2000, all the dumb bosses who are shipping 90-pound bags of pet food saying it's the future of the web went back home. And then these workers were sitting around with servers at 10 cents on the dollar and office space going begging. And they hired each other to build real things, which we call Web 2.0 and it was pretty cool. So probably some people build it. And what will they build it with? Well, the AI companies released a ton of software for free that's open source that anyone can maintain and anyone can improve. And they did it as a kind of demo but it turns out that software is a lot more powerful than they thought it was because they never bothered to optimise it. So, in a state of nature, that software runs pretty slowly unless you throw a lot of hardware at it. But when technologists actually examine the software and see if they can tweak it to make it more efficient, they get massive efficiencies out of it.

Most famously, there was a Chinese hedge fund that spun out this little skunk works called DeepSeek, and they gave them reportedly 6 million American dollars. And it was so efficient running on old chips of the sort that you can get in China, because China's embargoed for modern Nvidia chips, that Nvidia lost $600 billion off its share price in a day.

You can see what's going on there. And the reason that the AI companies never bothered to optimise these old models, the reason they don't care if they're data hungry, is they're effectively running a stock swindle. And the marks, the naive investors, they don't understand the technology. Their rule of thumb is the more money they're spending, the more money they expect to get. Google wouldn't spend $100 billion on AI unless they thought $2 trillion would come out the other side. Basically, it's an investment hypothesis that goes, if the pile of shit is big enough, there's a pony underneath it. And so why bother optimising it if the way you attract suckers is by setting money on fire?

So, we're going to have these models. We're going to make them run far more efficiently. We'll make incremental improvements to them. And we're not going to use it for so many frivolous and pointless things that are heavily subsidised that we need new chips every year. And it'll just become a normal technology. And if we're not careful when a third of the stock market is vaporised, when the Magnificent Seven, who are 35 per cent of the S&P 500 are all losing money on AI, when they burst. If we're not careful, we'll do austerity again.

You pointed out both in Enshittification and in this recent book that the internet is really not that much fun at the moment. But is there still a place on the internet that brings you joy?

Oh, I find joy all the time on the internet. It's full of weird and gnarly communities, some of which are on shitty websites. YouTube is full of great videos. I mean, the problem with YouTube isn't that it's not full of great videos. The problem is that they're siloed there. But I see wonderful things all day long. Mastodon has an algorithmic feed called Explore. I discovered Texture Tuesdays this week. And it's photographers who take pictures of really dramatic textures. I went down a rabbit hole. It was amazing. Public Domain Review just spelunks through the Welcome Trust and various state archives. New South Wales has a really good archive but also the Internet Archive and the Library of Congress highlights a couple of things every day and every day it's amazing and interesting and cool and weird.

Podcasts, God, there's this podcast I love called No Gods No Mayors and the thesis is that mayor is the highest office to which a true oaf can aspire. They've done some really funny Australian mayors as well. But they do mayors through history. It's so funny. Oh my God. And one of their corollaries is that because the Pope is sometimes in charge of the bins in Vatican City, popes is mayors. So every now and again, they'll do a Pope. It's really good.

You’ve said you like to start writing very early in the morning in your backyard hammock and that you have electrified undergarments and a survival so you can do it in all weather. And I had never heard of heated thermals, that sounds terrifying. Why do you like to work from a hammock?

I have chronic pain and I've had a double hip replacement. It hasn't really helped and sitting upright sucks. So being able to anteriorise my pelvis in a hammock is just nice. I'm now mostly living in London. I wrote that when I was living in LA. I don't think I'm going to do all weather hammocks in London. I think it's going to be harder in the winter. But in LA in the morning, the sun's coming up and we get critters, it's raccoons and then it's opossums and then there's rats and then there's a flock of wild parrots, pigeons, many kinds of birds, hummingbirds. And just being outside, watching the sky pinking and then turn blue and it's rising over the palm trees in my neighbour's backyard and, my God, it's just so lovely.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Cory Doctorow appears at Sydney's Festival of Dangerous Ideas from August 22-23 and Melbourne's The Capitol on 25 August. The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI is available now.

World.title: How to avoid the singles tax without finding a romantic partner
World.content:
Marni Trevena always assumed she would get married, have children and share life's costs with a partner.

Instead, at 39, she's navigating mortgages, bills and major life decisions alone, all while also contending with the emotional and financial impacts of the "singles tax".

The singles tax is the extra costs people pay when they can't split costs like rent, internet, insurance and other household bills the way couples can.

Marni Trevena wants all levels of government to be more aware of singles when providing cost-of-living support. (ABC News: Tim Morris)

"Having to pay for everything on your own with only one income is difficult," Ms Trevena said. "The economic pressure, it's a lot".

Ms Trevena, who contacted the ABC through Your Say, said she often feels like she is living in a world designed for pairs.

She said she could have settled down with someone less than compatible. Financially, it might have made sense.

"But instead I feel like I've been disadvantaged by being a responsible, conscious, self-reflective person," she said.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

What is singles tax?

First, it has nothing to do with the ATO.

Singles tax is a term used to refer to the extra money un-partnered people spend because they can't split costs like their paired-up counterparts.

Essentially, it's the extra financial burden you take on for not being in a relationship.

Single-person households are on the rise, and are projected to account for up to 28 per cent of households within the next 20 years.

More than half of Australians living alone are women, and around half of those women are aged 65 or older.

While more Australians are living alone than ever before, some argue society has been slow to adapt.

Bella DePaulo coined the term "singleism" and has written a number of books including Single At Heart. (Supplied: Doug Ellis Photography)

Social scientist Bella DePaulo coined the term "singleism" to describe what she sees as the stereotyping, marginalisation and discrimination faced by singles.

"I think most places around the world see couples and families as the norm and single people as outliers, despite the striking rise of single people over past decades," the American author said.

Dr DePaulo said the rise of "couple norm" as the natural and normal way of being can shape everything from social expectations to public policy.

"Single people have been ignored or treated unfairly for far too long," she said.

Bella DePaulo says she often goes out to dinner with other single women during each leg of her book tours. (Supplied: Bella DePaulo)

What's the cost of being single?

Managing a household budget alone naturally means fixed costs that could otherwise be shared like internet bills, insurances and rates are carried alone.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) an average one-person household spends $2,835 per month on living costs compared to couples who spend a combined $4,118 per month, or $2,059 per person.

That's a difference of $776.

At the same time, single-person households made up two thirds of low income households.

The impacts extend to the amount of money put aside for a rainy day per household.

The 2026 Finder Singles Tax Report found the average Australian with a partner has $50,192 in savings while the average single person has $30,932, a difference of $19,260.

RMIT academic Alicia Bubb has told The Conversation the average single person spends about 3.5 per cent more on goods and services than couples.

Loading...

How can singles save?

Money educator Lacey Filipich said the "singles tax" is real and most acutely felt in variable costs like hotel rooms, where twin-share accommodation is rarely twice the price of a solo room.

"When one person has to carry all the fixed and variable costs alone, it usually ends up more expensive per head than if the fixed costs can be spread across multiple people, which is why it can feel expensive to be single," she said.

Lacey Filipich says the singles tax is a very real thing for a growing number of Australians. (Supplied: Kelly Pimgrim-Byrne)

But while the numbers suggest living alone is more expensive, Ms Filipich said saving money was not a reason to settle for the wrong relationship.

"Choosing poorly for a partner is one of the most costly mistakes a person can make," she said.

"Paying the singles tax is probably better than rushing into something that's not a good fit for you."

Instead, she said singles should focus on the aspects of their finances they can control.

Here are some of her suggestions.

Building a bigger buffer

Singles don't have a second income to fall-back on if they lose their job or face an unexpected financial hit.

Ms Filipich said having a healthy cash buffer as particularly important for singles.

"For example, if you lose your job and you're alone, you might find yourself in a tight financial situation quicker than if you're in a couple where your partner can help cover any shortfall temporarily till you find another job.

"For this reason, singles may find they need a proportionally bigger cash buffer for emergencies."

Review fixed costs

Shopping around for better deals on insurance, utilities and other recurring bills can help reduce some of the costs that fall entirely on a single-income household.

"You can also work out where you could be getting a better price, especially on fixed costs," she said.

Ms FIlipich has summarised her approach into four words: Don't ask? Don't get.

You can read more of her bill-saving tips here.

Most budget benefits won't be in your tax return There was a lot of talk about the $1,000 instant tax reduction and the $250 Working Australians Tax Offset in the federal budget. But they won't be in play at tax time this year.

Don't forget tax time

Tax time can be a daunting time for many.

Ms Filipich said a tax deductions and voluntary super contributions are among the opportunities Australians often overlook.

"The place you make the biggest tax savings is in how you structure your tax affairs," she said.

"For example whether you use company or trust structures, which are not always accessible or necessary for employees but still worth considering every 10 years or so.

"There's a lot going on in this area with recent CGT (capital gains tax) changes, so definitely worth getting up-to-date advice from a qualified accountant."

Help is out there

If just thinking about money is hard, or you've found yourself in a debt you can't seem to shake, you're not alone.

Ms Filipich said anyone feeling the squeeze should consider calling a financial counsellor, the "MVPs (most valuable players) of Australian finance".

Lacey Filipich is the founder of Money School and the author of the book of the same name. (Supplied: Kelly Pilgrim-Byrne)

"Whether you're having trouble making ends meet or feeling overwhelmed by debt, including Buy Now Pay Later, a financial counsellor can help," she said.

"They're free and will help you work out where best to focus your energy to get into a better spot financially."

Speaking out

For Marni Trevena, her concerns about the singles tax aren't about special treatment as much as recognition.

Cost-of-living discussions tend to centre on families, she said, with little consideration given to singles.

"It feels like you're insignificant and not worth taking into consideration," she said.

"Why aren't I entitled to some relief from the costs that I have to bear on my own?"

Marni Trevena says the "tax" of being single has hit in a number of areas. (ABC News: Tim Morris)

With more Australians living alone, Ms Trevena said she hopes policymakers start paying attention.

By her own admission she's one of the lucky ones. She owns her home and has strong family support.

So she's speaking out, in part, on behalf of singles who are not as fortunate.

"If most single people aren't saying anything, then they [policy makers] are not going to know that we feel this way," she said.

" Single people without traditional partners and children are a growing cohort [and] we should not be ignored. "

What prompted this story? Marni Trevena reached out to the ABC through Your Say to bring up the topic of a singles tax. "One of the most frustrating aspects of my life, acknowledging the privilege I hold, is that I often miss out on any small element of support which will lighten the load," she said. "Every year, budgets both state and federal come out and provide relief for families, pensioners and disabled people. I am not asking the government to take from them to give to me, I am asking for the government to give to me as well. The singles tax is wearing, and it is inescapable if your relationship status doesn't change."

World.title: 'It's infuriating': The trapped and vulnerable feeling when you're hacked
World.content:
I do not own any cryptocurrency, nor do I drive a Range Rover.

I do though, according to my X account, which was hacked at some point late last month.

The story is straightforward.

A long-term trusted contact of mine, Sean Callow, sent me a direct message on X. At least I thought he had.

Sean Callow says the hack was a "wake-up" call. (ABC News: John Gunn)

It was in Sean's "voice".

He asked me to vote for him to host a podcast.

I thought the request was a little odd, but it was entirely plausible that Mr Callow could be in the running to host a finance or currency podcast given his role as a currency strategist at ITC Capital Markets.

I clicked the link, but it asked for too much authentication, so I bailed out. It was too hard.

A few days later "Sean" sent me another direct message, pulling on the heartstrings, saying he had noticed I hadn't voted for him, and he was disappointed.

Meta AI agent latest model to hack external company The incident will fan concerns about how developers can contain increasingly capable AI systems, after similar incidents at rival companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

So, naturally, I tried voting again, going through several links.

It felt odd again, so I bailed out. But I was too late. I had been hacked.

It has been a humbling experience because I had thought of myself as proficient in spotting a phishing exercise or hack a mile off.

Mr Callow, too, regrets getting trapped in the hacker's web.

"This episode has been a wakeup call for me in how sophisticated hackers have become," he said.

"This was not an email with spelling mistakes or a 'too good to be true' financial offer.

"It was presented as a favour to a friend of mine in the US who would very plausibly be preparing for a podcast."

Hack spreads through web of contacts

But the distinctive aspect of this hack is that neither Mr Callow nor I were aware an X account direct message could be infiltrated.

"My guard was also lowered by the message arriving in my X direct messages, which require a PIN for me just to read them," he said.

A trusted contact of Mr Callow's in the US appears to be the origin of the spread of this hack.

It then moved to myself, property investment adviser Pete Wargent, and then onto the X account of the Centre for Independent Studies' chief economist Peter Tulip.

Peter Tulip was eventually given the contact details of someone at X to complain about the hack. (Supplied)

From these contacts, hundreds and potentially thousands of Australians have received cyber security threats within their X direct messages.

Mr Tulip said the direct message he engaged with came directly from Mr Wargent.

The ABC has contacted Mr Wargent for comment.

Mr Wargent, however, is indeed a podcast host, making the direct message from him about asking for votes to host a podcast, on the surface, seem credible.

Peter Tulip says he received a direct message from another finance expert, Peter Wargent. (ABC: Dan Irvine)

Mr Tulip said he thought at the time it was "plausible" the direct message was authentic given Mr Wargent's occupation.

Mr Tulip has since been able to regain control of his X account, but he says the day his account was hacked was "extremely difficult".

"I've spent seven years accumulating 8,000 X followers and the prospect of losing communication with them and starting again would have been a huge loss," he said.

'Infuriating' lack of response from X

Mr Tulip said the most challenging aspect of the hack was that there was "no-one to talk to at Twitter [X]".

"It's just infuriating.

" It was a simple and common problem that couldn't be rectified. "

Musk's 'hardcore' ultimatum backfires The company tells employees it will close access to its offices after staff say security began kicking them out.

Mr Tulip was given the contact details of a representative at X by a member of the media.

He said it provided him with a "ray of sunshine" on an otherwise difficult day.

I can corroborate how hard it is to get action from X, formerly known as Twitter, having completed two incident reports with only an automated reply in response.

Unlike your average person, I was able to engage the help of the ABC's cyber team and I was given access to Mr Tulip's new-found contact at X to try to regain control of my account.

Thankfully, that correspondence was helpful and I regained control of my account on Friday evening.

How to avoid being hacked

Our world is dominated by digital applications, passwords, and the ever-present threat of a cyber attack.

An online attack could leave anyone in a constant state of digital fight or flight.

Fraud and scams increase A rise in organised, industrial-scale offshore scam centres and cybercriminals using AI to make scams harder to detect have played a part in an increase in online scams.

Cyber security expert Troy Hunt agreed it was an ongoing worry for anyone with a digital footprint.

And, he said, dodgy links from trusted direct messages were becoming increasingly common.

However, he also said cyber security "should be a shared responsibility".

He said if one of your online accounts was hacked you need to immediately "go through the account recovery process [provided by the platform host] as painful as that is.

"It's not going to be fun."

A reasonable approach is to remain cautious, but there are proven ways to protect your online presence.

The most obvious are changing passwords, and having two-factor authentication, among others.

A simple text message to Mr Callow after receiving his direct message on X would have also prevented the hack.

Many of my contacts have done precisely that with me.

But if you haven't, please don't click on the link. I'm already on a podcast, for the ABC, and you can listen to it here.

World.title: Inside the first week of Alan Jones's trial
World.content:
In a courtroom on level three of Sydney's Downing Centre, a man once considered among the most influential in Australian media has this week sat quietly in the public gallery, legs crossed, with a notebook and pen in hand.

It is only a couple of kilometres from radio station 2GB's Pyrmont studios, where veteran broadcaster Alan Jones previously commanded the attention of scores of listeners every morning from behind a microphone.

But this week, he was the one listening, sitting impassively as the first of six male complainants began testifying in his indecent assault trial.

Mr Jones is on trial over allegations he indecently assaulted and sexually touched a number of male complainants. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

The former Wallabies coach and teacher has waited over 18 months for his day in court after vowing to defend charges he has described as either baseless or a distortion of the truth — 20 counts of indecent assault and two of sexual touching linked to allegations spanning almost two decades to 2020.

After only its first week, the lengthy trial has already provided a rare glimpse into the 85-year-old's life, and the allegations plaguing it since they were reported in the Sydney Morning Herald (SMH) the year before his 2024 arrest.

The prosecution argues Mr Jones either knew he did not have consent, or was reckless to the issue of consent, in relation to all of the charges.

But his defence lawyers say media rivalries are partly to blame for the broadcaster's detractors, in particular 2GB host Ray Hadley, wanting to spread stories about alleged offending to "destroy" him.

Mr Jones's lawyers say his detractors, including 2GB's Ray Hadley, have spread stories about alleged offending to "destroy" him. (Facebook: Ray Hadley)

Defence counsel Gabrielle Bashir SC used her opening address to tell the judge that "rivalry, treachery, double dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more" were at the heart of the case, and her client had endured a trial by media.

Money, gifts and sexual touching

A man dubbed Complainant J, the first witness, has told the court of meeting Mr Jones as a high school student and doing an interview.

He testified that the broadcaster allegedly gifted him a phone when he was a teenager, paid the promising athlete $400 to $600 a week to "help with his training", and bought him a car.

The court heard Mr Jones kept in contact with Complainant J, and the pair would see each other at the defendant's Circular Quay apartment and now-former property at Fitzroy Falls in the NSW Southern Highlands.

Complainant J detailed a number of alleged incidents in 2003 and 2004 where Mr Jones kissed him with a "chomping" motion and sexually touched him, including on one trip to Fitzroy Falls, where it is alleged the broadcaster touched the man's genitalia several times, both outside and under his clothes.

The first witness told the court he met Mr Jones as a high school student. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

During a drive with Mr Jones prior to an increase in the weekly payments, he claimed Mr Jones told him he could have more money, because he had "been a good boy".

"I thought if I told someone about what was happening, I would lose everything, the car he purchased me, the payments would stop," Complainant J said.

He recalled a night at the Fitzroy Falls farm during which the broadcaster told him to have a shower and come out wearing "a robe and nothing else".

He said his "heart was racing" as he sat on the couch next to Mr Jones, who he alleges rubbed his genitals.

The court heard graphic allegations from Complainant J about further indecent assaults, including one where it was alleged Mr Jones and the complainant masturbated at the same time.

Complainant J said it was a moment where he felt "trapped" and "completely frozen".

At another point, he agreed to stay at Mr Jones's Circular Quay apartment and planned to "stand up" to him and tell him to stop, but remained disappointed in himself that he failed to do so.

The court heard Complainant J's payments stopped in 2012 after he had received an estimated $110,000.

Under cross-examination, he has denied reading SMH articles which included allegations against Mr Jones before he went to police in 2024, following the broadcaster's arrest.

He agreed that his allegations were similar to those contained in the articles, but has denied the news reports formed a base for his own accounts.

Claims of fabrication and false recollections

Over nearly four days, Ms Bashir has challenged the witness's reliability during cross-examination.

She has put to him that in 2024, he had lost his job as a police officer over a claim of misconduct, was under financial stress, and saw an opportunity for something "life changing" financially.

"I think I've been very clear … I don't want anything from this," he replied.

"If there is any opportunity to obtain finances for this or rewards I won't accept it …I don't want anything other than proper justice."

Ms Bashir accused Complainant J of fabricating" claims of sexual touching. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Ms Bashir has accused him of "fabricating" claims of sexual touching, which he firmly denied.

After the defence team produced documents about the registration of the car gifted to him and the date which the mobile phone service was connected, he conceded he could have had the dates wrong.

"The [alleged] offences are very clear, but the timelines are always going to be difficult, considering how long it's been," the witness said.

He denied falsely recalling when he received those items to "fit a schoolboy narrative" in connection with the allegations.

Complainant J tells Alan Jones trial of alleged robe request A man accusing Alan Jones of historical indecent assault has told a court he followed the broadcaster's alleged direction to have a shower and come out in a robe because he did not want to disappoint Mr Jones.

And he denied "recasting" the payments from Mr Jones as "something sinister" when they were, according to Ms Bashir, "anything but that".

The witness agreed that Mr Jones was "unfailingly generous", supported him through his career and recognised his potential as an athlete from a young age.

Ms Bashir put to him that "hugs and taps" were a common part of the "sporting world", and touches from Mr Jones were in the context of encouraging him to do his best.

But Complainant J insisted there were occasions where Mr Jones said "I love you" passionately.

'I don't want any of his money'

Throughout his evidence, Complainant J at times closed his eyes in an effort to replay memories and place himself in the moment he was recalling.

Ms Bashir put to him that one of those moments was a "performance for the court", and that he was simply "trying to recount something that you have memorised".

"No, I just recounted what happened," he replied.

Complainant J told the court he did not want "to sue" Mr Jones. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The court has seen messages between Complainant J and his former girlfriend, who he claimed to have briefly confided in when they were in a relationship many years before he came forward.

In one message, after she made a statement to police, he told her, "Once it's all over, I promise to look after you."

Again rejecting the idea of any monetary motive, the complainant denied the defence's suggestion that his message meant he intended to look after her financially.

"I don't want to sue him [Mr Jones], I don't want any of his money."

On Friday, Ms Bashir suggested parts of his account of one of the alleged Fitzroy Falls assaults, in a bedroom, were an attempt to humiliate Mr Jones with a "false narrative".

"No, I'm recounting what happened," he replied.

The trial, before Judge Glenn Walsh, continues next week and is expected to hear from more than 70 witnesses.

World.title: Dead AFL star's mother accuses league of 'cover up' on brain injury
World.content:
The late West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown has revealed AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother described the phone call as "too little, too late".

Mrs Brown also accused the league of a brain injury "cover up", dubbing it "disgusting".

The call to Mrs Brown came four weeks after Four Corners reported Adam Hunter was one of 33 Australian Rules players who have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), exposing the scale of the AFL's brain trauma crisis.

Adam Hunter was diagnosed with a degenerative brain disease after his death in February 2025. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

The Four Corners investigation has since triggered a WorkSafe Victoria investigation into the AFL over player safety and concussion management during contact training.

Mrs Brown told Four Corners she had not heard from the AFL since her son's death in February 2025 and subsequent CTE diagnosis.

Hunter was a West Coast Eagles premiership player and played 151 games.

But last week Mrs Brown said Ms Kane called and said the AFL had initially failed to reach out because the clubs "handled" grieving families "very well".

Joanne Brown described a phone call from Laura Kane, pictured, as "too little, too late". (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

"I said to [Ms Kane], ''It's been 17 months since Adam passed', and said this should have been done in the first month," Mrs Brown said.

"I said, 'Why didn't someone call then?'"

"Laura said, 'Oh, we thought the clubs handled this thing very well.'

"I said, 'But they play for you. You're the AFL. They play for you.'

"[Laura replied], 'Oh yes, I’ll take that on board and forward it on.'

"But it's too late. Too little too late."

Mrs Brown said Ms Kane told her the AFL was continuing to improve player health and safety and said it intended to reduce contact in training from this pre-season on in an attempt to decrease a footballer's exposure to repetitive hits.

CTE is linked to repetitive hits to the head and body.

A coroner looking into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck, who died by suicide at 38 and had CTE, recommended the AFL reduce contact in training back in 2023.

If you or someone you know needs help, call: Police: 000 (Triple Zero) in an emergency

Lifeline: 13 11 14

MensLine Australia: 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service: 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue: 1300 224 636

SANE: 1800 187 263

Shane Tuck took his own life after receiving repeated head knocks as a footballer and boxer The coroner investigating footballer Shane Tuck's death says the AFL should limit contact training sessions to reduce the risk of concussion.

Mrs Brown told the AFL that the league had failed to act fast enough on the coroner's key recommendation.

"She was going on about what they're trying to do not to combat head injuries and I said, 'But wasn't that in 2023 that you were supposed to stop physical contact at training?'

"And she goes, 'Yes, but we're working on it.'

"I said, 'That's three years ago. How many players have been affected in those three years?

"And she just waffled on like she did in the interview … that Four Corners did and I just went, 'They're just trying to cover up or make up' … and it's just disgusting."

The Herald Sun on Thursday revealed a Geelong player, with a history of concussion, had been presented with and signed a waiver.

The document the player signed waived his legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma.

Geelong dumped the waiver after the Herald Sun report. The AFL said it had not approved the arrangement.

Cats avoid sanction Geelong will not be penalised by the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

However, the agreement was signed off by Geelong's board, which was chaired by the current AFL Commission chair, Craig Drummond.

Mrs Brown said she found the story upsetting and believed her son would have done the same, signed a waiver, despite his history of head injuries.

"I felt disgusted, absolutely disgusted that that [waiver] was allowed to go ahead," she said.

"How can that go ahead?

"And gutted in my heart. I know Adam would have done the same thing [signed it]. Because you know how much they want to play, right?"

In a statement on Thursday night, the AFL and the AFL Players Association said it had not approved the agreement.

It also said Geelong was removing it and all other clubs would be advised not to strike similar deals with "at-risk" players to exonerate themselves from future legal action.

Mrs Brown's statement comes just a month after Adam Hunter's "grieving best mate" Dave Andrews penned an open letter to the AFL Commission saying it had "failed" in its duty of care to players.

"You have failed him," Mr Andrews wrote in the five-page letter that touches on Hunter's sacrifice for the game and pleads for the AFL leadership to better inform its players of the CTE risk.

Mr Andrews is yet to receive a response from the AFL Commission.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Enter the secret cave seen by fewer people than have walked on the moon
World.content:
Stephen Fordyce inside Elk River cave. ( )

"There is no greater feeling in the world than finding passage that no-one ever in the history of the world has seen before."

This sentiment by the late cave explorer Agnes Milowka is what drives adventurers to push the boundaries of human capacity in pursuit of new worlds.

But with very little of the Earth's surface left uncharted, the last frontier of true exploration has been forming in total darkness for hundreds of millions of years.

Going there comes with significant risk. And we're taking you with us.

Four hours from Melbourne, a small band of hard-hatted explorers makes its way towards a hidden portal to a subterranean world few humans have ever seen.

They leave the regularity of their day jobs behind to spend their weekends discovering new cave networks.

I'm in the small town of Buchan, in Victoria's East Gippsland, to experience firsthand the hidden world of a cave that has captivated explorers for the past two decades — Elk River.

Concealed beneath the undulating green hills of this bucolic landscape in Gunaikurnai Country, underground waterways have been carving out Elk River's limestone caverns for more than 350 million years.

Potholes Cave Reserve in Buchan, Victoria, conceals more than 100 known caves. ( )

It was only by chance that this labyrinthine system of dry and submerged chambers was discovered in 2006.

Some of Elk River's caverns soar like cathedral vaults; others can only be traversed with scuba diving equipment.

So far, 3.13 kilometres of Elk River have been explored, making it one of the longest caves in Victoria.

At a depth of 135 metres, it is also one of the deepest, and among the state's most important, as its discovery resolved century-old mysteries about the hydrology and geology of the region.

Elk River cave is in Victoria's East Gippsland region. ( )

Today, experienced cavers are taking me into Elk River via its original entrance — a concealed tunnel in a paddock that no-one has used for nearly 20 years.

Stephen Fordyce, one of the trip leaders, says the part of the cave they are taking me to is, in terms of human visitation, "probably still in the category of less people than have walked on the moon".

That's 12 humans to date.

Stephen became the key exploration diver in what became known as the Elk River project, and is the only person to have reached the furthest known point of this cave — an extraordinary feat we will come to later.

Stephen Fordyce hopes more sections of Elk River will be explored in his lifetime. ( )

The original entrance to Elk River is now closed with a metal lid and rarely used. ( )

Stephen Fordyce enters Elk River cave in Buchan, Victoria. ( )

He lives for the thrill of pushing the limits of human exploration to leave a legacy of discovery.

On each trip, despite meticulous planning, Stephen accepts there is a chance he may not return.

Before setting out, he “makes peace” with his loved ones and leaves an emergency plan with his support team.

The deaths of five Italian divers in a Maldives ocean cave system in May, and the loss of two cavers in Laos in June, are tragic reminders of the risks speleological explorers face.

When incidents like these, and the 2018 rescue of a junior soccer team from a flooded cave in Thailand, hit the news, the world sees a glimpse of this mysterious underground realm.

But beyond the headlines, cave exploration continues in quiet darkness, more frequently than you might think.

Stephen and two of the other cavers accompanying me, Josh Van Dyk and Tom Elms, are among the team of Victorian speleological experts who would be called to assist in a cave rescue.

Still, I can't help but feel nervous looking at the cave entrance — a narrow, 2-metre deep, vertical construction pipe inserted 20 years ago to prevent the entrance from caving in and filling with dirt.

Rochelle Hotchin enters Elk River cave through the original opening — a hole in a paddock. ( )

Loading...

I slide in off the edge feet first, swing my arms to prop me up as my feet dangle, and look for a way to safely shimmy to a point where I can rest my feet on the muddy rocks below.

The air gets damper, but it is a stable 17 degrees Celsius, on average, inside the caves at Buchan.

The next sections we navigate are tighter, and I can feel the limestone catching against my body as my feet drop into a small vertical hole amid a jumble of ancient boulders.

Loading...

With careful movements, I figure out which angles will work best as we venture further into the darkness.

Suddenly, there's space.

Not much, but enough for me to crouch next to Tom and look up at the breathtaking array of thousands of colourful stalactites above us.

They form an extraordinary ceiling of calcite shards reaching down to us through millions of years.

I feel goosebumps at the thought that I am one of the few people on Earth who has ever seen their beauty.

Loading...

I turn off my head torch and sit in the silent darkness.

It's difficult to imagine how it must have felt to be the very first person to see this cave.

And then I meet her.

Kim Van Dyk sits beside her walker on the verandah of Homeleigh, an 11-bedroom cottage bought by a group of cavers in the 1970s for use when exploring nearby.

We're on the edge of the Buchan township in Victoria's "home turf" of caving, and 9 kilometres south of Potholes Cave Reserve, a 48-hectare expanse riddled with more than 100 known caves, including Elk River.

Kim warns me she will likely cry as we chat.

Caving has been a major part of Kim Van Dyk's life. ( )

Kim Van Dyk recounts her exploring days while looking at old caving photos. ( )

Her eyes well up as she speaks of how illness has prematurely ended her dream of being able to go caving on her 80th birthday.

Now 68, Kim longs to go underground again, and recalls a distant conversation with her eldest son, who once told her she loved caves more than her children.

"I love my two boys. But I really did love my caves and my bats more," she admits.

Kim takes me back to 2006 and reveals how a slight movement in her peripheral vision led to the chance discovery of Elk River.

An entrance to Elk River cave was discovered by the Van Dyks in 2006. ( )

While walking through the Potholes reserve with her husband John, she noticed a patch of grass waving in a doline, a sunken section of ground.

As there was no wind and the surrounding grass was stationary, they knew it could mean a draft coming from underground.

Digging at the Elk River cave site at Buchan in 2006. ( )

It could mean a new cave.

"Our thing was finding new caves. Why go somewhere where 100 other people have gone before?" Kim says.

Since quitting their city jobs and moving to Buchan in 1990, Kim and John have discovered 66 new caves and have assisted in more than a dozen cave rescues.

But their discovery of Elk River was something special.

When digging beneath the waving grass revealed rock, they knew their suspicion was correct.*

After returning with caving equipment and friends Eric Munro and Laurie Brown, Kim was the first to enter their new find.

It was a tight shimmy down, crawling and squeezing her way through rocks, and using wire ladders to descend vertical pitches.

The night before, Kim had listened to an interview with pioneer caver Frank Moon, who was active in the early 1900s. If Kim is the mother of Buchan caving, Frank is the grandfather.

Frank Moon was a pioneer of cave exploration in Buchan in the early 1900s. ( )

In the interview, Frank was discussing his belief that a river must flow beneath this part of East Gippsland.

Cavers obsessed about that theory for the next 100 years, believing, like Frank, that there had to be a river and a "master cave system" into which all the water in the area drained.

Could this finally be it?

"Being the skinniest, I always copped the squeezes," Kim says.

Kim Van Dyk misses caving but says she is no longer able to head underground. ( )

"I am going through … then I saw what I thought was just a puddle, but I kept on going, and it's a flowing river.

"I sat down and cried. I was crying my eyes out thinking, 'Frank, you were right.'"

This elk antler formation prompted explorers to name the cave Elk River. ( )

The inspiration for the name Elk River came from an unusual speleothem formation they thought resembled an elk's horn, and a combination of the first letters of their names: Eric, Laurie and Kim.

Kim says finding the streamway flowing through the cave was one of the proudest moments of her life.

Another caving highlight was her and John's discovery of the best-preserved skull of Ice Age marsupial Palorchestes azael in a Buchan cave in 2000, which is now in the Melbourne Museum.

Exploration of the Buchan caves has led to other important fossil finds that have helped to paint a picture of how life evolved in Australia over hundreds of millions of years.

In 2011, the Van Dyks' son Josh found a 50,000-year-old short-faced kangaroo fossil in a newly discovered cave, Nightshade, while exploring with Eric Munro.

When Museums Victoria palaeontologists returned and completed the full extraction more than 10 years later, it was revealed that Josh and Eric had discovered one of the most complete fossils of Simosthenurus occidentalis ever found.

The Palorchestes azael skull fossil found in a Buchan cave in 2000. ( )

An illustration of what Palorchestes azael would have looked like. ( )

An artist's impression of what the short-faced kangaroo would have looked like. ( )

The short-faced kangaroo fossil found in Buchan is 71 per cent complete. ( )

It is extraordinary discoveries such as these that fuel the passion of weekend cave explorers.

Josh Van Dyk lives in Buchan with his own children now. He works at the local quarry and runs a fireworks business, but still spends most of his spare time caving.

After we reach the cave floor, Josh sits beside the Elk River streamway that brought his mother to tears 20 years ago.
