World.title: Country Life: Three native nurseries, a fridge full of seeds
World.content:
Clifton farmer Sandra Campbell tries not to take life too seriously, so there was room to experiment when she began planting the gullies on her dairy farm with native shrubs.

"Inevitably this improves water quality because no one's putting stock in here ... it should improve bird life at some stage. There's offsetting of emissions. There's all sorts.

"[But] we've just had a heap of fun along the way. We've met a heap of people, and it's made farming a little bit more exciting."

Sandra Campbell looks out over the gully - once an empty ditch covered with tall grass, and now a "pretty place to be". RNZ/Anisha Satya

The farmer with the seed fridge Country Life Download MP3 14m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

What began as an attempt to beautify some land has grown into three nurseries, a fridge full of seeds, and a blue Bedford named Beryl.

She's documented her and husband Chris' "water care journey" on Instagram, taking viewers through the challenges and triumphs of harvesting native seeds and then growing them.

She was inspired to try her hand at growing seedlings through her role as a catchment group facilitator.

"Covid happened and we were not in the financial position to buy lots of trees, so I figured that I could give it a go," she said.

"We started with one nursery, and then it extended to the other side of the shed and became a second nursery, and then it ended up in the tractor yard as a third nursery.

"We now grow about 4000 trees in the nursery on-farm as a hobby."

Some DIY growing beds using leftover gardening materials. RNZ/Anisha Satya

There is a DIY spirit about the nursery: seedling houses made from pellets, old water line and windbreak, a garden sprinkler and timer setup found on Temu.

Even the storage for the foraged seeds - the hand-collected jewels of the Campbells' operation - is a repurposed fridge.

"You used to come in here and it just smelled like mice. Granny's fridge broke down, so it got moved down here."

Containers full of southern rātā, ake ake (Dodonaea viscosa) and more seed sit along paper bags and pillowcases of mixed seeds, and a tub of unprocessed mānuka branches.

"Seed collecting takes over the shed normally, and also sometimes my house, because I'm drying a lot.

"There's a period of time between December to April that I'm very busy seed-collecting; I try and make weekends away to Te Anau or the Catlins so I can collect seed, and everybody I know who has ever holidayed with us has gotten roped in to helping."

Some seeds get potted for the nursery, to be hand-planted in the gullies, or donated to other farmers who want to start their native planting journey.

The seed mixes were used for drone seeding, which was not commonly done when planting natives, but Campbell said it was cost-efficient.

Sandra Campbell stores her foraged seed collection in an old, unplugged fridge - it keeps the rats out. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"You could solely drone seed and not plant. If we did that, we could probably almost do it for free, bar the first drone visit.

"But it's quite patchy... so it works well with the planting."

Drone seeds take time to "strike", some popping up years after they've been spread, but the plants that want to grow will, Campbell said.

"I just think nature sorts that out. If I plant something that shouldn't be [there], it'll die and then we try something else.

"And when you're growing it yourself, you get a bit less picky about things dying because you just haven't [gone] and spent $10 on a tree for it to die."

Aside from efficiency, Campbell said drone-seeded plants often passed the hand-planted ones, likely because they had not had their root structure handled.

She said six hectares of gully had been planted - but there were many more to go.

World.title: Timor-Leste: The new tourism frontier
World.content:
For the adventurous traveller, finding somewhere genuinely undiscovered has become almost impossible. Modern travel, globalisation and social media have left few blank spaces on the map. One country, however, has so far escaped mass tourism: Timor-Leste, a peaceful nation with a complicated history, a distinctive culture and a special bond with New Zealand. Anna Thomas reports.

Timor-Leste, or East Timor, is a name most New Zealanders would recognise but few could probably locate on a map. The most direct route is by flying to Bali, then taking a two-hour flight to the capital of Dili. But while Bali attracts 16 million visitors a year, Timor-Leste receives just 26,000, even then, most of those are ex-pats or business travellers.

Change, though, is arriving quickly. Since joining ASEAN in October 2025, development in this small South East Asian nation has accelerated. New hotels and restaurants are opening, roads are being sealed, and the international airport is undergoing a US$240 million upgrade.

With Timor-Leste due to chair ASEAN in 2029, a large convention centre is under construction on Dili's waterfront and thousands of political leaders, media and visitors are expected.

Supplied/Anna Thomas

Roughly the size of Hawke's Bay, the country has a population of 1.4 million. It has a rich and complex history marked by colonisation, conflict and occupation but as 'independent' Timor-Leste, its history is still being written.

It remains the poorest country in South East Asia, with almost half its people living below the poverty line. Ironically though it is also one of the most expensive countries with the majority of its goods imported. While oil and gas reserves remain the country's main revenue earner, tourism is increasingly seen as a potential golden goose.

A Kiwi connection

Diane Clayton has been living in Timor-Leste for a year. After 10 years with Tourism New Zealand, she and husband Tristam decided they needed an adventure. She signed up with Volunteer Service Abroad with the plan to help Timor-Leste develop eco-tourism. While the well-travelled couple were given a lengthy brief before arriving, she says nothing can quite prepare you.

"It's really quite a crazy place", she laughs "especially the lack of infrastructure, the heat, and the pollution. But very quickly we were made to feel at ease because the Timorese are so friendly."

VSA worker Diane Clayton with Timor-Leste Forestry Rangers. Supplied/Diane Clayton

Clayton has been working alongside tourism operators sharing her knowledge on everything from marketing to basic customer service. She explains that very few of the locals have experienced being a tourist themselves sowhen you're advising on hospitality you're starting from scratch.

And while health and safety wasn't part of her job description, Clayton discovered first hand, it needed to become a priority.

"On day two of my job I was asked if I'd like to join a group of Australian tour operators heading to Atauro Island."

The island is roughly 36km from Dili, about 1.5 hours by a small boat, and it has one of the world's most biodiverse coral reefs. The waters around Timor-Leste also have at least 24 species of whales and dolphins living or travelling through them. Clayton says the weather wasn't ideal and from the beginning she had a bad feeling.

"Because of the wind and swells the trip was on-again off-again but the call was made to proceed. There were 14 of us in a 10 person boat with no lifejackets.

The trip over was OK but when we arrived visibility wasn't good enough for snorkelling. So we had lunch and decided to return to Dili. However, halfway across the channel, the boat just stopped. We had run out of gas."

Diane and Tristram Clayton on Atauro Island. Supplied/Diane Clayton

The crew couldn't speak English and refused to use the boat radio but luckily there was some phone coverage. "Calls were being made but because of the deteriorating weather no one wanted to bring out extra fuel. As the hours ticked by, and the seas got rougher passengers were scared and a few of them were throwing up.

Finally, after waiting four hours, help arrived." Clayton told me it was the first time she had ever feared for her life.

As a result of that incident, Clayton has been working on health a safety protocols. But like most things in the country, developing industry standards is a work in progress.

One of the many picturesque rivers around Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

VSA volunteers like Clayton have been making a small but important contribution in the tourism sector. Clayton's predecessor, Jonty Crane, spent a year producing tourism videos and articles that remain the country's most visible promotional material online.

Australian expat Barry Hinton, who owns 'Barry's Place' one of Atauro Island's original eco-resorts credits Crane with doing more for Timorese tourism than anyone else. Hinton arrived in 2001 to teach English, later settling on Atauro and marrying locally.

Up to 85 percent of guests at 'Barry's Place' are Australians who are drawn to the island's marine environment.

Barry Hinton is an ex-pat Australian who owns the ecolodge Barry's Place on Atauro Island. Supplied/Anna Thomas

Hinton employs 30 local staff, doesn't advertise and books entirely through WhatsApp. His main frustration is bureaucracy. "The laws are changed all the time," he says.

"They (government) want investment, they want tourism, but they don't get how difficult they've made it." Still, he stays for the lifestyle. "It's just the rawness and the beauty of a very simple life and meeting guests who want an ethical holiday."

The next generation

'Friendly' and 'resilient' are the two words most commonly used to describe Timorese. Despite the poverty, the people of Timor-Leste are always smiling.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida is a 24-year-old tour guide from Dili. He is sharp, enthusiastic and hungry to learn. He started work in a car rental firm and when customers kept asking for recommendations of what to do and where to go, he saw an opportunity.

He's been running his business MaunTimor Guide for three years.

Varela Belo de Almeida says because Timor-Leste is an expensive country, it's not really suited to backpackers. Most of his clients are Australians and some New Zealanders, who want to learn more about the country where many of their soldiers served first in WWII and then again from 1999 as part of a multinational force restoring peace to the newly independent country.

Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida, 24, has been guiding tourists around Timor-Leste for three years. Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

Varela Belo de Almeida says an ideal itinerary is about six days; a couple of days in Dili, visiting Christo Rei (a smaller version of Rio's Christ the Redeemer), Santa Cruz cemetery, markets and museums, then Baucau to see Portuguese architecture, and then up to the remote and pristine Jaco Island.

Supplied/Mateus Varela Belo de Almeida

He says getting around the island can be challenging. "The roads can be dangerous at times and you could travel for hours only to discover the guest house you booked has increased the price, given away your room or has run out of food."

A typical washed out road in Timor-Leste. Supplied/Anna Thomas

While guiding can't support him full time yet, he says the knowledge and expertise he's received through Clayton has been invaluable. "I have learnt so much in her workshops on story-telling, hospitality and customer service, and especially marketing. I'm hoping as a result business will grow."

As Clayton's one year posting comes to an end she says volunteering gives you a rare insight and access to this young nation.

She is looking forward to returning in a few years to see how the country has developed. And for those considering visiting Timor-Leste, Clayton has some advice. "Come with your eyes wide open. Have low expectations and you'll be delighted."

World.title: Transport Agency refuses to release documents about tolling roads
World.content:
The Transport Agency is refusing to release briefings and records about tolling roads.

The government has moved to have tolls considered on all big projects and to change the rules so the revenue raised could be spent more widely.

RNZ asked Waka Kotahi for copies of any ministerial briefings on tolling this year and of any board minutes where tolling came up this year.

It identified two briefings and two lots of minutes from April and May.

But it has withheld all four on various grounds.

The first briefing, related to tolling consultation of the Belfast to Pegasus Motorway and Woodend Bypass project, where decisions had not been made, was withheld on constitutional conventions for the time being which protect the confidentiality of advice.

The second briefing and boths sets of minutes contained commercially sensitive information so were withheld, NZTA said.

World.title: In China-US rivalry, NZ remains isolated but not insulated
World.content:
With China and the US vying for status as the major world superpower, New Zealand is caught walking a careful line.

In China-US rivalry, NZ remains isolated but not insulated The Detail Download MP3 22m

China sees an opportunity - created by US President Donald Trump and the global chaos he is creating - to influence New Zealand's actions in the world, according to an expert on the Chinese Communist Party.

"If you're a propagandist sitting in Beijing, Trump is the gift you never thought you'd get," says Sam Chetwin George, a senior fellow at the Asia Society's Centre on US-China Relations in New York.

China has been issuing more critical statements about New Zealand in the past year or so, coinciding with a realignment in New Zealand's foreign policy towards a traditional, US-led security framework.

But with Trump's disregard for international rules, New Zealand could be feeling more exposed, says George.

George is a Kiwi: he was a New Zealand Prime Minister's Scholar, learning Mandarin in Taiwan, and he also studied at Oxford and Stanford. He recently published a piece in Foreign Affairs magazine about how Beijing is making the most of this "age of anarchy".

"The New Zealand economy is in difficulty," George says. "We're facing an energy crisis. Our manufacturing base is at risk. The global economy is not looking great, and so it might just be that [China thinks] there's strategically an opening to apply pressure in a way that might be more effective now."

Earlier this year, China sharply criticised New Zealand's participation in a United Nations sanctions-monitoring mission focused on North Korea, and put a travel ban on four New Zealand MPs who visited Taiwan, a self-governing island that Beijing considers part of its territory.

It has also been encroaching further into the Pacific diplomatically, economically, and militarily. Last year, a Chinese naval task force group conducted live fire exercises in the Tasman Sea between Australia and New Zealand. Last month, Beijing launched a nuclear-capable missile into the nuclear-free South Pacific.

Still, Chinese leader Xi Jinping is casting himself as the stable alternative to the unpredictable Trump.

The Chinese Communist Party has long portrayed the US as bullying, hegemonic, greedy and expansionist - and Trump is proving some of those stereotypes, George says.

Beijing is now benefiting from the geopolitical rivalry between the world's two superpowers that's playing out in public.

"Countries like New Zealand are in the unenviable position of having to navigate that."

A recent survey from the Asia NZ Foundation found that, for the first time in a decade, Kiwis are more likely to see China as a friend than the United States. Similar trends were reported in a Pew Research survey of 36 countries, which found views of China have improved while opinions of the US have worsened, to the point where China is now seen more positively than the US.

So is China the guardian of stability in the world?

"Of course they're not," George says. "They're like any big power: they are focused on their own interests and they're focused on their own objectives."

But they're just being smarter about it. For example, the way Beijing is funding and supporting Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.

"America is so overt in its military adventurism, and China has just very carefully and very cleverly, I think, kept its support at a level that's plausibly deniable," he says.

Xi is "obsessed with strength" and returning China to what he sees as its rightful position in the world as a great civilisation and a great country, George says. That means cementing the absolute leadership of the Chinese Communist Party but also challenging the leadership of the US, its principal adversary in the world.

World.title: The unexpected day jobs of Australia's female footballers
World.content:
When Caitlin Reid is not re-arranging her patient's vital organs you will find her on the training field.

Such is life for many professional female athletes, whose sporting income falls short of providing a sustainable living.

"A lot of us [AFLW players] don't earn enough to survive on the footy alone," she said.

The 29-year-old's typical day starts from first light at the SCG working on her ruck craft with the football.

After midday is usually when she heads off to St Vincent's Hospital to start her shift as a surgical registrar working on the frontline of patient care.

"I'm usually working if not seven days a week, six days a week," Reid said.

Caitlin Reid trains with the Sydney Swans several days a week while balancing her job as a surgical registrar. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Growing up, girls' football didn't exist for Reid. It was not until halfway through her medical degree that she discovered the league.

Initially the tall ruck said her passion was in basketball, but COVID cancelled the NBL1 star's season with the Albury Wodonga bandits.

So Reid took a chance playing in an AFL Nines competition to maintain her fitness through the season.

"By the time basketball was ready to go back I loved footy more than I loved basketball," she said.

'Double life'

Emily Pease followed her two passions in football and love for animals to get the best of both worlds. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Emily Pease is performing the same juggling act as a winger for GWS while wrangling wildlife at Sydney's Taronga zoo.

"It's my double life. I'll start with meetings, a gym session and a field session with the Giants, then flip it to the zoo greeting guests and interacting with the animals," Pease said.

"It's actually really cool having footy life and also having something outside of it which I'm really passionate about."

The 24-year-old started playing Aussie rules in Canberra and had the opportunity to train with the Giants academy before making her way to the team.

GWS Giants winger Emily Pease trains several days a week while balancing her job at Taronga Zoo. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Most of her co-workers at the zoo do not know about her double life.

"A lot of my colleagues kind of just go 'wow'. No-one really expects that I'm playing footy. It's like I'm revealing a superpower," Pease said.

She hopes to be a full-time zookeeper one day, preferably working with primates.

'It's a team sport'

According to data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

The latest data from the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) tracked that 3 per cent of AFLW players work full-time outside of playing on the field, down from 6 per cent last year.

Across 540 listed players in the women's league an additional 62 per cent work part-time or casual jobs.

And according to AFLPA data, the average wage of an AFLW player in the 2026 season is $79,414.

From 2027 AFLW players will move from the current four-tier system pay to a salary cap model similar to the men. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"Some people ask why I do both jobs. I think for me it's a bit of an outlet," Pease said.

"I'm able to take my mind off footy when I'm at the zoo and vice versa.

"I think just being given the opportunity to follow my passions. I had a passion for footy and for animals".

Reid has not had a holiday in two and half years, not because she does not want to, but because she has used most of her annual leave to accommodate her other career.

AFL strikes historic joint collective bargaining agreement The five-year collective bargaining agreement covering male and female players features significant wage rises and a longer AFLW season.

"There's certainly an element of guilt I feel playing football because I'm not at the hospital and we are short-staffed as is everywhere in New South Wales," Reid said.

"My co-workers have to work extra hours because I'm not there. I love my job at the hospital but I also love my job at the club.

"I've said it before, medicine is a team sport and the closeness you feel towards your footy teammates is the closeness I feel towards my co-workers."

The 11th AFLW season begins this Sunday with a clash between St Kilda and Carlton at Docklands Stadium.

World.title: Travis Head pips star duo to win second-straight Allan Border Medal
World.content:
Travis Head has pipped fellow Ashes hero Alex Carey to claim a second consecutive Allan Border Medal.

During a function in Brisbane on Friday night, held six months later than normal due to scheduling conflicts, the star batter was again crowned Australia's leading male cricketer.

Head had 153 votes, just ahead of his South Australian teammate Alex Carey on 152.

Player of the Ashes, Mitchell Starc, finished third on 150 votes despite having ditched one of the three international formats.

Head pipped Carey and Starc to the gong. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Still a force in Tests and ODIs, Starc ended his T20 international career last September in a bid to extend his red-ball career.

Starc won the Shane Warne Test player of the year award, while Mitchell Marsh took out the ODI award.

Big-hitting Tim David was named Australia's best T20 player.

Head joins Ricky Ponting, Michael Clarke, Shane Watson, Steve Smith and David Warner as multiple winners of the Allan Border Medal, which was first handed out in 2000.

The 32-year-old made 30 appearances for Australia across all three formats during the 2025/26 season, scoring 1,437 runs.

Head belted a famous 123 from 83 balls to guide Australia to a stunning victory in the opening Ashes Test in Perth.

He took that form into his home Test in Adelaide, flailing 170 in a memorable partnership with Carey.

During a career-best season, Carey scored 1,079 runs in 24 games across all formats.

Carey hit a stunning century at the Adelaide Oval, while his glovework during the Ashes was exceptional with 28 dismissals.

Normally held during a gala event in Melbourne at the end of summer, the Allan Border Medal was delayed due to organisers wanting the cricketers to be in the room for it.

Last year, the all-conquering women's team attended the event, but the men's players were in Sri Lanka for a Test tour, so Head had to accept the medal via video.

Earlier this year, Annabel Sutherland won a second-consecutive Belinda Clark Award and was also named the women's ODI player of the year.

AAP

World.title: Ruthless Lions send ominous warning to AFL rivals by dismantling Hawks
World.content:
Jarrod Berry (left) and Ryan Lester (right) celebrated their milestone matches in style as the Lions recorded a 67-point win. (Getty Images)

Brisbane has bounced back from last week's thumping by Carlton to thrash Hawthorn by 67 points at the Gabba.

Led by Kai Lohmann's five-goal haul, the premiers stayed firmly in the top four hunt with a convincing 18.17 (125) to 8.10 (58) win over the third-placed Hawks.

The victory was a perfect response to the 76-point loss to the Blues as the Lions celebrated a double milestone night with Jarrod Berry making his 200th AFL appearance and veteran defender Ryan Lester marking his 250th AFL game with a late goal that delighted the sell-out crowd.

Defeat for Sam Mitchell's team ends a four-game winning run ahead of next weekend's clash with Collingwood at the MCG and will raise questions heading into the finals about their genuine premiership credentials.

In a week where his own visit to Magpies HQ was a focus, Lachie Neale was a standout for the Lions with 35 disposals, seven marks, eight tackles and six clearances.

As well as Lohmann, the Lions had four multiple goalkickers with Logan Morris kicking four majors in the first half, Charlie Cameron booting three and Eric Hipwood scored two including a booming third-quarter shot from well outside 50.

Will Ashcroft had a game-high 39 disposals including 13 score involvements while Harris Andrews delivered another defensive masterclass, snaffling 10 marks as the Hawks forward line struggled to get clean ball all night.

Hawthorn was no match for the rampant reigning premiers at the Gabba. (Getty Images)

The Hawks though were also guilty of missing crucial chances in the opening two quarters with Harry Morrison and Sam Butler both offending as the Lions surged into a winning position.

The hosts were only six clear at the end of the first term but scored three quickfire goals at the start of the second to break the game open and never looked back, the Hawks unable to mount any meaningful resistance.

In the end Jack Gunston finished with three majors while Josh Ward had 28 disposals but it was a disappointing night for the Hawks who were simply second-best across the park.

AAP

World.title: New jumper revealed as NRL grants Perth Bears salary concessions
World.content:
The NRL's newest side, the Perth Bears, have unveiled their inaugural playing jersey on the same day they were granted salary cap concessions ahead of their entry to the competition in 2027.

In an event coordinated between Perth and North Sydney, where the unveiling was live-streamed, the Bears revealed the jersey by dropping the design from the famous WACA Ground light towers.

The design, which features red hoops on a black background, pays homage the North Sydney Bears, which left the NRL at the end of the 1999 season and currently play in the NSW Cup competition.

Peter V'landys (second from left) announced the concessions alongside WA Premier Roger Cook (speaking), Bears CEO Anthony De Ceglie, and Perth coach Mal Meninga (left). (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

The unveiling of the jersey marks a major step towards the Bears' entry into the NRL, which club chief executive Anthony De Ceglie said was on track to have 35,000 members by the beginning of the 2027 season.

Salary boost

In a big boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys announced the Bears would be granted a concession for signing a marquee player.

"They will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for any player above a million dollars [salary]," V'landys said.

"If the player is worth $1.5 million, they can pay another 20 per cent from a sponsor and that won't be counted in the salary cap.

" So that gives them the opportunity to get somebody because they've got a 20 per cent bonus for that player from the sponsor. "

The Perth Bears will play in the 2027 NRL season. (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

Additionally, the Bears will have first rights to any player who wants to leave their club but is under contract for 2027.

"You may have a marquee player that's not happy in a particular club and the club and the player want to separate. That player can only go to Perth in the first instance," V'landys said.

"There will be some good players that will come up and be given the opportunity to play in Perth."

The concessions will help the Bears land a high-profile player, which has so far being lacking in their signings.

Meninga happy with progress

Bears inaugural coach Mal Meninga says he is "really happy" with the club's progress to date and talked down the need for a marquee player.

"We've worked within the conditions of obviously our entry into the NRL and you know … let me be frank with this … I'm really excited about the roster we've built," he said.

"You look through the team, we've got some high-profile players already.

"We've certainly got players of the future, there's no doubt.

"I really appreciate Peter and the club's great concessions, but I'm really happy with where we are at the moment."

Bellamy excited

Veteran Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy said the arrival of the Bears was exciting for the league.

And he said the club was in good hands with coach Mal Meninga steering the ship.

"I worked with Mal, I played with Mal and I know the amount of work that he puts in and the amount of work he will put into the coaching," he said.

"I'm sure it will be a very successful venture."

The Storm has already seen two of their players, Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, sign on with the Bears, but the coach was magnanimous about their departure.

Tyran Wishart of the Storm will line up for the Bears next season. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

"They're very excited to be coming over here," he said.

"They're obviously doing what they think's best for them and best for their families.

"They're still doing a great job for us.

"That's just the way the game is."

World.title: 'Doesn't look great': Fears Penrith captain could miss rest of NRL season
World.content:
Penrith captain Isaah Yeo may miss the rest of the NRL season after injuring his pectoral muscle, while the Sydney Roosters joined the Panthers on top of the table after defeating the Canterbury Bulldogs.

Yeo came off in the first half of Penrith's 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland on Friday night, with the Auckland-based side solidifying their status as a genuine premiership threat in 2026.

Yeo was clutching his pectoral muscle after reeling out of a tackle, with scans needed to confirm if he has sustained a tear.

Should scans confirm a pectoral tear, he could be out for the rest of the season.

"It doesn't look great," Panthers coach Ivan Cleary said during his press conference.

"Obviously Yeoy's a big loss and hard to replace, but that's how it goes.

"If that's the case, we'll have to (replace him)."

The Roosters have joined the Panthers on 36 points at the top of the NRL ladder, surviving a scare to pip the Bulldogs 20-18.

The Roosters held an 8-2 lead at half-time, but the Bulldogs scored three tries in 11 minutes to take an 18-8 lead with 25 minutes to play.

But two quick tries in the final 15 minutes for the Roosters earned them a hard-fought win.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.

Relive all of Sunday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: De Minaur haunted by Montreal Masters double-fault drama
World.content:
A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Australians through in Montreal Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

World.title: Ex-AFLPA boss calls for independent tribunal over Cats concussion waiver
World.content:
Former Richmond player and AFL Players Association (AFLPA) chief Joel Bowden has criticised the AFL, Geelong and the AFLPA for their handling of the secret concussion waiver signed by an unknown Cats player, calling for a Senate committee hearing to investigate.

The Cats have avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Speaking to ABC Radio Melbourne on Friday, Bowden said he found it "absolutely outrageous that a young person's been taken advantage of", calling it "gambling with a young [player's] health and safety".

Dogs coach on concussion controversy Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Bowden — who is also a former trade unionist and member of the Northern Territory parliament — pointed to the close ties between the club and the AFL, with former Geelong president Craig Drummond the chairman of the AFL Commission and Geelong chief executive Steven Hocking being the former general manager of football at the AFL.

"How this has got through, how people have thought that this is possibly OK is now ever more outrageous with the facts that have been put on the table," Bowden said.

Loading...

"It's conduct unbecoming. The AFL will fine players, they will fine people who are involved in the community sport — if you breach the code of conduct anywhere in the AFL at a game of community football you can be brought in front of a tribunal.

"And this AFL club, Geelong, have gone and signed a contract outside the standard playing contract and I would say outside of WorkSafe Victoria's legislative framework to provide a duty of care and a safe workplace.

"And now they're going to say: 'Nothing to see here, let's move on and watch the footy.'"

Bowden took aim at his former organisation the AFLPA for putting out a joint statement with the AFL over the issue and saying that the association had to "act more like a union, the union they are."

"They [the AFLPA] are too close [to the AFL] and this example says to me that the industry has got control of the Players Association," Bowden said, citing the AFL's funding of the AFLPA "to the tune of millions of dollars per year".

He called for Geelong to be brought in front of an independent tribunal to get to the bottom of the issue.

"I don't think there's been a press conference where anyone from the AFL or Geelong has stood there and taken questions," he said.

"Concussion is the nmber one issue in the AFL at this point of time. It's going to be huge in years to come, the CTE research and understanding now, the history that we know.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They're all too close and the industry is too close at times so maybe it needs to go to a Senate estimates committee hearing or something and get David Pocock to ask some questions and get independent senators and Sarah Hanson-Young to level these to the AFL.

"A young man has been put at risk and been asked to sign a secret waiver that says he'll exonerate the club from any future issues with his health. That needs to be investigated and that's not OK."

Asked if he thought Geelong would end up being sanctioned over the waiver, he replied:

"Yes I do. I think the court of public opinion will demand that they be sanctioned because this type of behaviour in modern AFL but also in workplace safety laws is not acceptable. Independent separate contracts are unacceptable."

A Victorian government spokesperson responded on Friday.

"Players safety must never be compromised," the spokesperson said.

"The AFL must have evidence-based policies and procedures in place to protect their players.

"The AFL, as the governing body for Australian rules football, has responsibility for managing concussion within the code."

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

Tech.title: The only instant cameras worth your money
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There’s something magical about using instant cameras that smartphones can’t match. You can capture a moment, print it out, and then give the photo as a gift or hold onto it. Image quality won’t be all that good, but imperfections are part of the allure.

We tested instant camera models from popular brands and landed on a handful that we think are the best. Some aim to preserve the classic experience above all else, while others support companion apps and the ability to print stored photos.

Fujifilm’s latest Instax cameras are the best out there for most people. The company’s Instax Mini Evo is a bit pricey, but it produces great-looking images and offers a lot of creative control. If you’re shopping on a tighter budget, the Instax Mini 13 also takes good photos but has fewer features. The Polaroid Flip is the best retro-focused experience (be warned: prints are pricey!), while Kodak’s Mini Retro 3 might be a better purchase for some because its prints are quite affordable by comparison.

The best instant camera

Film type: Fujifilm Instax Mini film / Film size: 2 x 3 inches / Weight: 285 grams / Charging method: USB-C / Companion app: Yes / Other features: LCD screen, smartphone printing

Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo is a hybrid instant camera that bears a resemblance to its premium X100 line of cameras that cost hundreds more. Its vintage dials and buttons look so stylish that they caught the attention of passersby as I walked around Los Angeles.

It’s easy to balk at its price tag, but this camera offers a level of flexibility that sets it apart (and could save you from wasting a bunch of prints). The camera’s dials also let you apply lens options and effects, from retro filters to monochrome shades, and you can even remotely trigger shots from the app. Its 3-inch LCD screen can be used as a viewfinder, and it also lets you preview and select which images you want to print. The camera’s internal storage tops out at 45 images, which is more limited than we’d prefer, though you can send photos from a smartphone to print. Plus, unlike the Instax Mini 13 (a more budget-friendly pick mentioned below), the Evo uses a USB-C port for charging.

Being able to adjust the brightness of the prints helped me capture night photos and a low-light immersive exhibit a little more clearly and realistically. Image: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

The best instant cameras if you’re on a budget

Film type: Fujifilm Instax Mini film / Film size: 2 x 3 inches / Weight: 327 grams / Charging method: AA batteries / Companion app: None / Other features: Built-in selfie mirror, self-timer, film counter

Fujifilm’s Instax Mini 13 is a more budget-friendly option that can take great photos mostly on par with the Mini Evo. It’s easy to use (just twist its lens to turn the camera on or off), it outperforms other budget instant cameras we tested, and we like its bright, playful designs. Its biggest improvement over the Mini 12 is its self-timer, with both two- and 10-second countdown options. Meanwhile, the Instax Mini 41 looks more sleek, but it lacks the Mini 13’s self-timer and costs about $23 more usually.

The Mini 13 produced more true-to-life photos than the non-Fujifilm instant cameras I tested. I also appreciated the Mini 13’s generously sized physical viewfinder and that it shows your remaining shots, which is useful given that each print costs about $1.

For an instant camera, Fujifilm’s Instax Mini 13 produces vivid, relatively true-to-life photos. Photo: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

Like many instant cameras, it struggles in low light, though the built-in flash brightens dark scenes. The flash can’t be disabled, and it’s very powerful, which resulted in a handful of overexposed shots during testing. It lacks Bluetooth connectivity along with creative shooting modes found on pricier cameras, so you can’t edit photos, apply filters, or choose from different lens effects before printing.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The Kodak Mini Shot 3 Retro. Photo by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

Fujifilm’s Instax cameras produce excellent-looking photos, but each print costs around $1. Kodak’s hybrid Mini Shot 3 Retro is pricier up front (it retails for $159.99 but it often on sale for much less) but much cheaper to buy film for, making it the better budget pick (or beginner-friendly pick). Replacement cartridges are often around $20 for a 60-print pack. And, because you can preview photos before printing, you’re less likely to waste prints.

The Mini Shot 3 Retro affords you more controls than the Instax Mini 13; it sports an LCD screen for previewing photos, it lets you print photos from your phone via Bluetooth, and you can upload ones you shoot to social media using Kodak’s Photo Printer app. The companion app features frames, stickers, filters, and other effects that would look great in a scrapbook. There’s even a beauty mode and Snapchat-style filters. However, photos taken with the Mini Shot 3 Retro lack sharpness and sometimes have an excessive pink tint, and the prints also feel flimsier.

The best instant cameras for retro fans

Film type: Polaroid i-Type Color Film / Film size: 4.2 x 3.5 inches / Weight: 648 grams / Charging method: USB-C / Companion app: Yes / Other features: Scene Analysis

If you’re looking for an instant camera that offers a retro-inspired experience, the Polaroid Flip might be for you. Its classic design and flip-up lid resemble vintage instant cameras like the Polaroid 600, and its square I-Type film prints iconic white-framed photos that look like authentic Polaroids. Yet the camera has modern features like Bluetooth, USB-C charging, and a beginner-friendly companion app that adds convenience and creative control.

The Flip improves on my former retro pick, the third-gen Polaroid Now Plus, with clearer shots and fewer wasted photos. That’s important, as you don’t want to waste any of the eight I-Type sheets that come in a pack that’s $18.99. The Flip’s sonar autofocus and a four-lens hyperfocal system result in sharper images, plus it has an excellent flash — it’s the most powerful of any Polaroid camera I’ve tested. The Scene Analysis feature also helps by warning if a shot is likely to be over or underexposed, or if you’re too close to your subject (these warnings didn’t always get the exposure right).

A few outdoor examples I captured with the Polaroid Flip. Image: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

The Flip has a few downsides, in addition to its costly film. It’s the heaviest camera on this list, not to mention it’s awkwardly sized, making it tough to slip into a purse or easily carry around. Prints also take 15 minutes to develop, during which they must be shielded from light. Low-light performance remains a weak spot as well, and I struggled to capture indoor shots given the contrast and saturation are lower than with Instax film. Sometimes, this gave my pictures a more dreamy, vintage look that felt artistic, but you might not be into it.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Photo: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

If the Flip seems too bulky or expensive for you, the third-generation Polaroid Go is a smaller retro-inspired alternative. It weighs just over a pound and fits easily in the palm of my hand. At $89.99, the latest Go is the most affordable Polaroid camera available, with film that costs only a little more than Fujifilm’s Instax sheets (a 16-sheet pack runs $21.99).

The Go skips advanced features found in the Flip, including creative shooting modes, Bluetooth connectivity, and a companion app for editing photos. It’s a straightforward point-and-shoot camera with a self-timer and large selfie mirror. The smaller prints may disappoint those who prefer traditional Polaroid sizes, but its simplicity and portability make it an approachable way to enjoy the classic Polaroid experience at a much lower price.

What I’m looking for

Update, August 6: Added the Instax Mini 13 and Polaroid Go Gen 3, made the Instax Mini Evo our top pick, and designated the Kodak Mini Retro and Instax Mini 13 as our budget picks.

Tech.title: Disney Plus tries a new AI-powered search
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Disney is testing a new AI-powered tool for Disney Plus that uses a natural language search, a voice query, or a suggested prompt to create a customized row of show and movie recommendations.

Disney Plus, like other streaming services, can recommend shows to watch based on your viewing history. But the company says this new tool, which is “a limited beta experiment” that’s in testing with a “small group of select subscribers,” is intended to recommend content that “fits the moment.”

Sorry this is grainy; I grabbed it from a GIF. Image: Disney

The feature is the latest in a broader push to offer AI-powered recommendation tools that help you find something to watch among massive catalogs of streaming content. Netflix started testing an OpenAI-powered conversational search tool last year and also has a native voice search feature. Last week, Warner Bros. Discovery announced it is experimenting with a “conversational search experience” for HBO Max as well. Peacock even recently added an AI Andy Cohen that narrates Bravo clips.

In an earnings call this week, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro doubled down on plans to make Disney Plus the “digital centerpiece” of the company with “increased personalization, exclusivity, and benefits for subscribers.”

Disney is also introducing an “AI-assisted” conversational search experience for ESPN that looks more like a traditional AI chatbot. ESPN Search, which is in beta with a “subset” of users, lets users ask questions and get answers, stats, and recommendations “drawn from ESPN’s vast sports knowledge ecosystem,” the company says.

Disney has a GIF of ESPN Search in motion, too.

Tech.content:
Some of the biggest names on Google’s AI team got new jobs this week. In some cases, including for legendary Googler Jeff Dean, those jobs are no longer at Google. Given that Google’s models seem to be behind the best of what’s coming out of anthropic and OpenAI, is this a sign of Google in turmoil? Is it about Demis Hassabis wanting something more interesting to work on than virtual assistants? Or is there something else entirely happening here?

Tech.title: Sony could release a cheaper version of its WH-1000XM4 headphones, according to leaks
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Following the release of its premium and very expensive $650 The Collexion headphones in May, Sony could be taking its 1000X line of wireless noise-canceling headphones in a cheaper direction next month. The company is reportedly planning a refreshed and more affordable version of its six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones that will feature similar performance and specs as the original but at a lower price point, according to reliable leaker billbil-kun.

The WH-1000XM4C are expected to launch in early September 2026 in black, silver, and lavender color options for €249.99 or £219.99, which is around $289 to $297 after currency conversion.

The original WH-1000XM4 launched in 2020 for $349.99, while the WH-1000XM6 debuted at a much steeper $449 last year. The new 1000XM4C’s features will include ANC powered by Sony’s QN1 chip (the 1000XM6 use its newer QN3 chip), spatial audio, support for hi-res audio, and earcup touch controls. The only compromise, according to the leaks, is slightly reduced battery life on the new version. The original 1000XM4 maxed out at up to 38 hours with ANC off, or up to 30 hours with noise-canceling on. The 1000XM4C will only offer up to 34 hours of playback, or up to 27 with ANC.

Although there have been two major updates to Sony’s 1000X headphone line since the 1000XM4 first launched, there are still devoted fans of the older model’s design. Sony introduced a major redesign of the line with 2022’s 1000XM5 that eliminated the folding earcups necessitating a much larger carrying case. The company reintroduced the folding mechanism with last year’s 1000XM6 that also added a wider and more comfortable headband, but some (myself included) still prefer the 1000XM4’s design. For those of us with the aging older models suffering from reduced battery life, the 1000XM4C could be a solid replacement.

Tech.title: Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra is more of the same, but better than ever
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What makes the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra so Ultra? Samsung’s first foldable with the Ultra name isn’t a souped-up version of the regular Fold 8, as you might expect. Where the Z Fold 8 is squat and wide, the Fold 8 Ultra retains the thin outer screen and square inner panel of the previous Folds. It does have a substantially better triple rear camera system and a slightly larger battery. But with no support for the S Pen stylus and no Privacy Display, it’s not Ultra in the same way as the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

But compare it to last year’s Z Fold 7 and the upgrades look more substantial. Samsung has improved the displays, battery, charging, cameras, chipset, and crease. Most of these are only iterative, but taken together the package is impressive.

Does that make it Ultra? I don’t know, and it doesn’t really matter. This is a meaningfully more capable phone than last year’s, albeit for $100 more, and it offers something different than its wider new sibling. Samsung will have to hope that’s enough to hold up against whatever Apple has coming with its expected foldable iPhone next month.

Closed, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 6.5-inch cover screen that’s taller than most phones but skinnier too; open, there’s an 8-inch flexible display that’s almost square in its aspect ratio.

At a glance, you’d struggle to tell it apart from last year’s Z Fold 7. It’s the same size, shape, and weight, apart from being fractionally thinner at 4.1mm thick when open. The cameras are in the same spot and look just about identical. In fact, the new set of colors — dark grey, cream, purple, and green — is really the only way to differentiate the two generations by sight.

Closed, it feels unusually thin and tall. Open, it’s good for split-screen work but less well-suited to video.

Samsung argues that while the new Z Fold 8 is designed for content consumption, the taller Ultra is more useful for productivity. The extra vertical space helps if you’re trying to cross-reference documents or navigate multiple inboxes. Personally, I’m more likely to use the larger inner screen for watching video, so I would take the Z Fold 8 over this, but I do see the benefits of the larger space. I wrote two whole articles for my food newsletter across a couple of flights using the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s on-screen keyboard, something I would never consider with a regular phone or even the smaller Z Fold 8.

Both displays are brighter than before, now with a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, making them easier to use outside. The inner screen benefits further from a new anti-reflective coating and a small resolution bump to 2256 x 2504.

Just as importantly, Samsung has reworked the main screen’s innards, incorporating a new titanium alloy film and a flexible titanium plate. These make the foldable screen thinner and more durable — and combined with the anti-reflective coating, they also make the crease harder to see and feel. Head-on, it’s now almost invisible, though still relatively clear when the light catches it at an off angle. Oppo’s solution in the Find N6, which involves using 3D printing to fill surface-level gaps in the hinge, seems more effective at eliminating the crease, but it’s hard to imagine anyone finding this version especially bothersome.

As ever, Samsung offers seven years of software support with its flagship foldable. AI features including Now Brief return, though new additions are limited.

The biggest year-over-year upgrade is the battery. For the first time, Samsung has adopted silicon-carbon battery chemistry, which makes it possible to fit higher-capacity batteries into the same-size space. As a result, the Z Fold 8 Ultra has jumped from a 4,400mAh battery last year to 5,000mAh, despite being fractionally thinner. The phone easily lasts a day, even with a few hours of inner screen use, and I usually have 30 to 40 percent left when I head to bed.

The bigger battery has been bolstered by faster charging — 45W wired and 20W wireless — though the phone is still only Qi2 Ready, meaning there are no charging magnets inside, and it requires a Qi2 case to hit top wireless charging speeds. That helps keep it thin, in fairness, so may be a worthy tradeoff.

An IP68 rating is another major omission; the IP48 rating here means good water protection but limited guarantees against dust and sand. Samsung removed S Pen support in last year’s Z Fold 7, and it’s still missing here. There’s also no sign of the impressive Privacy Display technology introduced in this year’s S26 Ultra.

Unlike the regular Z Fold 8, you get three rear cameras on this phone.

Then there are the cameras. If you’re picking between the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, then form factor aside, this is the only difference that matters. The Ultra gets the same 50-megapixel, f/1.9 ultrawide as the Fold 8, but its 200-megapixel main camera is substantially superior in both detail and light capture. And the presence of a 10-megapixel, 3x telephoto adds a welcome versatility that the regular Fold 8 lacks. It’s far from the best telephoto in any phone — it’s an area where manufacturers like Vivo and Xiaomi have devoted considerable resources, including larger sensors and superior stabilization — but just having the option makes this a more flexible camera. I wouldn’t push the zoom much beyond its 3x optical range though, with significant noise creeping in above 6x or so.

There’s an impressive level of consistency between the three lenses in most conditions, though just occasionally the ultrawide comes out a little differently. It’s usually more muted, though at least once, it took the most vivid shot. Low-light performance across all three lenses is good, though they’re all guilty of over-lightening the nighttime sky and creating flare around brighter lights.

Previous Next















































1 / 25 The Z Fold 8 Ultra’s main camera is the same as the Z Fold 7’s, and just as capable.

Samsung’s software updates this year are relatively slight. There’s My FanCam, a video editing feature that uses AI to crop videos in on a specific person. Google’s Gemini Intelligence task automation is supported, but so far isn’t available in the UK, meaning I haven’t tested it. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel Magic Cue, has apparently been updated to suggest helpful contextual actions (like adding an event to your calendar) to carry out in split-screen. In a week of using the phone, I haven’t seen it pop up once, even after subjecting myself to Samsung Keyboard the whole time because some reports suggest that’s a requirement.

Samsung’s stark and simple design language is still among the best out there.

I’ve been more impressed than I expected by the Z Fold 8 Ultra. I thought it would struggle to compete with recent excellent foldables from Oppo and Honor, but in reality, it’s a fairly close contest — and unlike those phones, it’s actually on sale in the US.

Its cameras still aren’t at the level of Oppo and Honor’s, and without an S Pen or a Privacy Display, I’d quibble over how Ultra it all really is. But for those who prefer the tall, square foldable form factor, this is a worthy follow-up to the Z Fold 7. The substantially larger battery alone justifies the $100 price hike.

I don’t know which of Samsung’s two Z Fold 8 phones I’d buy this year — really, I want the Z Fold 8’s form factor with the Ultra’s cameras squeezed in — but that indecision is testament to the fact that you can’t go too far wrong with either.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Tech.title: Cloudflare launches Kitesurf, a browser built for AI agents
Tech.content:
Cloudflare is the latest company to join the race to build a new web browser. But instead of pitching a Chrome alternative to consumers, the internet infrastructure provider launched Kitesurf, a cloud-hosted browser designed specifically for AI agents.

AI software is evolving from chatbots that answer questions to agents that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. Browsers are a critical part of this transition, as they’ll need to navigate the web and use websites, as humans do.

Unlike traditional web browsers built for humans, a browser built for AI agents doesn’t care about visual elements, like themes, tabs, or browser extensions, Cloudflare explained in its announcement. A browser designed for AI agents needs to manage context windows, performance, token costs, and scalability. It also faces a different threat model because an AI browser could be subject to vulnerabilities like prompt injection attacks and more, the company noted.

With Kitesurf, AI developers will be able to build software that can navigate websites, fill out forms, and complete other browser-based tasks, without having to build their own browser software.

Cloudflare says it decided to build Kitesurf just 12 weeks ago, and it runs entirely on top of the company’s serverless platform, called Workers. Kitesurf is available for free while in beta in Browser Run, which lets developers programmatically control and interact with headless browser instances on Cloudflare’s network.

For developers, Cloudflare’s pitch is that this enables AI agents to use the web more efficiently while using less computing power than Chromium, which keeps costs down.

“Kitesurf is significantly more efficient in CPU and memory consumption than Chromium for common agentic tasks like screenshots and HTML extraction,” according to the company.

Image Credits:Cloudflare

The browser itself was built from other technologies, including a modular rendering engine from Blitz; Firefox’s CSS parser, Stylo; and Boa JS, a Rust ECMAScript engine. Everything else runs inside Cloudflare Workers. Although still new, Cloudflare says Kitesurf already passes around 215,000+ web platform tests, and it’s adding hundreds more, passing tests every week.

Cloudflare also credited the open source Rust headless engine, Obscura, for inspiring it to develop Kitesurf, noting that the first proof of concept was a port of Obscura to Workers.

The company said the browser correctly renders pages like TodoMVC, a popular benchmark application for comparing JavaScript frameworks, along with Wikipedia, Hacker News, the Cloudflare Blog, and much of the Cloudflare dashboard.

Tech.title: Computer maker Framework notifies ‘all customers’ of a data breach
Tech.content:
In Brief

Framework, a company that makes modular repairable computers, said it has notified all of its customers that hackers stole their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses, due to an incident at a company that provides business intelligence.

On Thursday, several Framework customers said on social media that they had received an email from the company notifying them of the data breach.

Framework’s spokesperson Eric Schumacher told TechCrunch that the breach affected “all customers,” but declined to specify a specific number. Framework computers are relatively niche products, but some estimates say the company sold hundreds of thousands of devices.

According to the notification seen by TechCrunch, the company blamed the data breach on an upstream cyberattack at Metabase.

Metabase disclosed its own breach in a blog post on its official website, where it said that it was hacked by someone using an unknown security flaw, a so-called zero-day. The company said the hackers exploited the bug to give them the ability to access customers’ databases stored on Metabase’s cloud servers.

In its email to customers, Framework also included the email Metabase sent to the company, which says hackers accessed Framework’s cloud instance. The computer maker said it investigated the incident and found that hackers had stolen its customers’ personal data, but did not include their payment information.

Metabase did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Trump administration has spent nearly $4B to cancel offshore wind farms
Tech.content:
In Brief

The Trump administration is paying another $1.2 billion to cancel an offshore wind lease, this time to German utility RWE.

The energy company said in an announcement that the wind farms would have been built off the coasts of California, Louisiana, and New York. Instead, RWE will spend $900 million to buy a small stake in a Louisiana liquid natural gas export terminal.

The New York wind farm would have generated more than 3 gigawatts, according to Heatmap News.

The remaining $300 million will go toward buying natural gas turbines to power 15 peaking power plants around the country. Peaking power plants are among the most expensive and most polluting natural gas power plants to operate. It’s unclear when those will be completed — there’s currently a backlog for new turbines stretching into the early 2030s.

RWE isn’t backing off its offshore wind investments elsewhere, though. The company said it bought 6.9 gigawatts of capacity in the U.K.’s recent auction.

The Trump administration has paid $3.93 billion for the 12 leases it has coaxed developers into abandoning.
